# TO THE READERS,
## Desirous of true Wisdom,
->Greetings<- <note>original: "S.", an abbreviation for "Salutem," a standard Latin greeting wishing health or prosperity to the reader.</note>

The **P R E L U D E S** or **F O R E R U N N E R** of the most distinguished **C O M E N I U S**'s <term>Universal Wisdom</term> <note>original: "Pansophiæ." From the Greek words for "all" and "wisdom," this was Comenius’s lifelong project to organize all human knowledge into a single, pedagogical system that would lead to world peace and Christian unity.</note>, *which about two years ago, at the urging of many and without the Author’s knowledge, we released into the light somewhat timidly, we now expose more confidently to the sight of all. We do so having obtained both the Author's own approval for our previous daring effort and the applause of very many other excellent men. We could have refrained from this labor until the works promised in that volume were* <term>brought to completion</term> <note>original: "ad umbilicum deducerentur," literally "brought to the navel." This is a Roman idiom for finishing a book, referring to the decorative knobs at the ends of the rod around which a papyrus scroll was wound.</note>, *if that first edition had elicited for the Author those supports which such an arduous and remarkable undertaking no less required than deserved. Now, however, we have discovered that the generosity of many was restricted by nothing more than the fact that they were either still entirely ignorant of* **C O M E N I U S**'s *goal, or desired to be more certain of his intent and capabilities. Therefore, we have worked diligently so that everyone might be satisfied, so to speak, by this second edition. For we have seen to it not only that everything contained in the first edition should appear here again—and indeed far more correctly—but also that other matters of no less importance from the workshop of the same Craftsman should be added to them. These will easily provide proof for those matters which previously seemed beyond belief, even to many who are not unlearned. In this, it happened by a certain good fortune that we were able to be more generous than we had at first hoped. For besides*

# PREFACE.

<meta>catchword: from which</meta>

...you have observed that **everything rests [upon this]**, strive all the more so that by your counsel and your help—and most especially your financial aid—these things, having been well-founded, may finally begin to rise. Or will you be reluctant to bind the **Architect** <note>Referring to Jan Amos Comenius (1592–1671), the philosopher and educator often described as the "Architect" of this new system of knowledge.</note> to you in return for a few coins? Especially since you have already received for free the **Ground Plan** <term>ground plan</term> <note>original: "Ichnographiam." In architectural terms, a floor plan or blueprint; here used metaphorically for the intellectual framework of his system.</note> of such a distinguished work and many other no less important things from the storehouse of that rich genius. With those few coins, he might buy the stones, timber, and other necessities for such a great structure, and hire porters and co-workers, etc. Does he not deserve the generosity of any person of heart, if only for his exceptional piety and the hardships of his long exile? 

Will you permit, **Great and Noble Souls**, that **Wisdom** <note>original: "Sapientia."</note>—which is greater than any price—should offer herself to you for such a low cost and find no buyer among you? Will you allow such noble and otherwise immortal offspring to be extinguished for lack of **midwifery** <note>The author uses the metaphor of birth ("obstetricationis") to describe the publishing and realization of Comenius's ideas—suggesting that without funding, these ideas will be "stillborn."</note>? May God, the thrice Greatest and Best, forbid that the fear of Him and respect for future generations should so vanish from your minds that you would rather be stained with the shameful mark of greed upon your conscience and reputation, than to secure eternal peace for both through the surplus of your wealth. 

For, make no mistake: it is not the cause of Comenius, but the cause of **GOD** and of His people that is being weighed. His glory, and their peace and safety, are advanced by nothing more effectively than by this extraordinary **restoration of universal wisdom** <note>original: "sapientiæ omnimodæ instauratione." This refers to Comenius's concept of Pansophy, or a total reform of human knowledge.</note>. No Christian heart should hold the care of these things in low regard. As for Comenius, he will easily find a way to live; but see to it that you, by scorning this rare treasure, do not one day lack **from which** <note>The catchword "unde" indicates the text continues: "from which [you might seek help/relief]."</note>

# PREFACE

Since you have observed that everything depends on this, strive instead to ensure that through your counsel and your assistance—and most especially your financial support—these things may finally begin to rise from a solid foundation. You have already received, free of charge, the **Ground Plan** <note>original: "Ichnographiam." In architectural terms, a ground plan or blueprint; here, it refers to the conceptual outline of Comenius’s universal philosophy.</note> of such a distinguished work, along with many other no less significant things from the storehouse of that rich genius. Will you now find it a burden to support the **Architect** <note>The "Architect" is Comenius himself, framed here as a master-builder of human knowledge.</note> in return with a few coins? With these, he might purchase the stones, timber, and other materials necessary for such a great structure, and hire porters and laborers. Has he not earned the generosity of any wise person through his exceptional piety alone, and through the hardships of his long exile?

Will you allow, **Great and Generous Souls**, that **Wisdom**—which is greater than any price—should stand before you for sale at such a low cost and yet find no buyer among you? Will you permit such noble and otherwise immortal offspring to be extinguished for lack of a **midwife’s help**? <note>original: "obstetricationis." A Socratic metaphor suggesting that even great ideas need assistance to be "born" into the world through publication and teaching.</note> May **God, Thrice Best and Greatest** <note>original: "Deus ter Opt. Max." (Deus Optimus Maximus), a traditional honorific title for God borrowed from Roman descriptions of Jupiter and adopted by Christian scholars.</note>, forbid that the fear of Him and reverence for future generations should so depart from your hearts that you would prefer to be stained with the perpetual blot of a shameful stinginess upon your conscience and reputation, rather than achieve a lasting serenity for both by giving from the surplus of your wealth.

For, make no mistake, this is not the cause of Comenius, but the cause of **GOD** and of His people. His glory, and their peace and salvation, are promoted by nothing more directly than by this unusual **restoration of all-encompassing wisdom**. <note>original: "sapientiæ omnimodæ instauratione." The word *instauratio* (restoration) echoes Francis Bacon’s *Instauratio Magna*, a contemporary movement to overhaul all human learning.</note> No Christian heart should disregard the care of such things. As for Comenius, he will certainly find a way to live; you must see to it that, by scorning this rare treasure, there does not one day lack...

...from which you may live well. Regarding the fruit of the generosity you have expended thus far, there will never be a reason for you to justly doubt: *He who has freely bestowed so much from the harvest of his own genius upon you, what will he not do when spurred by your kindness?* O that it might happen one day to see that most beautiful pair—so worthy of our century which shudders with so many calamities—not, as that man <note>Likely a reference to the Roman philosopher Seneca, who frequently wrote about the Stoic ideal of the "wise man" struggling against misfortune.</note> says, the **Wise Man joined with ill fortune**, but **Comenius’s diligence** joined with the **munificence of patrons** <note>original: "Mecænatum." <margin>* Praises of Wisdom.</margin>
<image-desc>A large decorative square woodcut initial 'S' featuring ornate foliate and floral scrollwork designs.</image-desc>
That Wisdom—which for Aristotle is the knowledge of many and wonderful things; for Cicero <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman orator whose definitions of philosophy were standard in 17th-century education.</note>, however, it is the knowledge of things divine and human, and of the causes by which these are contained; and finally for Solomon, the craftswoman of all things, teaching all things <note>A reference to the Book of Wisdom, where Wisdom is personified as a female figure who assisted God in creation.</note>—was celebrated in antiquity with great * Eulogies <note>original: "Elogiis"</note>, cannot be unknown to those who pursue the study of wisdom. "She is more precious than all riches," (says the Wisest of mortals <note>Referring to King Solomon, traditionally considered the author of the biblical books of Proverbs and Ecclesiastes.</note>) "and all things that can be desired are not worthy to be compared to her. Length of days is in her right hand, and" <note>The text continues on the next page, following the catchword "in."</note>

<summary>Jan Amos Comenius introduces his "Pansophia" by defining Wisdom through the lenses of classical philosophy and biblical tradition, asserting its supreme value over all material wealth. This serves as the opening argument for his project to unify all human knowledge.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the opening sequence of classical and biblical citations regarding the nature and value of Wisdom. The previous page ended with a quote from Proverbs 3:16 regarding Wisdom's right hand; this page begins with the description of her left hand.</meta>

# J. A. COMENIUS

*in her left hand are riches and glory. Her ways are beautiful ways, and all her paths are peaceful. She is a tree of life to those who take hold of her, and those who possess her are blessed.* Proverbs 3:15-18. <note>Comenius is quoting from the Latin Vulgate Bible; in modern English translations, these verses are numbered 16–18.</note> Cicero <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BCE), a Roman statesman and philosopher whose writings were the bedrock of Latin education in the 17th century.</note> moreover says: *No more excellent good has been given to the race of mortals, nor ever will be given.* Horace <note>Quintus Horatius Flaccus (65–8 BCE), a leading Roman lyric poet.</note> indeed says it thus:

> ->*To sum up, the wise man is second only to Jupiter:*<- <note>original: "Ad summum sapiens uno minor est Iove." Jupiter was the king of the gods in Roman mythology; Horace uses this to show the near-divine status of the philosopher.</note>
> ->*Rich,*<-
> ->*Free, honored, beautiful, and finally a king of kings.*<-

<margin>2</margin> If you ask the reason why they value this one virtue so highly, Seneca <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca (c. 4 BCE – 65 CE), a Stoic philosopher and advisor to Emperor Nero.</note> will answer: *Without the study of wisdom, no one can live well, nor even passably.* Cicero adds: *Wisdom is the mother of all the arts: she instructs us first in the worship of God, then in human law—which is rooted in the society of the human race—then in modesty and greatness of soul. She also dispels the darkness from the mind as if from the eye, so that we may see all things—above, below, first, last, and middle. For God loves no one except him who lives with wisdom.* (Wisdom of Solomon 7:14, 28).

## PRECURSOR TO UNIVERSAL WISDOM <note>original: *PANSOPHIAE PRODROMUS*. "Pansophia" was Comenius's lifelong project to create a "Universal Wisdom" that would synthesize all human knowledge—scientific, philosophical, and theological—into a single, harmonious system.</note>

A 2

<margin>* The pursuit of wisdom.</margin>
3 * Justly, therefore, the most excellent of men in every age—having set aside care for transitory things, for riches, desires, and honors—directed their thoughts, prayers, and studies toward this: that by devoting themselves to the contemplation of things, they might grasp whatever can be understood by the mind, and by that means <term>subdue the world</term> <note>To "subdue the world" in this context refers to the intellectual mastery of nature, a common theme in 17th-century thought (similar to Francis Bacon) where knowledge is seen as the tool to restore humanity's dominion over the earth.</note>. Such men, amidst the remaining crowd of mortals, are truly what the gift of wisdom itself is among the other goods granted to mortals: the most brilliant of gems, or rather, stars dispelling the fog of worldly darkness. We must, therefore, gratefully acknowledge the work of divine mercy, not only because God has opened to us the theaters of His wisdom—Nature and Scripture <note>Comenius refers to the popular early modern concept of the "Two Books" of God: the physical world (Nature) and the Bible (Scripture). He believed both must be studied together to reach truth.</note>—but also because He has equipped us with the instruments for observing them and for gathering the <term>light of wisdom</term>: our senses and our reason, along with His divine revelation, which supplies what is lacking in sense and reason. We also owe it to divine benevolence that the study of letters <note>original: *literarum studia*, referring to the whole tradition of scholarship, literature, and formal education.</note>, by which the pursuit of wisdom is nurtured and passed from others into us, has been preserved until our own age. Indeed, in our century, these studies flourish as never before, so that the present age may, with good reason, both take pride in and congratulate itself on the name of learning, and the hope for even greater light shines forth.

*   There are many complaints from many people that *Erudition* <term>Erudition: Formal, scholarly learning and the body of knowledge taught in schools.</term>, in the form that schools are now swollen with and which they propose, is a thing too lengthy for the shortness of our fleeting life, too laborious for the measure of ordinary minds; too narrow for the breadth of reality; and in many ways crippled and defective regarding the subtlety and solidity of the truth of things. II. *To our talent, because of their difficulty.*
III. *To things themselves, because of frequent deviation.*
IV. *To the use of life, because of the near alienation of the things being taught from those things which happen in common life.*

Not that I dream that one man can excel in all things; but I am certain that to be able to know all things as far as necessity requires, while excelling in one's own profession, is both possible and necessary for anyone equipped with even a mediocre intellect.

# J. A. COMENIUS

<meta>catchword: folly,</meta>

learned men excel the unlearned, but in the skillful handling of affairs, they are mostly surpassed by them. Nor do I speak only of mere grammarians <note>original: *literonibus* — a term for those who have only a superficial or "alphabetical" knowledge of letters</note>, since it is often the case with sublime Philosophers and Theologians that, while they seem like Eagles to themselves in their abstract speculations, they are moles in matters of life and in serving human society. From this has arisen the mockery: *A good scholar is a bad politician* <note>original: *Bonus Scholasticus, malus Politicus*. In this era, "politician" referred generally to anyone skilled in civic life and practical social interaction</note>: even though a school ought to be a prelude to life.

But to touch upon something specific, it is well known with what great praise the study of Metaphysics is raised even to the heavens, as if it were the firmest basis and the most splendid summit of all wisdom. And if we judge the matter correctly, this is indeed the case. But because that same "Queen of Sciences" <note>original: *Regina scientiarum*. Metaphysics was traditionally granted this title because it deals with the primary causes and principles of things</note> bristles with so many thorns and is involved in such darkness that few grasp those subtleties—and those who do grasp them are utterly ignorant of how to apply them to the lower sciences—it happens that the study ends with itself. Beyond a momentary pleasure, with which it tickles its practitioners for a little while, it brings no use to human affairs. From this it further happens that some desert it and plainly outlaw it, not only from the circle of Philosophy (namely the *Ramists* <note>original: *Ramæi*. Followers of Petrus Ramus, a reformer who sought to replace abstract Aristotelian logic with a more practical, streamlined method</note>) but even from the Universities, as if it were the useless equipment of a most sterile vanity. For [it is said that] the King of Sweden, **Gustavus Adolphus**, of glorious me- <note>The text cuts off mid-word: *gloriosæ memoriæ*, meaning "of glorious memory." Gustavus Adolphus was a contemporary hero to Protestants like Comenius, known for his practical and military leadership.</note>

<summary>Comenius argues that ivory-tower scholars are often useless in practical society and critiques Metaphysics for being an overly complex "Queen of Sciences" that offers no real-world benefit.</summary>

...memory (to which end, his deeds show he was not born for trifles: by a public edict he banished the entire study of Metaphysics from his kingdom, so that no bookseller, under penalty of confiscation, would dare to import such books, and no subject would even dare to read them, lest his kingdom be bewitched by a new Barbarism, and lest he, in the conduct of affairs, should find himself with empty disputers and commentators instead of practical men of business), as Johannes Angelius Werdenhagen <note>Johannes Angelius Werdenhagen (1581–1652) was a German diplomat and political philosopher known for his works on "universal" politics</note> testifies.

<margin>14</margin>
The study of Logic and Rhetoric ought to approach more closely the affairs of life, since they profess to explain reason and speech (the two bonds by which human society is held together). But that the testimony of Jacobus Acontius <note>Giacomo Aconcio (1492–1566) was an Italian jurist and philosopher who argued that the excessive rules of logic often hindered true understanding</note> is most true, the reality of the situation clearly proves.

> "The number of Dialecticians <note>original: *Dialecticorum* — those who practice formal logic and debate</note>," he says, "is abundant everywhere. But if you observe their writings and disputes, you will find nothing less than true dialecticians. Likewise: you may see many well-instructed in the precepts of Rhetoric, whose speech, though it may be proper, ornate, elegant, and copious, yet you will find lacking in them the force and strength required for persuasion."

The same judgment applies to the other Arts and Sciences: we are occupied by them more than we are prepared by them to skillfully undertake the occupations of life.

<meta>This page continues Comenius’s critique of the educational systems of his time. <header>JOHANN AMOS COMENIUS</header>

<margin>15</margin>
* Finally, our scholarly pursuits are not yet arranged in such a way that they lead us by a straight and infallible path to our ultimate goal, **GOD**. What need is there for witnesses? The profanity of our Academies is openly evident, being greater than any witness; it is full of luxury, pride, gluttony, brawls, and every kind of insolence. Furthermore, the very doctrine gathered there—alas!—for how many does it become nothing but a whetstone <note>original: *cos* — a stone used for sharpening tools; here meaning a way to sharpen one's capacity for evil</note> for malice, an instrument for practicing iniquity throughout their entire lives? Thus, for the majority of our scholars, what God laments is most true: *They are wise in doing evil, but to do good they have no knowledge*, Jeremiah 4:22. And for such men, their wisdom is a guide to destruction.

For this is the source of that voice of God: *Not many wise are chosen, because the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God*, 1 Corinthians 1. Indeed, we interpret this securely as referring to Pagan <note>original: *Gentili* — referring to non-Christian or classical Greek and Roman philosophy</note> wisdom, so that we do not feel ourselves pressed by that voice of God; yet we still do not apply ourselves to any other kind of wisdom. 

In truth, that very wisdom which the schools have offered us until now is drawn from Paganism <note>original: *Gentilismo*</note> and infected with serpentine venom; it strives only for the knowledge of good and evil, which "puffs up," rather than working for charity, which "builds up." <note>Comenius is referencing 1 Corinthians 8:1: "Knowledge puffs up, but charity edifies."</note> And because, through our hereditary perversity, we always prefer to excuse our faults rather than to correct them...

->### A PRECURSOR TO UNIVERSAL WISDOM<-

...we are more prepared [to persist in our ways]; and it further happens that we flatter ourselves by using the corruption of nature as an excuse, thinking it impossible to be transformed because we are depraved. As if, indeed, the **Fear of the Lord**—which God has protested over and over again to be both the beginning and the end of **Wisdom** <term>sapientia — in this context, the highest form of knowledge that integrates intellectual and spiritual truth</term>—should not be the antidote to that corruption. It is true, therefore, that the common studies of learning <note>original: *literarum vulgata studia* — the standard academic curriculum of the 17th century</note> are:

I. An infinite occupation.
II. A most perplexing distraction of the intellect.
III. A perpetual wrestling-ground <note>original: *palaestram* — a gymnasium or school for wrestling; here used metaphorically for a place of struggle and competition</note> of errors.
IV. A hindrance to the affairs of life.
V. Finally, a multiform occasion for wandering from God; which is most to be deplored.

<margin>Consultation on remedies.</margin>
Since some excellent men have long ago begun to take pity on this calamitous state of Learning and the Learned, various people have attempted to seek remedies for those diseases in various ways. Some, indeed, advising that the entire apparatus of ancient wisdom borrowed from the Pagans <note>original: *gentilibus* — referring to classical Greek and Roman authors like Aristotle and Cicero</note> be cast aside; others maintaining that a selection should be made, and that the Arts and Philosophy should only be used sparingly; some beginning to attempt a kind of transfusion and transformation of all the sciences; another in this way,

<meta>This page continues Comenius's argument for educational reform. ### J. A. COMENIUS

...one person in one way, another in another. And truly, it is more than necessary that whoever can bring any counsel or help here, should bring it. First, so that such a small amount of wisdom—of the kind provided by common letters <note>original: *literæ* — here referring to the standard curriculum of grammar and basic literature</note>—should not cost so much and such great sweat; or certainly, if labors must be spent, that they might return a more abundant fruit. Secondly, so that we may vindicate ourselves and learning from the reproach of the unlettered common people: who, while they see those preferred above them in the name of erudition <term>eruditio — formal schooling and scholarly training</term>, notice that they do not at all excel in practical experience, in the honesty of their morals, or in the zeal of their piety <note>original: *pietas* — in the 17th century, this meant a combination of religious devotion and moral duty to society</note>. They see that these "learned" men often barely follow in the footsteps of simpler folk, and thus the commoners either dissolve into laughter or are stirred to contempt for the world of letters. Finally, lest we incur the wrath of God—who wishes to restore His image in us through the gift of wisdom sent down from heaven—by not dispensing such a divine gift for His glory.

<margin>* An investigation of the causes of such great evil.</margin>

* But in truth, because the cure of a disease is undertaken rashly when the cause of the disease is not yet understood; let us see whether, by a certain investigation, we can penetrate to the roots of such great evil by which the world of letters <term>res literaria — the "Republic of Letters," or the entire system of scholarship and education</term> is oppressed, and uncover them: so that from there the transition to remedies may be safer. I will say, therefore, what cause I think lies beneath each of those evils we have already recounted—

->### FORERUNNER OF UNIVERSAL WISDOM 19<-

evils: and at the same time, I will explain what should be applied by way of a remedy.

* The **excessive length of studies** <term>prolixity — the state of being drawn out to a tedious length</term>, as they are commonly handled, seems to arise from three sources. First, from a careless failure to distinguish necessary things from those that are unnecessary. From this it happens, according to the complaint of *Seneca* <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca (c. 4 BC – 65 AD), a Roman philosopher whom Comenius often cites to argue that education should be practical and concise</note>, that we are ignorant of necessary things because we are learning unnecessary ones.

This is entirely true. If the less necessary matters were separated from our studies, we would have twice as much time (to put it very mildly) and half as much of a burden. Truly, the following must be considered unnecessary. First: whatever can be ignored without damaging one's education <term>eruditio — formal scholarly training</term>, such as the many trifles of the pagans, the names of petty deities <note>original: *Deastrorum* — a mocking term for minor or false gods</note> along with their lying stories and similar fables. Second: whatever tires the mind with no significant use, such as most of the rules of the grammarians <note>original: *Grammaticorum* — referring to the heavy emphasis on complex Latin grammar in the 17th century</note>, by which the minds of children are tormented <note>original: *macerantur* — literally "softened" or "soaked," here meaning worn down or exhausted</note> and years are wasted; and other things of that same sort <note>original: *similis farinae* — literally "of the same flour," an idiom meaning "of the same kind"</note> that will have no use outside of the school. Finally, all the wordy evasions of things and words, which do not bring out the kernel, but only grasp at it while it is covered by a thousand layers <note>original: *volucris* — wrappings or envelopes; Comenius uses the metaphor of a nut kernel to describe essential truth</note>. And yet most schoolbooks <term>scholastici libelli — the standard textbooks of the day</term> are filled with such things, and therefore they occupy and distract the youth for the greatest part of their time with useless and unnecessary matters.

# THE WORKS OF JAN AMOS COMENIUS

...-fuse. And is it any wonder that a person rarely arrives at any solid learning <term>eruditio — formal scholarly training and well-rounded education</term>?

The remedy, therefore, will be to construct a **Seminary of Learning** <term>Seminarium Eruditionis — a metaphorical "seedbed" or nursery where the essential foundations of knowledge are planted</term> from the most solid things and words—those that will be of nothing but the truest use. For you will reap just as much fruit if you sow an acre of field with one measure of pure wheat, as if you were to scatter that wheat mixed with ten measures of chaff <note>original: *paleis* — the husks of grain, which are useless as food and represent the "unnecessary things" Comenius wants to remove from the curriculum</note> over ten acres with ten times the labor.

<margin>20 *</margin> * Secondly, because literary labors **are a kind of inextricable labyrinth in which most people wander without end; and the confusion of studies creates a widely diffused variety of things—a kind of ocean which is easier to be swallowed by than to drain**, because the things to be learned have not, until now, been reduced into a sufficiently certain and evident order. It is inevitable that whatever things are scattered appear to be many, while those collected together are compressed into a small space.

The remedy will be if all things to be learned, from the greatest to the smallest, are arranged in such a clear series that students <note>original: *literarum candidati* — literally "candidates of letters," meaning those aspiring to scholarship</note> have them as plainly before them as their own fingers. Thus, they might see through the material from the very beginning, right through the middle and to the end; certain that the whole ocean of learning, by this very path which they have em- <note>The text breaks off mid-word: *conscensuri* — "embarked upon"</note>

# PRELUDE TO UNIVERSAL WISDOM

...-through, and like a ship, they shall sail forth to the very harbor of desired perfection.

->* III. *The excessive pursuit of trivialities.*<-

Thirdly, the pursuit of all kinds of useless trivialities <term>minutiarum confectatio — the act of chasing after small, insignificant details at the expense of the big picture</term> makes the study of literature monstrously diffuse. For in such *things and words* (since the play and chance of both nature and wit are infinite), there is no end or limit. Therefore, those who devote themselves to the detailed description of things in any branch of the Sciences and Arts, and grow accustomed to either laboring or delighting in them, find a journey pleasant enough for the mind, yet they necessarily suffer a delay <note>original: *remoram* — literally a "remora," a sucking-fish believed in antiquity to slow down ships by clinging to them; here meaning a conceptual drag or obstacle</note> in their training for universal wisdom <term>Pansophia — Comenius’s concept of a "universal wisdom" that unites all knowledge into a single, divine system</term>. Indeed, they ensure that because the mind is filled with specific details of a certain kind, other things can scarcely find a place.

The remedy will be the *preparation of a small book*, in which, through a *true and established Anatomy* <note>original: *Anatome* — Comenius uses the metaphor of dissection to describe a systematic analysis that breaks down complex subjects into their essential parts</note> of all things that are and can be thought, all things are brought back to their true classes and types. And this should be done in such a way that whatever is to be said about any one thing is said at one and the same time about all things of which it can be said. Thus, all things will be shorter and more solid than expected: because the intellect, through a few rules, can be freed from infinite barriers <note>original: *repagulis* — gates or bars; Comenius envisions the mind breaking through the "fences" of fragmented knowledge</note>, so that by its own power it may be carried through all things and penetrate everywhere. For truly, as *Seneca* says: There is no need for many things (namely, for...

# J. A. COMENIUS

...wisdom) through precepts, but effective ones. They must be scattered in the manner of a seed; although it is tiny, once it has occupied a suitable place, it unfolds its powers, and from the smallest beginning spreads out into the greatest actions.

As to why the path of studies has seemed *obstructed and rough*, I believe the cause was this: First, that a worthy preparation of minds to eagerly drink in the teachings did not come first, nor was the useful sufficiently mixed with the sweet <note>original: *miscebatur satis utile dulci* — a reference to the Roman poet Horace’s famous advice that art should both instruct and delight</note> to entice their talents; instead, everyone was approached just as they were, and admitted just as they arrived. Moreover, students were treated not as guests usually are at a banquet, with kindness and delights, but as slaves are in a grinding-mill <term>pistrino — a mill powered by humans or animals, used in Roman times as a place of grueling labor and punishment for slaves</term>, with shouting, force, and beatings. 

For fists and canes, rods and whips were the most common "feasts" in schools, and their daily "desserts." And would it be any wonder if someone should feel sick or grow faint! Truly, nothing is so easy that it does not become difficult if you do it against your will. How then can letters be easy to learn amidst such trembling? This occurs in the learning of no mechanical art. Severity necessarily brings about fear; fear, however, necessarily confuses and entangles the mind, so that the mind does not know where it is, and if it is a little weaker, it suffers a certain dizziness.

# THE PRECURSOR TO UNIVERSAL WISDOM

...is affected. Therefore, there is a need for an art to capture, entice, and soothe the minds of students. This art will consist partly of the kindness of the teachers, and partly of the wisdom of the method; thus, the study of letters may become an allure for their talents and appear as mere play.

<margin>* 2. Superficial explanation of things.</margin>
* Second, a large part of the difficulty lies in the fact that things are not taught to students through first-hand observation <term>autopsia — from the Greek for "seeing for oneself"; the principle that knowledge should come from direct sensory experience of an object</term>, but through roundabout explanations. By these, the images of things are only with difficulty imprinted on the intellect, and they stick weakly in the memory, so that they either vanish again easily or are confused in various ways.

The remedy for this will be to offer everything through first-hand observation and the present senses: visible things to sight, things that can be tasted to taste, and things that can be touched to touch. For a single inspection of an elephant (or at least of its image) would impress its likeness upon me more easily and firmly than if it had been described to me ten times, because

> *Things sent through the ears stir the mind more slowly,*
> *Than those committed to the faithful eyes.*
<note>original: "Segnius irritant animos demissa per aures, Quàm quae sunt oculis commissa fidelibus" — a famous maxim from the Roman poet Horace’s *Ars Poetica* regarding the power of visual media over spoken words.</note>

† The third and greatest factor in this difficulty arises from the method by which the Sciences and Arts are commonly delivered, which is not sufficiently proportioned either to the things themselves or to the human intellect. ...the later parts, from general principles to more specific details, and finally from the known to the unknown. But who provides this? We see nothing of the sort as of yet: <gloss><unclear>often as if</unclear></gloss> all the Arts and Sciences, if you except *Mathematics* <note>original: *Mathesin* — Comenius frequently highlights mathematics as the only discipline with a truly logical, step-by-step progression at this time.</note>, are in truth shrouded in darkness. For if the books we currently possess led our talents gently from the known to the unknown, with a never-interrupted pace, then readers eager for knowledge would be led to even the most obscure matters as surely as anyone equipped with legs can be guided up the highest cliff, provided that steps are built into it. 

Since this does not happen, and no one understands what those books are teaching (unless they are remarkably gifted, penetrating the matter with their own sharp wit and raising themselves by their own power, or unless the same things are drummed into them by a living voice in various ways until they begin to see something as if through a mist), it is certain proof that the intellect is not being led step-by-step along a level path, but is being dragged through rugged terrain, pits, caves, and chasms.

The remedy will be such a shaping of all Sciences and Arts that everywhere one begins with the most familiar things, and a gradual, slow progression toward the unknown takes place: in such a way, indeed, that the first things provide light to the second, the second to the third, and the third to the fourth, carrying that light forward to the very end; just as in a chain, one link catches and pulls the next. <margin>* The threefold cause of Truth struggling throughout all literature.</margin>
* Of **Truth** deserting us everywhere throughout the whole range of the sciences, a most true threefold cause can be assigned: namely,
I. *The tearing apart of the sciences.* <note>Comenius refers here to the fragmentation of knowledge, where subjects are studied in isolation rather than as a unified whole.</note>
II. *A method not most deeply bound to the things themselves.*
III. *Carelessness of words and style on one hand, and untimely luxury on the other.*

<margin>† I. The tearing apart of the sciences.</margin>
† For first, I testify before my conscience that in the books I have happened to see, I have yet seen nothing that sufficiently corresponds to the magnitude of things, which might exhaust the whole <term>universe of things</term> <note>original: *universitatem rerum* — the totality of all that exists.</note>: regardless of the titles some books might bear—whether *Universal Wisdoms* [Pansophias], or *Encyclopedias*, or the *Systematic Arrangement* <note>original: *Syntaxeōs* — from the Greek word for a systematic composition or ordering.</note> *of the Admirable Art*—and whatever other titles they may display. Much less have I seen the entire apparatus of the human intellect so constructed from its own certain and unmoved principles of eternal truth, that all things were mutually linked from the first to the last without any gap in the truth. For perhaps no one has yet attempted this: having established universal principles of things and balanced them in every proportion to one another, to [bind] the variety of things flowing in every direction with certain reason...

...would surround it with boundaries: so that through a universal and proportionate harmony among all things, the hidden, yet invariable and invincible truth of things might reveal itself. That, I say, no one seems to have sought yet: namely, to open some universal way for knowing the truth of things through the most universal principles of knowledge, and through those methods of correctly deducing down to the very last conclusions. The <term>Metaphysicians</term> <note>Scholars who study the fundamental nature of reality and being beyond the physical world.</note> hum to themselves; the <term>Physicists</term> <note>Natural philosophers who study the physical world and its laws.</note> applaud themselves; the <term>Ethicists</term> <note>Philosophers of morals and conduct.</note> set laws for themselves; the <term>Politicians</term> <note>Those who study the art of governing the state.</note> fashion foundations for themselves; the <term>Mathematicians</term> triumph for themselves; and the <term>Theologians</term> <note>Scholars of divinity and religious doctrine.</note> reign for themselves. Indeed, in individual faculties and sciences, almost every individual establishes particular principles for themselves from which they might build and defend their own opinions, treating with indifference <note>original: *fúsque déque* — a Latin idiom meaning to treat something as indifferent or to regard it with unconcern, literally "up and down."</note> whatever others elicit from their own presuppositions.

Yet it is impossible for the truth—which in this way is hidden and scattered through all things, and longing to be gathered from everywhere—to be unearthed. For while each person pays attention only to himself and his own imagination, dissonance is no more avoided than in a choir of musicians if everyone were to sing for himself, disregarding any respect for a common rhythm <note>original: *modulum* — a measure, melody, or rhythmic standard.</note>; or who would believe that a well-ordered republic <note>original: *rempublicam* — here meaning a commonwealth or a structured society.</note> could exist where people do not live by common laws, but everyone acts according to their own whim! Do we not see that the branches of a tree can only live if they all [draw] equally from a common trunk [supported] by common roots...

<summary>Comenius critiques the fragmentation of academic disciplines, arguing that scholars in different fields work in isolation rather than seeking a unified "universal truth." ...draw sap from the roots! And can it be hoped that the branches of wisdom can be torn away from the truth while their life remains intact? That is, can someone be a <term>Physicist</term> <note>A natural philosopher who studies the physical world and its laws.</note> who is not also a <term>Metaphysician</term> <note>A scholar who studies the fundamental nature of reality and being beyond the physical world.</note>? Or a <term>Logician</term> who is not skilled in the real sciences? Or a <term>Theologian</term>, a Lawyer, or a Physician who was not first a Philosopher? Or an Orator or a Poet who is not all those things at once? Whoever removes any part of what can be known from himself deprives himself of light, a helping hand, and a standard of measurement.

Certainly, <term>Astronomers</term> (to add this by way of example) would never have dared to introduce and defend such contrary and absurd hypotheses if their ideas had to be drawn from a common foundation of truth. Nor would other things be so uncertain and slippery—or at least almost everything currently taught seems to be so. For they are taught in such a way that almost no one establishes anything that another does not then destroy, or labor to destroy.

The philosophy of *Plato* indeed seemed elegant and divine; but how the school of the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>The followers of Aristotle, known for their habit of walking while discussing philosophy.</note> proved it to be empty speculation! The philosophy of *Aristotle* seemed refined enough to itself; but Christian philosophers have found that it does not correspond in any way to the Holy Scriptures, nor does it match the truth of things in all respects. Astronomers, with their eccentric spheres and <term>epicycles</term> <note>Complex geometric models used in ancient astronomy to explain the seemingly irregular movements of planets.</note>, have applauded themselves for so many centuries, but by—

Indeed, if everyone derived their ideas from the same common principles, it would be impossible for them to fall into such contradictions. Such conflicts cause a manifest delay for those listening and a loss of truth itself, which is usually lost in the heat of argument. For as long as useless things are proposed—not built upon a universal foundation—they cannot help but seem obscure and ambiguous, and they breed hesitation in the minds of the audience. Furthermore, to draw people into agreement, principles are adopted that have been snatched from wherever; they are not well enough known, nor agreed upon by others, nor are they truths beyond doubt in themselves. This is because they are subject to various limitations and exceptions—as are most of the rules of common <term>Philosophy</term> and <term>Theology</term> <note>Comenius is criticizing the "Scholastic" method of his day, which relied on complex logical distinctions and "canons" rather than direct, universal truths.</note> of our day. <margin>27</margin>
Therefore, the matter must be managed in an entirely different way. We must ensure that the truth of things, coming in clear light, can escape the pits of hesitation and the darts of contradiction, and struggle out from all errors. We believe this cannot happen unless the scattered rays of truth everywhere come together into one, so that in all things—the sensory, the intellectual, and those coming from divine revelation—one and the same symmetry appears. Only the balancing of the principles of knowledge—for what can there be but three: *Sense, Reason*, and divine *Revelation* <note>Comenius believed that God reveals truth through three "books": the world of nature (perceived by the senses), the human mind (reason), and the Holy Scriptures (revelation).</note>—and their consolidation into an immovable strength will be able to reveal this, and through it, remove controversies about things. For once the foundation of things is revealed, the error of one of the opposing parties will necessarily become clear, or the reason for the diversity of the sciences will be made plain. This would show that both sides may perhaps think and speak correctly in different respects, even if they do not understand each other because the foundation of those different perspectives has not been perceived. 

Certainly, either by this way can the errors that occupy the minds of mortals in various ways be conquered and minds placed in clear light, or by no other. For it is necessary that, once the clear sun of truth has risen, the mists of infinite opinions will vanish of their own accord; indeed, even the darkness of Atheism itself <note>In the 17th century, "Atheism" often referred to any philosophy that denied God’s active providence or failed to acknowledge the divine origin of the world's order.</note> will finally be dispelled with God’s help.

\* I have identified the second cause of the truth wavering everywhere as the *instability of methods*, because writers do not bind themselves entirely to the things themselves so as to pass them down in an unchangeable manner—exactly as they exist within themselves—but instead they drag and distort things in a thousand ways toward some artificial and self-invented elegance. This is nothing other than distorting things in the mind's view and transforming them from their native form into others. And then, what can appear in place of things but monsters! Furthermore, it is certain that a method entirely parallel to things cannot be given, unless all things are reduced in the intellect to the same degree of harmony with which they bind and connect themselves outside the intellect. I have just pointed out that, until now, many philosophical systems <note>original: "Philosophemata"</note> have been devised at will, and then torn down by others. Let it be understood that the same can happen with the dogmas of theology, or even entire methods: they can be built up and destroyed, since they were fashioned not according to the unchangeable norm of things, but according to the "leaden rule" <note>original: "plumbeam regulam." This refers to the ancient "Rule of Lesbos," a flexible leaden ruler that could be bent to fit any shape; Comenius uses it as a metaphor for a standard of truth that is bent to suit a person's whims rather than being a fixed, objective measure.</note> of this or that little brain <note>original: "cerebelli." Comenius uses the diminutive "little brain" to dismissively refer to subjective, individual human intellects that lack universal perspective.</note>.

...all may begin to be handed down in a single, unified order of things. 
And such a <term>Christian Philosophy</term>, or rather <term>Pansophia</term> <note>original: "Pansophiam," meaning "Universal Wisdom." Comenius envisioned a system where all knowledge—scientific, philosophical, and theological—formed a single, harmonious whole.</note> we teach is to be sought: a place where all things rise from immovable principles into immovable truth, and connect themselves in such perpetual harmony that this work of the mind is as indestructible as the <term>machinery of the world</term> <note>original: "mundi machina." Truly, just as the universe of things is not governed by our whim, but proceeds unchangeably according to its own laws; so must its mirror, *Pansophia*, be passed down by a method from which one cannot depart, even if one were bursting with the desire for variation. This will be achieved if all things are handed down demonstratively through their immediate causes and effects. 

But for this purpose, it will be absolutely necessary that things be taught and learned not through external testimonies about things—that is, traditions—but through the things themselves. For authorities can just as easily disguise things <note>original: "fucum facere," literally "to apply dye/makeup," implying a false or artificial appearance.</note> as they can illuminate them; at the very least, they certainly distract the learner and call them away from the objects of study to the authorities themselves. However, things themselves cannot impress themselves upon the senses in any way other than as they actually are. Or, if the senses fail in any way, reason must be applied, equipped with certain standards so that it cannot go astray. Finally, where reason also leaves a gap, divine revelation should come to the rescue. These three principles of cognition—<term>sense, reason, and revelation</term>—are to be established as the bases of Pansophia, so that hereafter, whatever has fallen from the mouth or pen of any philosopher or theologian is not held as an oracle [ha-] <note>The text cuts off here at "ha-", likely leading to "habeatur" (be held) on the next page.</note>

\* Finally, as to the fact that scholarship does not sufficiently lead its pupils toward God, what wonder is it? These studies have not yet cast off their pagan <note>original: "gentilem." Referring to the pre-Christian Greek and Roman educational traditions which Comenius felt still dominated the schools.</note> profanity—the rashness of handling God’s works, and indeed God Himself, without a sense of God, and of transforming the glory of the incorruptible into the likeness of corruptible things. 

For this reason, the Apostle <note>Saint Paul.</note> testifies that the pagan philosophers "became vain in their thoughts," and while they thought themselves wise, they became fools, and were "handed over by God to the desires of their heart for impurity"; because they served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever. *Romans 1.* 

But what else, I ask, happens even today? Most of our "wise men" are just as wise without God as those pagans were: certainly neither drawing their wisdom from Him, nor directing it toward Him. Instead, they move from one created thing to another—that is, they conduct all their affairs with a deep forgetfulness of God, focusing only on themselves and other...

# I. A. COMENIUS

...regarding corruptible things; serving themselves and those things. God has declared that He is the Alpha and the Omega <note>original: "α & ω." The first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, representing the beginning and the end of all things.</note>, the Beginning and the End of all things: from whom, through whom, and in whom all things exist. 

But who begins their own wisdom from Him—that is, from the fear of Him? Who seeks to be wise through Him—that is, to be governed by the guidance of His Word and Spirit? Who desires their wisdom to end in Him—that is, to devote themselves and all they possess to His glory alone? 

These things are hidden from the eyes of most people. We begin with ourselves, we make progress by our own efforts, and we move toward our own ends. We start with self-confidence, rely on our own strength, and by our own light we strive for our own comfort and glory. Thus, we fall back from ourselves into ourselves; we are dragged and swept this way and that by the vanities of created things, until we ourselves vanish as well. This is the saddest path of all flesh, by which even the wisest of men unhappily stray from God.

\* The Remedy will be to scatter the seeds of the true knowledge and fear of God throughout the whole of Universal Wisdom <note>original: "Pansophiam." This is Comenius's core concept: a "full" or "all-encompassing" wisdom that connects all branches of knowledge to a divine purpose.</note> in such a way that wherever a person turns, they may see that all things are nothing without God. Indeed, it is necessary that this Christian Universal Wisdom of ours be organized so that it consists of nothing but constant reminders to seek God everywhere, precise signs for finding the God we seek everywhere, and a reliable way to [find] God...

### PRECURSOR TO UNIVERSAL WISDOM

...found everywhere to be embraced; and in such a way that there may be a certain holy ladder <note>original: "sancta scala." Unless we obtain this (as with the things mentioned above), all our efforts are in vain, we ourselves are in vain, and finally, whatever we do is in vain. Those pseudo-scholars <note>original: "sapientuli." A diminutive, mocking term for those who possess a shallow or false cleverness rather than true wisdom.</note> will continue to wander through their own labyrinths; the schools will continue to roll their stones of Sisyphus <note>In Greek mythology, Sisyphus was condemned to roll a boulder up a hill for eternity, only for it to roll back down; Comenius uses this to describe the fruitless, repetitive labor of traditional education.</note>; and the world will continue to rave and walk in a dizzying whirl.

<margin>Therefore, it is necessary that help now finally be given more correctly to the struggling state of learning.</margin>

* But since this is a matter of the utmost seriousness, in which the glory of God and the salvation of the human race are at stake, we must most ardently call upon God, so that, having mercy on us, He may open our darkened eyes, that in His light we may see light. And because Christ did not only say: "Ask, and you shall receive," but also, "Seek, and you shall find; Knock, and it shall be opened to you" (*Matthew 7:7*), we must join tireless efforts to our prayers and sighs, to find a way to pull the veils from things, and to lead men toward...

# J. A. COMENIUS

I. Let all things—wherever they are, will be, or have been—be brought under numbers, so that nothing may escape our understanding.

II. So that the measured proportion of all things, both in relation to the whole universe and to one another, may be laid open to our eyes.

III. And finally, so that the weight of causes may be clearly visible, for the sake of accurately perceiving the truth of all things.

The first point will ensure that **Learning** is **Universal**: which is our primary aim.

The second: that it be clear and distinct; which we eagerly pursue.

The third: that it be true and solid; which we most greatly desire.

I say, we desire such a book to be constructed, which might stand as **One** in place of all—a truly **Universal Repository of Learning** <term>promptuarium: literally a storehouse or larder; a place where everything is ready at hand.</term>: in which you could rightfully desire nothing more, and from the reading of which wisdom might flow into minds of its own accord. This is surely because of the perpetual, clear, and distinct coherence of things, with everything arising from its own proper roots and veins. Thus, it should be apparent that each thing is exactly as it is described, and cannot be otherwise than it is, because of the immutable truth of things that connects itself everywhere. Nevertheless, all these things must be presented concisely, because we must serve a brief and fleeting life. Everything must be presented accessibly <note>original: "populariter," meaning in a way that is clear and available to the common people rather than just elite scholars</note>, because light is to be brought into minds, not darkness. And everything must be presented solidly through causes and effects...

# THE FORERUNNER OF UNIVERSAL WISDOM <note>original: *Pansophiae Prodromus*</note>

...[if only] all standards might be reduced to one standard, and all weights to one weight? The more candles there are, the more light there is. If only a way can be found by which all lights can merge into one light: that is, how those so diverse and almost infinite discoveries, things known, and things thought, can be reduced into one perpetual, immutable, and eternal form of thinking, knowing, and discovering. For once this is discovered, we shall possess that which is sought.

And why should it not be found? We certainly already possess a not-to-be-despised forest <note>original: *sylvam*. In the tradition of Francis Bacon, this refers to a "Sylva Sylvarum" or a vast collection of natural facts and observations.</note> of known things, and a clear light of method for proceeding toward the rest. Let us therefore attempt to go "further beyond" <note>original: *plus ultra*. This was the motto of the Spanish Empire and the burgeoning Scientific Revolution, challenging the ancient "non plus ultra" (nothing further beyond).</note> to the ultimate goal of both things and method. For where there is a "further," there is also an "ultimate." # I. A. COMENIUS

For once this is done, only then will defects, redundancies, and errors become apparent; and only then can they be removed, corrected, or supplemented—and not before. 

But which mortal will be sufficient for such a labor? This is due, of course, to the infinite multitude as well as the variety of things: **natural, supernatural, moral, and artificial.** For if those earlier investigators of things found so many and such great "knots" <note>This refers to intellectual difficulties or complexities that are hard to untie</note> in every specific subject, the diligence of most ended only in a complaint—concerning the insuperable subtlety of nature, the inscrutable complication of causes, the implacable hostility of opposing forces which occur everywhere, and finally, the excessive weakness of the **human mind** <note>original: "ingenii humani"</note> in the face of all these things. To us, however, it brings little help for the construction of **Pansophia** <term>Universal Wisdom: Comenius's grand project to organize all human knowledge into a single, cohesive system</term>, because (as I said) it is directed only toward unlocking the secrets of nature, whereas we are concerned with the **universality of all things**. 

Therefore, there will be a need for some other altogether **universal rule**, which our merciful God may perhaps not disdain to show us as we seek: He who hides Himself so that He may be sought; and wishes to be sought so that He may be found. ## I. * There are three things which complete our human knowledge—and even a certain kind of omniscience—the knowledge of *God, Nature, and Art*.

By **Art** <note>original: "artem" — in this period, "Art" refers to any human skill, craft, or systematic method of doing something, rather than just "fine arts" like painting</note> I mean whatever is made by human industry, including thoughts, speech, and works; by **Nature**, whatever is born and happens by its own spontaneously implanted force; by **God**, whatever of His eternal, hidden power, wisdom, and goodness has revealed itself until now through words and works. He who knows these three knows everything: because the universe of things consists of this triple category.

## II. Perfect knowledge of these three must be sought.

<meta>This page continues Comenius's logical sequence of aphorisms. While page 62 established that universal knowledge encompasses God, Nature, and Art, page 63 defines the criteria for "perfect" knowledge—moving from mere acquaintance with a subject to understanding the divine "Idea" or blueprint behind its creation.</meta>

<page-num>63</page-num>

<header>PRECURSOR TO UNIVERSAL WISDOM.</header>

It should not be considered enough to know something about ***God***, something about ***Nature***, and something about ***Art*** <note>original: "Arte" — referring here to human skill and systematic invention</note> (a thing which happens even to the most ignorant and even to fools); rather, we should fully and exactly understand all things that can be understood.

### *III. The knowledge of things is perfect when it is true.*

For if it is not true, it presents phantoms <note>original: "spectra" — used here to mean deceptive appearances or illusions</note> instead of actual things, and it ends in mockery.

### *IV. Knowledge is true when things are known exactly as they are.*

For if they are known otherwise than they are, it will not be knowledge, but error.

### *V. Things are known as they are, when they are known as they were made.*

For everything is exactly as it was made; because if it is not as it was made, it has degenerated <note>Comenius argues that to understand a thing's essence, one must understand its original purpose or "manufacture" by God or man</note>.

### *VI. Every thing is made according to its own Idea; that is, according to a certain reason through which it could become what it is.*

For unless a thing were able to be made, it would not be made; and unless it were able to be made in a certain way, it would not be made in that way.

### I. * There are three things which complete our human knowledge—and indeed a certain omniscience <note>In this context, "omniscience" refers to "Pansophia" or Universal Wisdom: knowing all things necessary for a human to understand their place in the world.</note>: the knowledge of **God, Nature,** and **Art**.

By **art** <note>original: "artem" — in the 17th century, this meant "human industry" or "technology," encompassing everything humans design or build, from logic to machines.</note> I mean whatever is made by human industry—thoughts, speeches, and works. By **Nature**, I mean whatever is born and happens by its own accord through a force implanted in things. By **God**, I mean whatever of His hidden power, wisdom, and goodness from eternity has revealed itself through words and works up to this point. He who knows these three knows all things: because the universe of things consists of this threefold genus.

...ly; therefore, that <term>τῆς</term> <note>original Greek: "the" — here used to emphasize the specific quality of possibility</note> possibility of such a thing is called an **Idea**, through which a thing is exactly what it is.

*VII. Therefore, all things that are made are made according to Ideas, whether they be the works of God, of Nature, or of Art.*

For since an Idea is a certain **Reason** <note>original: "ratio" — meaning a governing principle, logic, or blueprint</note> for things, God cannot even be conceived of as doing anything without Ideas—that is, without a fixed reason—as he is himself the Reason of all reasons. Similarly, Nature, since it produces the most orderly works, just like Art which rivals it, cannot operate without reason.

*VIII. Art borrows the Ideas for its works from Nature; Nature from God; God from himself.*

That first point is well known, as these common sayings show: *Art can do nothing without nature*; *Art is the rival of Nature*; *Art imitates Nature*; *Art is the daughter of Nature*. But these sayings are no less true: *Nature can do nothing without God*; *Nature is the rival of God*; *Nature is the daughter of God*; *Nature imitates God*. God, finally, imitates no one except himself, because he neither can nor wishes to do otherwise. He cannot do otherwise because he has nothing besides himself in his eternity: from where else, then, could he take the beginning or the form of his works?

He does not wish it, because since He is the best, He cannot wish for anything but the best. However, nothing is the "best" except for that one, sole, eternal Good, which He Himself is. If someone were to say that God freely devised the <term>reasons</term> <note>original: "rationes" — the logical principles or blueprints</note> for producing things: I ask, to what end? If God now does nothing in vain through Nature, why would He have done so from the beginning? Was it so that, despite possessing Himself as the most perfect <term>exemplar</term> <note>original: "exemplar" — a model or pattern to be imitated</note> of all perfection, He might devise another? Or was it to spare His majesty? And yet He gave this majesty visibly expressed. *Romans 1:20.* <note>Comenius references the biblical idea that God's invisible nature is understood through the things He has made.</note> Or was it to show the depth of His wisdom by that departure from Himself? But in this way, the fullness of His glory would be diminished, as if there were some perfection that did not exist within Him.

But this is impossible. It is certain, therefore, that just as the creatures <note>meaning all created things, living or inanimate</note> flowed from this source, so too did the **Ideas** of those creatures. And since among created things every agent <note>one who acts or produces an effect</note> seeks to make the object like itself, why should we not recognize the same in the Creator, by whom that very characteristic was impressed upon creatures? Especially since God can have absolutely nothing that He might establish as the <term>end</term> <note>original: "finem" — the ultimate purpose or goal</note> of His works, except for Himself. Let it stand, therefore, that God takes the source of His works from nowhere else than from Himself—including the purpose, the power of making them, and the form; taking from nothingness only the **matter**, by which the creature <term>subjectively</term> <note>original: "subjectivè" — here meaning in its physical substance or underlying material</note> differs from the Creator.

### IX. Therefore, by fashioning the world, God models it after Himself, so that the Creature <note>In this context, "Creature" refers to anything created by God, including inanimate objects and nature, not just animals.</note> might be entirely proportionate to the Creator.

For it is necessary that the thing formed corresponds to its own form: even though there are degrees of that proportion, depending on whether the resemblance is more or less obvious. In this way, the Son of God is called the **character** (or the **expressed image**) of the Father. *Hebrews 1:3.* And yet, humanity is also said to be the image of God. *Genesis 1:26; 1 Corinthians 11:7.* <note>The original text cites 1 Cor 11:6, though the reference to man as the image of God is found in verse 7.</note> Furthermore, all other things are compared to a certain image, since it is said that the invisible things of God have been clearly seen through the things that have been made since the creation of the world, *Romans 1:20,* and that from the greatness of the beauty and of the creature, their Creator can be known and seen. *Wisdom of Solomon 13:5.* <note>The Wisdom of Solomon is a book of the Biblical Apocrypha, often cited by scholars of this period.</note> And from this it happened that the Gentiles <note>The "Gentiles" here refers to pre-Christian Greek and Roman philosophers.</note> called nature not only the daughter of God, but even God Himself.

Because those things which agree with a third thing, agree with one another. <note>original: "Quia quæ conveniunt in uno tertio, inter ſe conveniunt." This is a fundamental axiom of logic.</note>

*XI.* Accordingly, the underlying reasons <term>rationes: the logical principles or "blueprints"</term> of things are the same; they do not differ except in their form of existence. This is because they exist in **God** as the **Archetype** <term>Archetype: the original divine pattern or "Master Idea"</term>, in **Nature** as the **Ectype** <term>Ectype: a direct copy or physical manifestation of the original pattern</term>, and in **Art** <note>In this context, "Art" refers to any human craft, technology, or creative endeavor.</note> as the **Antitype** <term>Antitype: a secondary reproduction or human imitation of nature’s patterns</term>.

Consider, for example, how the same form exists in a seal. First, it is conceived in the mind of the person who creates it, or who orders it to be created. Next, it is engraved into metal. Finally, it is impressed upon wax. Although the form is threefold in its manifestation, it is nonetheless one and the same. This is because the second is formed from the first, and the third from the second—each subsequent form according to the image of the one before it. In the same way, the **Ideas** conceived in the Divine mind <note>original: "Ideæ in mente conceptæ"</note> impress their likeness upon created things. Then, those creatures who act with reason <note>Meaning human beings.</note> impress that same likeness upon the things they produce themselves.

*XII.* Therefore, the foundation of all things—both of those that are to be built and those that are to be known—is **Harmony**.

Musicians define **Harmony** as a pleasant consonance <term>consonance: a harmonious combination of sounds or voices</term> of many voices. Such is the nature of the eternal virtues in God, the created virtues in Nature, and the expressed virtues in Art: a through-and-through accor— <note>The text breaks here mid-word; the Latin "concor-" likely concludes as "concordance" or "agreement" on the following page.</note>

[...to be known, all] produce harmony <note>original: "dans concentus." ## XIII. The first requirement of harmony is that nothing be dissonant.

Musical harmony is composed of voices that are very different, and even contrary to one another; and yet, this contrariety is brought back into consonance <term>consonance: a pleasing agreement of sounds</term>. In the same way, the entire world consists of contraries—for without contraries, neither truth, nor order, nor indeed the very essence of the world could exist. This is just as **Scripture** contains many things that seem to conflict on the surface. Yet, all these things return to a state of concord within themselves, and they must be brought back to that same concord in our own minds if **Panharmony** <term>Panharmonia: Comenius’s concept of "Universal Harmony" where all knowledge, faith, and nature align</term> is to emerge. This Panharmony should win universal agreement for our works, our opinions, and our words—just as it does for divine works—so that any apparent dissonance vanishes. 

Because this mystery is not commonly understood, philosophers snatch certain ideas from nature and theologians take others from Scripture—each choosing this or that piece. They then pit nature against nature and scriptures against scriptures, drawing out contrary meanings and stirring up quarrels and battles. All of this must vanish when the light of universal harmony appears. For **Truth** is consistent with itself from every side.

# XIV. The second requirement of Harmony is that nothing should be discordant.

Regarding **natural** things and **artificial** <term>Art / Artificial: in the 17th century, this refers to "Artifice" or human skill, including science, technology, and crafts</term> things, it is manifest that all things are created according to harmony. In an **Animal**, a **Tree**, a **Musical Instrument**, a **Ship**, a **Course** <note>original: "Cursu," which can mean a race, a journey, or a rhythmic movement</note>, a **Book**, a **House**, etc., it is necessary that all parts are proportioned both to the whole and to one another. 

But regarding **divine** things, some might doubt whether they enter into any proportion with natural and artificial things. One might think it a matter of God's majesty to share nothing in common with His creatures. However, it must truly be known that whatever exists in the **Ectype** <term>Ectype: the copy, reflection, or physical manifestation of a pattern</term> must necessarily be found first, and indeed in a more excellent way, in the **Archetype** <term>Archetype: the original divine model or blueprint in the mind of God</term>. This is because the river receives from the spring, the shadow from the body, and the mirror from the image whatever it possesses. 

Furthermore, *“if the works of nature are so precise that no room is left for even imagining a better construction”* (which **Galen** <note>Claudius Galenus (129–216 AD), a prominent Greek physician and philosopher</note> admits in *The Use of the Parts*, Book 6, Chapter 1), *“and if the nature of Nature is immutable and beyond reform”* (as **Tertullian** <note>An early Christian author from Carthage (c. 155–220 AD)</note> testifies in *Against the Valentinians*, Chapter 29), what then is Nature but a living image of Him in whom all things are primarily and excellently best, immutable, and beyond reform? Finally, God Himself in **Scripture** attributes to Himself ears, eyes, a mouth,

### XVII. And such common principles of things are to be drawn out from the things themselves, through a process of induction, and established as the standards for all things.

### Let the materials of **Universal Wisdom** contain nothing but serious knowledge.

\* V. The general precepts of **Universal Wisdom** <note>original: "Panſophiæ"</note> should be nothing other than real and practical **axioms** <term>Axiom: A statement or principle that is established, accepted, or self-evidently true without needing a complex proof.</term>: that is, statements worthy of belief in their own right, which do not need to be proven by prior arguments, but are only to be illustrated by examples. This is because the human **intellect**, as soon as it perceives such truths, accepts them as a standard of variety. For such insights, divinely imprinted upon our minds, will be the torches to be lit to understand every particular detail, and the keys to our practical operations. But the greatest care must be taken not to admit anything as an axiom unless it truly is one. Indeed, it is not in vain that **Verulamius** <note>Francis Bacon, Lord Verulam (1561–1626), the English philosopher who championed inductive reasoning and the "Advancement of Learning."</note>, **Streso** <note>Caspar Streso (1603–1664), a Dutch theologian known for his work on logic and rhetoric.</note>, and others complain that the common rules of **Logic** rashly affirm or deny just anything. They argue that traditional logic rarely serves for actual demonstration, but mostly only for **disputation**—which is carried out by making exceptions, limiting, insisting, and retorting; in other words, by bickering.

† VI. All particulars throughout the whole of **Universal Wisdom** should bring nothing new; instead, they should only be a more specific deduction of the general principles that preceded them, just as we see happening in the growth of a tree or an animal. In these, new limbs or branches do not sprout every year; rather, the original parts are simply brought to perfection.

---

\* *General Theorems are pure axioms.*
† *Particulars are pure Demonstrations.*

Organized in this way, **Universal Wisdom** will be:
1. **Easy to perceive.** For one thing will flow naturally from another.
2. **Solid in truth.** Everything that follows will be founded upon what came before.
3. **Remarkable in use.** For the underlying reasons <note>original: "rationes"</note> of all thinkable things will be excellently revealed.

And such a book will truly be not only a **seedbed** <term>Seedbed (seminarium): A place where the "seeds" of knowledge are planted to grow into full understanding.</term> for every kind of science, but also a kind of **irrigation system** that causes everything to take deep root. The result is that learners are not merely lured by persuasions, but are compelled to give their assent by **demonstrations** <note>In this context, a "demonstration" is a logical proof that shows a conclusion must be true based on its premises.</note>. This is what finally makes learning firm and lasting.

Just as, therefore, among mathematicians no one says: ***Pythagoras*** <note>An ancient Greek philosopher and mathematician (c. 570–495 BC).</note> teaches that three times three is nine; or ***Euclid*** <note>A Greek mathematician (c. 300 BC), often called the "Father of Geometry."</note> establishes three types of continuous quantity—the line, the surface, and the solid body. All **geometers** agree on this: that in a triangle, the three internal angles are equal to two right angles. Indeed, a person would be laughed at who so foolishly rattled off "authorities" for such things.

Instead, they demonstrate that it is so, and that it cannot be otherwise, even if no ***Pythagoras*** or ***Euclid*** had ever been born. Likewise, from now on, in **Metaphysics**, **Physics**, **Ethics**, and **Politics**, let it be a source of shame to cite authorities where the matter can be settled by **reason** <note>original: "rationibus"</note>.

But we also intend, by using such a method, that the entire work of **Universal Wisdom** may proceed without any repetition. This will allow for a brevity that—although the whole work is a very compact structure of dense, solid facts—will hinder nothing...

**Note Well.** Nevertheless, in more serious matters, the **Authority of Holy Scripture** must be added, as a testimony from the mouth of God. The goal is this: just as mathematicians find that once a **Theorem** <note>A statement that has been proven to be true based on previously established statements.</note> is proven, certain knowledge follows, and once a **Problem** is demonstrated, a certain result follows; so too, through the principles of **Universal Wisdom** <note>original: "Pansophia"</note>, both the knowledge and the practical handling of things will follow without fail.
