### 86

...as I was reasoning: If that most nimble language, the interpreter of the mind, eager to spread itself out in infinite profusion, could nevertheless be enclosed within such limits that, with a finite number of words, it must necessarily express all the primary concepts of the mind: why could not the concepts of our wandering mind likewise be constrained by the barriers of the things themselves? For even though things, situated outside the intellect, seem to be something infinite, they are not; since the world itself, the stupendous work of God, consists of a few elements <note>original: "elementis"; the fundamental building blocks of nature, which in the 17th century were still often thought of as earth, air, fire, and water.</note> and a few differences of forms, and whatever has been devised in the arts can be reduced to certain classes and certain sums. 

Since, therefore, **THINGS** *and the **CONCEPTS of Things***, and the images of concepts—**WORDS**—correspond in parallel, and in each of them there are certain fundamental elements from which the rest result, I thought that those very fundamentals could be taught equally in things and concepts as in speech. 

It also came to mind that the *Chemists* <note>original: "Chymicos"; early modern scientists and alchemists who sought to understand the world through the purification and distillation of substances.</note> had discovered a way to liberate the essences—or spirits—of things from the excess of matter, so that in a tiny drop a huge power of *Minerals* or *Vegetables* might be concentrated, and could be administered in medicines with greater efficacy than when they are offered in their entire bulk. And I thought that nothing could be devised by which the precepts of wisdom, scattered through such wide territories <note>original: "pomœria"; a classical term referring to the sacred boundary or limits of a city.</note> of the sciences...

<margin>100</margin>
And so, I began this web <note>original: "telam"; a metaphor for the intricate weaving of a complex intellectual project.</note> in the name of God, proposing for myself the same method to be observed here which I used in weaving together the Gate of Languages <note>original: "linguarum januâ"; referring to his revolutionary 1631 textbook *Janua linguarum reserata*, which taught Latin through descriptions of the world.</note>.

First, just as all the words of the Latin language were gathered there, so here all **THINGS** <note>original: "RES"</note> worthy of human knowledge should be brought together, as if into a Treasury.

Second, that nothing should be placed more than once, except for connecting terms and those things without mention of which others cannot be explained. 

Third, that nothing should be placed except in its own place and proper sense—that is, in the most natural order of things and the clearest sense of words—so that whatever notable thing the universe of things possesses, and all that books and libraries provide, may all be learned here in summary, briefly and lucidly. 

If we could achieve this, so that through this Gate of ours a passage might be prepared into all Things, and all books might be understood even without a teacher, then of praise...

<margin>16 6</margin> Indeed, we deliver none of these things—though they possess evident truth in themselves—by presupposing anything, as if we were begging for agreement. This could not be sufficiently observed in the books of "pre-cognitions" <term>precognita: the preliminary principles or basic foundational knowledge required before a deeper study</term> alone, because the causes of things had not yet been delivered. 

Therefore, we deal with the human intellect there just as those who break in young colts are accustomed to do. For they first use softer bits, which delight the horses rather than press upon them; and they train them to run through flat and pleasant places before they force them into tight circles.

### PRECURSOR TO UNIVERSAL WISDOM
<note>original title: "PANSOPHIAE PRODROMUS"</note>

...not <note>The previous page ends with "press upon the," referring to the mouths of young horses. This page completes the thought: it was not...</note> sought by me through some superstition or affectation. Rather, in every most important and weighty matter—from the very first attributes of things (the **one**, the **true**, and the **good**) <term>The One, the True, the Good: In classical philosophy, these are the "transcendentals," properties that belong to everything that exists.</term>—this structure offered itself so spontaneously that I stood astonished for a while, stunned by the novelty of the discovery. 

And when, encouraged by these examples, I tested the same approach elsewhere, I saw it succeed everywhere. Therefore, I did not dare to resist the truth of things, which so often presents itself in a **triple mystery**. Instead, joyfully embracing such a great harmony of the **sacred ternary** <note>original: "sacri ternarii"; the "rule of three" or the idea that reality is structured in threes, reflecting the Holy Trinity.</note>, I eagerly followed it through the remaining subjects. Nor was any force applied to the facts (I firmly believe), but they seemed to divide themselves of their own accord. 

I also believed that this would be greatly beneficial to learners. First, as an aid to **memory**, which delights in proceeding through structured boundaries <note>original: "cancellos"; literally "lattices" or "railings," suggesting that the mind remembers better when it has a clear framework to follow.</note>, both in discovering and in remembering. Second, for the **understanding** of things themselves, as the nature of things reveals itself most excellently in this way. 

Regarding this matter, I call upon the judgments of all who will weigh these things piously and attentively in the fear of the Lord. I am confident that they will find not a vanity of fantasies, but the truth of the things themselves. 

*Let this Christian **Universal Wisdom** <term>Pansophia: "All-wisdom" or a system of universal knowledge that integrates all fields of learning with spiritual truth.</term>, revealing **Ternary mysteries**, be sacred to the eternal, **Triune Jehovah**, the only Powerful, Wise, Good, and eternally to be adored God.*

### PRECURSOR TO UNIVERSAL WISDOM

...the Church is divine revelation given, nor without this can the human senses penetrate beyond the present life. <margin>113</margin>
Therefore, I do not apologize for the fact that I, a man of Theology, should attempt to map out the boundaries of such **Polymatheia** <note>original: *Polymatheiæ*; from the Greek for "wide-ranging knowledge" or "much learning."</note>, or more truly **Pammatheia** <note>original: *Pammatheiæ*; from the Greek for "universal or all-encompassing knowledge." The sacred Gospel which Jesus Christ entrusted to me is holy to me and dearer than life itself; I desire and labor for nothing else than to be found a faithful steward of His mysteries. But because I know the Lord said to Peter not only, "*Feed my sheep,*" but also, "*Feed my lambs*" (John 21:15), I am fully convinced that it is the duty of theologians to be earnestly concerned with leading both the former and the latter back *to the richest pastures on the mountains of Israel, where they may rest in green grass and feed in fat pastures* (Ezekiel 34:13-14). This is especially necessary after the scattering of God's flock—whenever that has happened because of the "beasts of the field"—so that the sheep and the lambs of God may be gathered together as quickly as possible. Therefore, with the Prophet, I will bless the Lord who "tugs at my ear" <note>original: *vellicat aurem*; a reference to Isaiah 50:4-5, suggesting God awakens the author's understanding to listen as a disciple.</note> so that I may be like one who pays attention and learns.

# FORERUNNER OF UNIVERSAL WISDOM

...[the deliberations of mortals] are timid, and our foresight is uncertain. <margin>Wisdom 9:14</margin> <note>Comenius is quoting the deuterocanonical Book of Wisdom: "For the deliberations of mortals are timid, and our plans are unsure."</note> I gladly invite all to an examination—those whom God has endowed with a lively wit and sharp judgment—so that they may inquire into the universality, brevity, and truth of things. 

And I wish to ask them, first, that they set aside the spectacles of preconceived opinions and come with a free mind and light to view this entire **Little Theater** <term>Theatriolum</term> <note>A "little theater" refers to a condensed, visual, or systematic representation of the world, a common metaphor for an encyclopedia or a comprehensive textbook in the 17th century.</note>: they should judge things not according to what they have heard before, but according to the things themselves, just as we offer them to be seen and touched. 

For unless they observe this, they will create a deception not for the things themselves, but for themselves; just like one who looks through colored glass does not color or deceive the things he sees, but rather deceives his own sight. Therefore, one must take care not to stand in one's own way by attending more to one's own opinions than to the truth of things. 

I hope it will be a greater pleasure to all wise people if, relying on the privilege with which we are all equally endowed, we may observe things freely without outside judges. To those who are learning, we should offer not just opinions about things, but the things themselves to be seen, handled, mastered, and possessed. 

Nor should anyone suspect that we are removing the views of others just so that room may be made for our own. Far be that vanity from us! We do nothing else, nor shall we do anything else, except what we transcribe onto our own tablet from the **Books of God, of Nature, and of Scripture** <note>Comenius famously believed that God revealed truth through three "books": the world of Nature, the written Bible (Scripture), and the human Mind (often called the "inner book").</note>: the things of this world and the world to come, simply as they occur. Several years ago, divine providence offered an opportunity to compose a small work which prescribes a more concise method of teaching the Latin language (and any other language) through the very order of Things. I thought that an opportunity was being given to supply these missing pieces, so that we might have a collection of whatever is necessary to be taught and learned in Christian schools gathered into a single volume. This would be done using a method that would instill all these things into our youth more briefly, more truly, and more effectively—that is, more suitably for the goals of both the present and the future life.

The aim was (to repeat it in passing) to complete a summary of the books of God: **Nature**, **Scripture**, and the human **Conscience**. The goal was that: whatever exists in the world would be described here in one continuous series; whatever exists of divine Revelations would be applied here to illustrate the nature of things; and whatever common notions are born into the human Mind would be arranged here for their proper uses. Through these means, we wished:

<page-num>128</page-num>

<header>->PREFACE.<-</header>

...the study of grasping Truth <note>original: [perci]piendae Veritatis; the first word is partially cut off from the previous page</note>, however much it binds and enslaves even the most ingenious minds. I attack no one: why then should anyone attack me? I am handing over a way of reconciling all who have sacrificed to Truth in any part: and why should anyone declare irreconcilable anger against me? Even if (I confess) I myself am less than my own advice: is it for that reason that I am worthy of hatred? For certainly, relying on no apparatus of erudition or sharpness of talent, I have set out to mark the boundaries of **Universal Wisdom** <term>Universal Wisdom: translated from "Universali Sapientiae," referring to "Pansophia," the 17th-century ideal of a single, unified system of all human knowledge.</term>. 

But because I know that what **GOD** <note>original: DEVS</note> has granted me to think will be most beneficial for the world, I have judged that opportunities for stimulating others—who can handle so great a matter more successfully—must not be passed by. Hence it happens that I have preferred to expose myself <note>original: prostituere me; in the sense of making his reputation vulnerable to public scrutiny</note> rather than fail to scatter that harvest of goads into the minds of men. Because, you see, I set before myself a high goal, and one deservedly desirable for the entire human race, if I fail in the midst of it, I shall be more worthy of pity than of hatred. 

It is far too inhuman to strike with blows one who is trying to be of use; but it is full of fairness that he who walks by the public way should enjoy public safety: and he who seeks to promote common interests should be defended and protected by common patronage. But let us come to the matter itself, so that we may again set forth our vows for the growth of the Church. I shall close this Preface, however, with the words of *Augustine* <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational theologian for both Catholic and Protestant traditions.</note>.

> *I shall speak with these before Thee, my* **GOD**, *who [know] that all these things are true, which* **Thy Truth** <note>original: Veritas Tua</note> *does not keep silent within my mind...*

# ELUCIDATION
# OF PANSOPHIC
## ENDEAVORS.

<margin>*</margin>Great men have long attempted to gather a certain comprehensive collection of all Learning; realizing well enough that the light of the mind does not stand firm unless the rays of the Truth of Things <note>original: "Veritatis Rerum"</note> come together from every side. Aristotle himself wrote that *the Wise Man ought to KNOW ALL THINGS, as much as is possible: and he ought to establish such principles through which he may satisfy all inquiries: and he ought to begin from those things which are better known, and therefore from the more universal: and it is necessary that he possess a great certainty of things, and that not just in any way, but through causes.* (*As Giovanni Bellarini* <note>original: "Ioh. Bellarinus"; a 17th-century theologian and author of "The Practice of the Sciences" (Praxi scientiarum)</note> *has collected these points from Aristotle in "The Practice of the Sciences," Book 4, Distinction 1, Number 1.*) Where, regarding the OMNISCIENCE <note>original: "OMNISCIENTIAM"; meaning "all-knowledge" or universal wisdom</note> *which is possible for Man*, the Philosopher <note>Commonly referring to Aristotle</note> requires these three things:

1. *Universality of Principles.*
2. *A true Method of Order.*
3. *Infallible certainty of Truth.*
* According to these laws, not only *Aristotle* himself and other ancients attempted to construct systematic arrangements of teachings; but also—

---

* <margin>Foundations of universal learning.</margin>
* <margin>And various attempts by various people.</margin>

The reasons and foundations of this project were directed there so generally that many already agree with us that there is no room for doubt regarding the necessity and possibility of the matter. 

But because some fear a certain confusion of divine wisdom with human wisdom, the occasion has been given to propose these things somewhat more distinctly, and from such a foundation that even the title of the Book may be changed. Namely, that it be titled:

# * THE TEMPLE OF CHRISTIAN ALL-KNOWLEDGE, according to the ideas of the supreme Architect Himself, Almighty GOD,

<meta>This page continues Comenius's etymological and philosophical justification for calling his project a "Temple." It expands on the usage of the term "Temple" in scripture, classical poetry, Roman law, and philosophy to show how it represents a space of both vision and sacred judgment.</meta>

<page-num>126</page-num>
<header>CONTINUATION OF J. A. COMENIUS</header>

In this sense, the title of "Temple" most greatly fits the Heavens: because it lies open everywhere to our view, and because GOD from there freely observes all things. Just as David speaks: *The Lord is in his holy Temple, his throne is in heaven; his eyes see, and his eyelids test the sons of men* (Psalm 11:4 and Psalm 33:13). So too did Lucretius <note>Titus Lucretius Carus (c. 99–55 BC), a Roman poet and philosopher.</note> speak of the *Bright temples of the heaven* <note>original: "Lucida cœli Templa"</note>. And Ennius <note>Quintus Ennius (c. 239–169 BC), often called the father of Roman poetry.</note> wrote: *The great temple of high-thundering Jove trembled* <note>original: "Contremuit Templum magnum Iovis altitonantis"</note>. 

However, because the ancients used to consecrate the higher places of the earth—the hills and mounds from which a pleasant view was provided—to the worship of the divinity, and marked them for sacred use by erecting Altars there, eventually surrounding the Altars themselves with enclosures: it happened that the name "Temple" shifted to signify primarily a building destined for divine worship, and it is in that sense that the word is now most commonly used. 

It is clear, however, from the writings of Cicero <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BC), the famous Roman orator and statesman.</note>, that the Senate House <note>original: "Curia," the meeting place of the Roman Senate.</note>—where the Senate gathers for deliberation as if in the sight of God—was also honored with the title of "Temple." He says, *The Senate House is the seat and Temple of public counsel*. And elsewhere (in his speech *Pro Milone*), he calls the Senate House the *Temple of Sanctity*. 

Finally, the Poet <note>Likely referring to a Neo-Latin or classical poet's metaphor for the soul.</note> calls the innermost recesses of the human soul (especially that of the Wise man) the *Temples of the mind*: from which the Mind, as if from a high watchtower <note>original: "edita specula." Comenius views the mind as an observatory for understanding the universe.</note>, contemplates all things, and even makes decrees regarding what it perceives, according to the conscience.

<summary>Comenius traces the term "Temple" from its origins as a high viewing point to its application to the heavens, physical churches, the Roman Senate, and finally the human mind. He argues that a "Temple" is essentially a place of elevated observation and divine judgment.</summary>

These are the reasons why this Theater of Wisdom should be distinguished by the illustrious name of **TEMPLE**. † It must now be explained why we do not call it simply Wisdom, but All-Wisdom, or Universal Wisdom (or, more elegantly in Greek, *Pansophia*). I will not put forward examples (such as those of Laurenbergius <note>Peter Laurenberg (1575–1639), a German polymath and professor.</note> and Alsted <note>Johann Heinrich Alsted (1588–1638), a famous encyclopedist and teacher of Comenius.</note>, who recommends five types of knowledge <note>original: "τῶν γνώσεων" (tōn gnōseōn)</note> to anyone who wishes to become and be called "all-knowing" or "Wise" <note>original: "πανεπιστήμων ἐπὰν Σοφὸς" (panepistēmōn epan Sophos)</note>, in his *Archilogia* <note>A work by Alsted on the principles of knowledge.</note>, chapter 1). For us, our own reasoning remains firm, and it is threefold, drawn from the subject, the object, and the manner of teaching Wisdom here. As for the subject: the custom has prevailed for several centuries that those things in which the mysteries of Wisdom were believed to be contained were not handed down in vernacular languages, understood by the common people, but in foreign ones (Latin and Greek), which had to be learned specifically for that purpose. By that reasoning, Wisdom itself was held as the private property of a certain few—namely, those admitted to those sources. * But we contend that it is a possession granted to the whole human community, which ought by right to be reclaimed for public law and use—we pray—

<header>I. A. COMENIUS: PANSOPHIA <note>original: "I. A. COMENI PAN." Short for Johann Amos Comenius's *Pansophiae Dilucidatio* (The Elucidation of Universal Wisdom).</note></header>

For God, being the author of both His **Works** <note>Creation/Nature</note> and His **Words** <note>Scripture</note>, wishes to be—and can be—recognized and celebrated in both. For although He prepares us for the future life, He nevertheless educates and instructs us for that life through the things He does here; He does not only speak, but He also acts. Therefore, He not only commands us to hear His voice, but He also orders us to gaze upon His **Works**. 

Therefore, so that we may reconcile **Philosophy** with **Theology**—that is, the Works of God with the Words of God, or the Truth imprinted on **Things** with the Truth expressed in **Words**—and thereby subordinate **Reason** to **Faith**, we urge that among Christians, neither **Philosophy** should be taught separately, nor **Theosophy** <note>original: "Theosophiam." Here meaning "divine wisdom" or the study of God, rather than the later 19th-century occult movement.</note> separately, but both together; that is, <term>Pansophia</term> <note>Universal Wisdom: a system of education that seeks to harmonize all human knowledge under a single divine framework.</note>. For this will be, properly speaking, our **All-Wisdom**: *to be wise for the future life, and not to be foolish in the present; to have GOD and the future life in our sights, and yet to feel how His majesty, diffused through all things, surrounds us on every side even now.* <note>original: "sapere ad vitam futuram, & non desipere in præsenti : habere DEVM & vitam futuram in prospectu, & sentire tamen quomodo nos jam nunc undique circumstet per omnia diffusa majestas ejus."</note>

<header>CONTINUATION OF J. A. COMENIUS</header>

[igno]rance, so it may be said: we most gladly profess with Socrates <note>Socrates (c. 470–399 BCE) was famous for his "Socratic irony"—the claim that his only wisdom was knowing he knew nothing.</note> that we know this one thing: that we know nothing. <margin>* Why is it to be built according to the Ideas of God?</margin>
It follows that we must explain why we say this **Temple of Universal Wisdom** <note>Comenius uses the "Temple" as a metaphor for his systematic organization of all knowledge. Just as a temple is a physical dwelling for God, "Universal Wisdom" is an intellectual dwelling for Divine Truth.</note> is to be constructed according to the ideas, standards, and laws of the supreme architect, God Himself. The reason is ready at hand: because in the dimensions of the whole and the number, position, and use of its parts, we follow the pattern <note>original Latin: *exemplar*. This refers to a perfect archetype or blueprint.</note> which the Wisdom of God has delineated for itself. 

First, this was seen with **Moses**, in the raising of the **Tabernacle**; then with **Solomon** in the building of the **Temple**; and finally with **Ezekiel**, in the more glorious restoration of the destroyed Temple. For first, the Lord spoke thus to Moses: *They shall make for me a Sanctuary, so that I may dwell among them, entirely according to the likeness which I shall show you.* And afterwards: *Look and do according to the pattern, which was shown to you on the mountain.* [Exodus 25:9, 40]. Then, God sent to **David** (through **Nathan the Prophet**, as it is believed) the pattern of the Temple and all its parts; David, handing this to Solomon, commanded him not to depart from that form, declaring thus: *All these things came written by the hand of the Lord to me, so that I might understand the whole...* <note>original: *univer-[sa operis]*—all the works/details. ...all these exemplary works. [1 Chron. 28:19] <note>This citation refers to King David receiving the plans for the Temple "in writing from the hand of the Lord."</note>
Finally, He showed to **Ezekiel** the form of the **mystical temple**—that is, the new Church under Christ—with an express command to receive everything attentively and announce it to the House of Israel. [Ezek. 40:4]

**N.B.** <note>Latin: *nota bene*, or "note well."</note> It must be observed, however, that each subsequent form was fuller and more perfect than the one before it. This is not because God makes progress over time or improves His works as He goes—as happens to human architects, whose later thoughts often seem to be (and indeed are) better—but because He wished to prefigure the progress of His Church that would unfold in time. The **Mosaic Tabernacle**, therefore, was only tripartite <note>Divided into three parts.</note>, consisting of the **Outer Court**, the **Sanctuary**, and the **Holy of Holies**, as is clear from Exodus Chapter 40.

**Solomon’s Temple** possessed, before that final and innermost shrine <note>original Latin: *penetrale*</note> (called the **Holy of Holies**), three outer courts: the **Court of the Common People**, the **Court of the Levites**, and the **Court of the Priests**; and finally that Holy of Holies, open only to the High Priest once a year.

# 141 PANSOPHIC CLARIFICATION 141

->141<-

**Solomon’s** <note>The Latin text begins with the fragment "monicum," completing "Salomonicum" from the previous page.</note> Temple lay on Mount Moriah, but it was situated entirely on the level plain of the mountain. In contrast, the outer parts of **Ezekiel’s Temple** were situated on the slope of the mountain, with each inner court elevated several steps above the one preceding it; so that finally the Temple itself—that is, the **Holy of Holies**—situated at the very summit of the mountain, might shine most splendidly in every direction. 

This differing structure of God’s dwellings among men demonstrated the various stages of growth of the Church of God, always moving toward something greater: both in terms of its expansion through peoples and languages, and in terms of the increase of knowledge and science as the ages of the Church progress. 

For just as the World itself has its own ages, so too does the Church: infancy, childhood, manhood, and finally a declining age, old age. And just as old age suffers a decrease in bodily strength, it generally intensifies the powers of the mind. This is due to the temperament shifting toward "dryness" <note>In the medical theory of Comenius's time, a "dry" temperament in old age was believed to settle the mind and make it more reflective.</note>, by which the movements of the soul become calmer and the **animal spirits** <note>term: animal spirits. In 17th-century physiology, these were believed to be subtle fluids that traveled through the nerves to produce sensation and movement.</note> become more stable. 

Since, therefore, it is fitting for the Church of the New Testament—especially in this era when the World is verging toward its old age—to be fully mature in its understanding [1 Cor. 14:20; Ephes. 4:14], we borrow the form for this **Temple of Christian Wisdom** from the outline of the final Temple given to **Ezekiel**:

## CLARIFICATION OF UNIVERSAL WISDOM
<note>original: PANS. DILUCIDATIO.</note>

...destines man for His fellowship and draws him toward it. In this Theater, Man, by contemplating the **archetype** <note>original: *archetypum*; the original divine blueprint or pattern in the mind of God</note> of himself and of the World, shall acknowledge how truly all the works of God reflect God in their own way, and yet how infinitely more sublime all things are in God than whatever good, beautiful, pleasant, and desirable things are found in **Created Beings** <note>original: *Creaturis*; referring to all things created by God, including nature and humanity</note>. <margin>Why the Temple of Wisdom must be dedicated to the Universal Church.</margin>

<header>PANSOPHIC ELUCIDATION. 153 <note>original: *PANS. DILUCIDATIO.*; a shortened title for Comenius's work explaining his system of universal wisdom.</note></header>

to fear or suspect that sacred things will here be confused with profane ones. <note>In this context, "profane" simply means "secular" or "non-religious" knowledge, such as physics or logic.</note> For first, ***“To the pure, all things are pure” (Titus 1:15).*** Nothing defiled the Israelites, nor the structure of the Tabernacle, in the Gold and Silver taken from the impure Egyptians, etc. Secondly, nothing is confused here; rather, remedies are prepared for the confusions with which the minds of men labor. This is achieved through a distinct knowledge of all things that can be known, deserve to be known, and ought to be known—a knowledge that rises by its own steps to its own heights.

Therefore, we first show those most general and well-known things which are clear in themselves to be true by the testimony of common sense <term>sensus communis; in the 17th century, this referred to the internal faculty that unites the data from the five senses</term> itself. Then we bring forward those things which the external Senses see and touch, and which they know they see and touch. Presently, we show those things which are deduced from these by certain Reason; but in such a way that their truth is also traced back to sensory experiments. Finally, we present those things which come from divine Revelation and are grasped by faith alone; but in such a way that, at the same time, Reason and sense are taught to bear witness to God, and to recognize the truth of invisible revealed things through the analogy of visible things. Thus, the one eternal harmony <note>original: *concentus*</note> of the whole eternal Truth, scattered through all things, may be consistent with itself everywhere. ***What confusion is there here, where there is pure harmony?***

But they say that Christ did not teach such things; He handed down only the way of salvation. *Response 1:* Why then do you teach even those lesser things pertaining to life...

<header>THE ENDEAVORS OF J. A. COMENIUS</header>

### CHAPTER HEADINGS
# THE GREAT
## DIDACTIC

*In the Preface of this work, the care of the diligent education of children is seriously commended to the Magistrate <note>The civil authorities or governing officials.</note>, to Parents, and to Teachers, through various reasons and examples. In the work itself, the following topics are treated:*

**Chapter I.** It is proven that Man is the last, the most absolute, and the most excellent of all Creatures.

**Chapter II.** That the ultimate end of Man lies beyond this life.

**Chapter III.** That this life is nothing but a preparation for the eternal life.

**Chapter IV.** That there are three stages of preparation for eternity: (1) To **KNOW** oneself (and all things with oneself), (2) To **RULE** oneself, and (3) To **DIRECT** oneself toward **GOD**.
<note>In the original Latin, these three stages correspond to "Eruditio" (Learning/Instruction), "Mores" (Morals/Conduct), and "Religio" (Religion/Piety).</note>

**Chapter V.** That the seeds of these three things (Learning, Morals, and Religion) are implanted in us by Nature.

**Chapter VI.** That Man, if he is to become a man, must be formed <note>Or "educated/shaped." Comenius believed that human nature is a potential that must be actively developed through teaching.</note>.

**Chapter VII.** That the formation of Man is most conveniently achieved in early childhood; and unless it happens then, it can scarcely be done successfully.

<meta>catchword: Chapter VIII.</meta>

<summary>This page outlines the first seven chapters of the Great Didactic, establishing Comenius’s theological and philosophical premise: that humans are created for eternity and must be "formed" through education in knowledge, virtue, and piety from a young age.</summary>

<keywords>Table of Contents, human nature, purpose of life, preparation for eternity, self-knowledge, self-governance, early childhood education, nature vs. nurture, pedagogical philosophy</keywords>

<page-num>169</page-num>
<header>HEADINGS OF THE GREAT DIDACTIC</header>

**Chapter VIII.** Youth must be educated together, and there is a need for Schools. <note>Comenius argues that while parents are the primary educators, the specialized work of instruction is best handled by collective institutions.</note>

**Chapter IX.** All the youth of both sexes should be committed to Schools. <note>This was a radical proposition in the 17th century; Comenius insisted that girls, like boys, were created in God's image and possessed capable minds.</note>

**Chapter X.** Instruction in Schools must be Universal; that is, in Schools, everyone should be taught all things. <note>This refers to "Pansophy," or the idea that every person should be introduced to the fundamental principles of all areas of knowledge.</note>

**Chapter XI.** Perfect Schools have been lacking until now.

**Chapter XII.** Schools can be reformed for the better.

**Chapter XIII.** The foundation for reforming Schools is a precise order in all things.

**Chapter XIV.** The precise order of the School is to be borrowed from Nature. Therefore:

**Chapter XV.** The foundations for prolonging life <note>original: "vitæ prolongandæ." Comenius believed that physical health and longevity were essential prerequisites for a complete education.</note> are demonstrated from Nature.

**Chapter XVI.** General requirements for teaching and learning; that is, how teaching and learning may be done with **Certainty**, so that a successful result cannot fail to follow.

**Chapter XVII.** Foundations of **Ease** in teaching and learning.

**Chapter XVIII.** Foundations of **Thoroughness** <note>original: "Soliditatis." This implies a deep, lasting foundation of knowledge rather than rote memorization.</note> in teaching and learning.

**Chapter XIX.** Foundations of Concise **Speed** in teaching. Where, among other things, it is shown how a single Teacher can be sufficient for any number of pupils. <note>Comenius here introduces the concept of group instruction and the use of monitors to manage large classes.</note>

**Chapter XX.**

<summary>This page outlines the structural and methodological chapters of the Great Didactic, advocating for universal co-education and a teaching system based on the certain laws of Nature. It introduces Comenius’s "triad" of effective instruction: Certainty, Ease, and Thoroughness.</summary>

## *Most Distinguished* LORDS,

That the undertaking of those who labor to bring the long, winding, and harsh path of childhood studies <note>original: "puerilium studiorum." Comenius refers to the standard curriculum of the 17th century, which he famously criticized for being overly difficult and tedious for children.</note> back to brevity, ease, and enjoyment by some art of method <note>original: "methodi." Here used in the sense of a systematic or scientific approach to teaching.</note> is praiseworthy; no one among all those who wish for human affairs to be as well-provided for as possible would deny it.

For because human life <note>original: "Vita hominum"</note> is to be spent not in the act of learning, but in acting and doing: and truly only he is able to act and do who has learned: and only he has truly learned who has been correctly taught: it is clear that those who work with some happy success toward the goal that both teachers <note>original: "docentibus"</note> and learners <note>original: "discentibus"</note>

<header>BY J. A. COMENIUS</header>

## CONCERNING
# THE STUDY OF THE LATIN LANGUAGE
### *To be perfectly established*
#### A Didactic Dissertation.

Pliny is our authority <note>Pliny the Elder, in his *Natural History*, recorded many anecdotes about ancient Greek artists.</note> that Apelles, the painter, was accustomed to display his finished works in a gallery, and then hide behind the painting to overhear the judgments passed upon them. He did this not so much to tickle his own vanity with whatever praise he might hear, but rather so that he might correct any faults noticed by the public, who are often curious censors of things.

2. *Since any person attempting a work of art is permitted to follow this example—using public criticism for the advancement of their craft—I believed it was also permitted for me to do the same regarding a matter of public utility I recently devised and completed. I refer to that new, more concise method of teaching languages which (following the example of others who attempted the same before us) happened to be called the* Gate of Languages. <note>original: "Linguarum Ianuam." This refers to Comenius's most famous work, *Janua linguarum reserata* (1631), which revolutionized language learning by teaching words through descriptions of the world.</note>

3. *Accordingly, I brought my little work into the light, and for six whole years I remained in hiding, exploring the various judgments of different people. These opinions generally fell into three distinct categories.*

4. *For some, and indeed the majority, [found] the invention*

<meta>catchword: then</meta>

<summary>In this opening to his dissertation, Comenius uses the anecdote of the Greek painter Apelles to explain why he spent six years observing public reaction to his revolutionary textbook, the Gate of Languages. He introduces his intent to categorize and address the feedback he received to further improve the teaching of Latin.</summary>

--- Page 206 ---
<meta>This page continues Comenius’s reflection on the reception of his "Gate of Languages" (Janua Linguarum). He categorizes the public response into three groups: enthusiastic adopters, critics who saw the work as unfinished, and skeptics who doubted its practical efficiency in preparing students for classical literature.</meta>

<page-num>181</page-num>
<header>CONCERNING THE STUDY OF THE LANGUAGE, etc.</header>

...then praised it, judging this method of teaching and learning languages to be such that no better could be found: for it was, they said, adapted to the pattern of Things themselves. <note>This refers to Comenius's "realist" educational philosophy, where words are learned through the study of the physical objects and concepts they represent (the "pattern of things") rather than through abstract grammar.</note>

5. As a result, the work was not only graced with translations into various languages and printed in many different places, but it was also widely adopted in schools—not just the common elementary ones, but the most illustrious academies as well.

*6. Yet one or two individuals were found who began to point out defects and to warn that the work should not be so universally applauded. They argued that the work was merely a beginning, not a finished product, and that the common welfare of literature demanded it be perfected and corrected.*

*7. Finally, there were those who could bring themselves neither to praise nor to blame the work. They only whispered their doubts that they could not see how this little book could fulfill its promised purpose: namely, that by its benefit, a beginner in Latin* <note>original: "Latinitatis tyro"</note> *might be more easily, pleasantly, and quickly introduced to the reading of classical authors.*

8. This caused some to receive the work with more hesitation. They were, it seems, waiting for either a more polished work better suited to the objective, or at least for clearer instructions on the true and proper use of this little volume. I have received such advice from many places, even from across the sea. <note>Comenius had a significant following in England and the Netherlands; "across the sea" likely refers to his English correspondents like Samuel Hartlib.</note>

9. What then is my response to all of this? First, I am content that whatever useful discovery the Giver of all things <note>A reference to God.</note> has granted me should become common property; indeed, I rejoice that it has done so.

<meta>catchword: 10 Not</meta>

10. For even *Bezalel* and *Oholiab* <note>Biblical craftsmen chosen by God to build the Tabernacle (Exodus 31).</note> cannot have the wisdom to devise whatever can be skillfully fashioned (*Exodus* 31, v. 2) except by the gift of Him who makes the mute and the deaf, the seeing and the blind (*Ibid.* 4:11).

11. And because our Savior said: *I have come to bring fire to the earth, and how I wish it were already kindled!* (*Luke* 12:49), it is right for all servants of Christ to imitate this warmth of charity, so that whatever sparks of light the Father of Lights <note>original: "luminum Pater"; a reference to God as the source of all intellectual and spiritual enlightenment.</note> has granted to be struck out, they may desire and rejoice to see them grow into a flame.

12. As for those who find something to criticize, their work is also welcome, provided they do what they do not out of envy, but out of love for public progress; (though one can be polished even by the tooth of a *Zoilus* <note>A term for a harsh, nitpicking critic, named after a Greek grammarian famous for his biting critiques of Homer.</note> if one has the spirit to seize opportunities for improvement from any source). Thus, whatever faults or defects they notice, they may go about correcting and completing them: whether by advising the Author, or those who assist <note>original: "succentùriant"; literally those who fill the ranks or act as substitutes/assistants.</note> him, or by composing something more elaborate themselves, to which these works of ours ought rightly and deservedly to give way.

13. Whosoever shall have done this, let him believe that I will not waste a single word in defense of my own works: I will rather praise the author of a better invention; and I will congratulate the progress of the age; and the goodness of GOD, which thus gradually [communicates] His gifts to the common...

...communicates to mortals, I will celebrate; and finally, I myself will be a more earnest encourager for everyone to follow (as far as it shall lie in me) those things which shall prove to be of more certain use.

14 In the meantime, however, while such a thing is being prepared, I am pleased to gratify those who are hesitating over the use of our works, by demonstrating more clearly that which they admit they do not sufficiently see.

15 To do this conveniently, it will be necessary to review the reasoning of our entire proposal more fully: not only in what has already been done (the building of that ***GATEWAY*** <note>original: "IANVA"; referring to Comenius's famous textbook *Janua linguarum reserata* (The Door of Languages Unlocked).</note> of the Latin Language, and the ***VESTIBULE*** <note>original: "VESTIBVLO"; referring to the *Vestibulum*, his introductory primer that preceded the *Janua*.</note> constructed before it) but also what else can—and indeed should—be done, as time has taught us, and as the didactic light <note>The "didactic light" refers to the art and theory of teaching, which Comenius believed was becoming clearer and more refined through practice.</note> itself has now been rendered more increased and purified.

16. I shall speak, therefore, distinctly. First, *Concerning the scope and end of our endeavors*. Second, *Concerning the Means toward this end*. Finally, *Concerning the manner or reasoning of the Means and the Method of dispensing the given means in such a way that there can be no straying from the goal*.

17. The *Goal* of this Didactic inquiry is: *that the study of the Latin Language (which, after it ceased to be the property of a single nation, has become the common messenger <note>original: "Mercurius"; Mercury was the Roman messenger god. Comenius means Latin is the shared language for communication across Europe.</note> of European nations, and, being enclosed in Schools, has become the bond of the learned and the vehicle of learning) may be rendered more expeditious: that is, easier, faster, and more fruitful than it has been hitherto*.

<meta>catchword: 18 Nem-</meta>

<summary>Comenius introduces his plan to refine Latin instruction by reviewing his previous works and outlining a new, three-part method focused on goals, means, and technique. He defines Latin as the essential shared "vehicle of learning" for all of Europe.</summary>

<header>J. A. COMENIUS</header>

18. To be sure, this is done so that one does not arrive at the mastery of this language with such great trouble, disgust, and nausea for both teachers and students; nor with such a massive waste of years and life; nor, finally, with such a delay and loss of the **knowledge of real things** <note>original: "scientiarum realium"; this refers to Comenius's belief that students should learn about the physical world and practical subjects alongside grammar.</note>, as is currently the case. Instead, the Christian Youth should be led quickly and safely, easily and pleasantly, into the works of the best authors, and through their help, into the knowledge of both divine and human affairs.

19. For we do not undertake to train ***parrots*** <note>original: "Psittacos"</note>, for whom it would be enough to rattle off sounds without any meaning behind them. Rather, we are training a ***rational creature, a master of things, a spectator, witness, and interpreter of the wisdom of God spread through all creation***. To stretch this creature out with ***Words*** while not filling them with ***Things*** <note>original: "Rebus"; Comenius uses "Things" to mean the actual objects or concepts that words represent.</note> is to wander away from the goal of the divine plan. It diminishes the majesty of the human being and shamefully deceives the mind by instilling mere images and shadows instead of the knowledge of ***Reality***.

20. Therefore, our aim must be this: that the ***study of languages (especially Latin) should focus on Things***, so that it results not in empty chatter, but in ***wise Eloquence***.

21. We shall achieve this by no other means than by ensuring that words are always taught in connection with the things they represent, so that by one and the same effort, the ***Mind and the Tongue*** are always educated together.

22. ***Words without Things*** are shells without a kernel, a scabbard without a sword, a shadow without a body, and a heart without a soul.

<summary>Comenius argues that language instruction must be tied to the study of the physical world, asserting that learning words without understanding the "things" they represent is a waste of human potential and a failure of education.</summary>

23. Accordingly, anyone who measures learning by a mere abundance of words does nothing but talk whenever he speaks—that is to say, he merely chatters.

24. Wisdom consists of ***Things***, not ***Words***; a wise and truly educated person thinks about things, speaks of things, and acts upon things.

25. It follows from this that we must ***avoid a divorce of Words from Things***. Books that deal only with vocabulary and consume the time of the young are useless for this sacred purpose. By this, understand the common ***Vocabularies***: ***Dictionaries***, ***Nomenclators*** <note>original: "Nomenclatores"; a type of dictionary organized by subject matter rather than alphabetically.</note>, ***Collections of Expressions*** <note>original: "Sylvas"; literally "woods" or "forests," used in this period to refer to unorganized collections of raw literary materials or miscellanies.</note>, ***Phrasebooks***, and those various, laborious, and abstract ***speculations*** and ***commentaries*** produced by ***Grammarians***.

26. ***Things should be learned from the things themselves***; but speech about things should be learned from suitable ***Authors*** who have described those things. From these authors—through a refined summary and the most solid practice—we can simultaneously acquire both a knowledge of things and the ability to discuss those things wisely, eloquently, and readily. There is no other way.

27. Let this then remain a fixed principle: if the ***Latin Language is to be a practical tool for acquiring practical learning, it must be learned from Authors***. Consequently, the explanation of good authors is the ***entirety of the matter*** <note>original: "τὸ πᾶν" (to pan); a Greek phrase meaning "the all" or "the whole thing." Comenius is saying that studying primary texts is the most important part of education.</note> for our schools.

28. Every effort must therefore be made to select the very best authors who have treated subjects necessary for education, and to present them through a remarkably easy method...

<page-num>186</page-num>
<header>-> I. A. COMENIUS <-</header>

...to be taught to be converted into the very essence <note>original: "succum & sanguinem"; literally "juice and blood." This is a physiological metaphor for deep internalization, suggesting knowledge should become part of one’s very being.</note> of the mind. In this way, when young people leave school, they will be found ready and capable in mind, hand, and tongue alike—prepared both to judge matters wisely and to begin their station in life successfully.

29. Indeed, this is and ought to be the ***true goal of schools: to prepare us for life and to make every person equal to the duties of their calling.*** This cannot be achieved in any other way than by using the thoughts, observations, and discoveries of others to awaken our own spirit and shape our intellect, so that we may think, speak, and act upon all the best things in a similar fashion (for every person born also fosters within themselves their own divine sparks).

30. For just as light is kindled by light, and the power of a magnet is drawn out by the proximity of iron, so too are minds excited by the friction <note>original: "affrictu"; the rubbing together or contact of two things.</note> of other minds, thereby putting forth their own strength.

31. Let it remain fixed, therefore, that ***the Latin language is not to be taught or learned except through Things and alongside Things***—namely, from authors who deal with Reality <note>original: "Res"; Comenius uses this term to mean the physical world and factual subjects as opposed to abstract grammar.</note>.

32. But in truth, because whatever is done is done step-by-step (as the examples of Nature and Art <note>original: "Artis"; in this context, "Art" refers to human skill, industry, or systematic methods.</note> show), and therefore whatever is learned ***can only be learned step-by-step***, it is evident that a beginner <note>original: "tyronem"; a novice or recruit.</note> in Latin cannot be thrust into that vast sea of authors...

33. Otherwise, he will either be dashed against the rocks of difficulties (which he has not yet learned to overcome), or he will be swallowed by the waves of a variety that is still unfamiliar and gaping like an abyss.

34. Therefore, let him learn to play in a small boat on a lake before he commits himself to the open sea.

35. Let the little boy be permitted to ride first on a long reed <note>original: "arundine longa"; a classical reference to a child's hobby-horse or toy.</note>, before he mounts caparisoned steeds that bite at their bits <note>original: "sonipedes"; literally "noisy-footed ones," a poetic Latin term for spirited horses.</note>.

36. Let the infant learn to babble before speaking; and the boy to speak, before he practices oratory <note>original: "dicere"; Comenius distinguishes here between *loqui* (basic communication) and *dicere* (formal, rhetorical speech or "oratory").</note>. For even Cicero (otherwise such a great master of the art of teaching) denies that he can teach a man how to deliver an oration if that man does not first know how to speak.

37. And how could it be otherwise? Nothing goes upward except step by step <note>original: "gradatim".</note>.

38. From the seed or kernel of a plant <note>original: "Plantæ"</note>, nothing can be born at first except a small shoot <note>original: "Virga"</note>. From the shoot, by slow growth, comes a young tree <note>original: "Arbuscula"</note>, and from this, a full tree.

39. And in human life, no one attains a man’s years, stature, or strength, unless he was first an embryo <note>original: "embryon"</note>, an infant, a boy, and a youth.

40. Nor do buildings rise in any other way than this: in the first place, a rough but solid foundation is laid; upon this, the walls are then erected; to the walls are added the beams or...

<meta>catchword: forni- (likely "fornicibus," referring to arches or vaults)</meta>

<summary>Comenius argues that education must follow a natural progression, moving from simple foundations to complex skills just as a plant grows from a seed or a child matures into a man. He emphasizes that one cannot master formal oratory or difficult Latin texts without first mastering basic speech and preparatory exercises.</summary>

...the vaulting of the arches; and in the final place, all those things are protected by a roof.

41. Even one who climbs to the summit of a tower, a cliff, or some mountain can only ascend by rising step by step <note>original: "gradatim"</note>: thus *Nature* and *Art* *never make a leap, and never allow one.* <note>This is a fundamental principle for Comenius: learning should be a smooth, continuous slope rather than a series of steep hurdles.</note>

42. It becomes clear from this that the study of the *Latin Language* should not be begun from whole and complete works—namely, the *Authors*—but from certain rudiments and beginner exercises <note>original: "tyrociniis"; literally the training of a recruit or apprentice.</note> which may rightly predispose and prepare the minds for those greater things.

43. But it is also clear that these *Preparatory Steps* cannot be of only one kind: because things that are very distant can hardly be joined together by the intervention of a single thing.

44. Certainly, while a tall building is being erected, the workers have need of several different stories <note>original: "contignationibus"; referring to the structural levels or floor-framing of a building.</note> before they place the summit upon it.

45. And just as there are certain levels or ages of a person's *Life*, clearly distinct: so in the cultivation of Minds and Language, it is necessary to establish certain levels, and to coordinate them so that one rises from the other.

46. For just as the dawn is not sent before the day so that it may remain dawn, but so that by gradually brightening it may change darkness into light, and night into day; and a Painter does not draw the first outlines for the purpose [of leaving them as they are]...

50. The third, even higher step will teach the student how to express one and the same thing—and the concept of that thing—in various ways, painting it, as it were, in different colors <note>original: "coloribus variis variè pingere." Comenius uses the metaphor of painting to describe "copia," or the ability to rephrase and embellish a thought without losing its core meaning.</note>.

51. Finally, the fourth and supreme step will be to have learned how speech should not merely spread itself out and become diluted in excess <note>original: "luxuriem"; referring to flowery or over-embellished rhetoric that lacks substance.</note>; but rather, by making an accurate *selection of words and sentences*, it should know how to contract itself and solidify around *the Things* being discussed. In this way, it may powerfully impress itself, and the **THINGS** themselves, upon the mind.

52. This is the very peak of Eloquence: to depict every subject to the life in its own natural colors, rather than with false or feigned ones, and thereby to be able to captivate minds under the empire of the Truth. From this comes that saying of Solomon:
> *The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails fixed deep.* Ecclesiastes 12:11.

53. Thus, there will be four distinct levels, as if they were **Schools or Classes of Latinity**: the first for *stammering* <note>original: "balbutie"; the rudimentary first attempts at speech.</note>, the second for *ordinary speech*, the third for *fluency*, and the fourth for acquiring Latin *Eloquence*.

54. To each of these levels, its own portions and goals must be assigned—where it should begin and how far it should progress—and a certain and refined method must be described, so that within the given time, the goal is necessarily reached by all.

55. Let these goals, as well as the means and the method of applying those means, be distinct and specific to each level; yet they should be harmoniously...

56. For we want this to be common to all those classes: that they be equipped proportionately with the same aids. Specifically, with books that present everything to be known step-by-step, always with greater fullness, and with almost identical types of exercises to be worked through.

57. We have given the name **THE VESTIBULE** <note>original: "VESTIBULI"; referring to the entrance court or porch of a house.</note> to the book for the First Class; **THE DOORWAY** <note>original: "JANUAE"</note> for the Second; **THE PALACE** <note>original: "PALATII"</note> for the Third; and **THE TREASURY** <note>original: "THESAURI"</note> of Latinity for the Fourth.

58. It is appropriate for the structure of each of these to be tripartite <note>divided into three parts.</note>.

59. The first and fundamental part should contain *the material essence or the measure of things* and *Words* assigned to that Class; *that is, the Text or the Author*. The second part should explain *the formal essence, or the measure* and *director of words—that is, the precepts* and *Rules* <note>Comenius refers to grammar and syntax rules here.</note>, by which the logic of the constructed speech in the preceding Author is revealed, for an easier and truer understanding of it. Finally, an Index of *contents* should be added, which serves as a *Repository* <note>original: "Repertorium"; a finding aid or inventory.</note> for everything preceding, aiding in their rapid use and practice.

60. The first reason for this method is that we teach more gently, better, and more effectively through examples than through precepts. (*For Examples form the understanding through the senses, which is natural; Precepts form the senses through the understanding, which is contrary to nature.*) Therefore, *Actual Speech* <note>original: "Oratio facta"; literally "made speech," referring to complete, meaningful sentences or texts rather than abstract grammar rules.</note> should come first; and then finally *the Precepts on how it was made*,

NB. I say *illustrations*: for such things ought to be of the kind that bring light to this study, not darkness; they should be a help to it, not a hindrance; nor should they offer a new struggle to young minds, heavier than the text itself, but rather they should resolve the struggle brought on by the words.

61. Next, because not all things can be impressed upon the memory all at once so that they can be promptly retrieved for use, the weakness [of memory] must be aided by an attached *Inventory, so that whatever needs to be retrieved is ready at hand.*

62. For with the help of these, we will reach the goal beautifully: nor is there any need for the book to be increased by any useless additions—which would be a burden to the book's size, a labor for minds, and a difficulty for the purses of the poor to afford.

...expressed with a simple and natural appearance.

64. Therefore, nothing metaphorical, figurative, unusual, or too specialized should be mixed in here. For we are currently focused on something else: opening the **Doorway** <note>original: "Ianua"; referring to Comenius's famous textbook *Janua linguarum reserata* (The Doorway of Languages Unlocked), which revolutionized language learning by teaching words through descriptions of the world.</note>, so that in due time and place, things may be more distinctly understood and spoken. Some people, unmindful or careless of this plan, have burdened this "Doorway" with useless additions; I do not know what they were trying to stuff in here, but it certainly causes delay and disgust for the learners. This must be avoided from now on.

65. Rather, we must strive to have a true **DOORWAY OF THINGS** (as I promised in its first preface), well-fastened with the solid posts of the **things** themselves; easily opened by the smooth hinges of a **DICTIONARY** <note>original: "Lexicon"</note>; and ready to be unlocked by the immediate key of **GRAMMAR**. That is: we should add grammatical rules and that promised dictionary to the text of the *Doorway*, so that whatever the needs of this level require may be found all in one place.

66. Specifically, *grammatical rules must be established that are very brief and clear, showing most plainly the true, genuine, and simple method of writing, pronouncing, forming, and constructing the Latin language.* Yet, these rules should not touch upon anything unusual, figurative, or highly irregular <note>original: "anomalum"</note>. For the rules must be illustrated with examples taken solely from the text of the **DOORWAY** (where nothing so irregular or figurative is included).

72. Namely, so that candidates of Latinity <note>Those aspiring to master the Latin language</note> may learn, in the **PALACE** first, the *Epistolary style*: a "running" style that is somewhat more casual and informal, yet pure and fluid. Second, they learn the *Historical style*, rising a little higher in tone and more carefully crafted. Third, the *Oratory style*, which is fully precise, weighty, and sublime. Finally, the *Poetic style*, bound by meter: both the simpler and more level kind (such as is found in *Elegiac* verse) and the grand and stately kind (such as is found in *Heroic*, *Lyric*, and *Tragic* poems).

73. *All of these, however, should be practiced not with our own words and sentences, but with those of the classical authors.*

74. Thus, led slowly step-by-step through the railings <note>An image of a guided path or a child's walking frame, suggesting the student is supported as they learn to "walk" in the language</note>, they will more easily learn both to distinguish the character of a style and to imitate it distinctly and consistently.

75. **THE EPISTOLARY PALACE** should therefore contain one hundred letters, each corresponding to the individual headings of the **DOORWAY** <note>The *Janua*, Comenius's previous textbook level</note>: through these letters should be distributed whatever elegant formulas exist for greeting, responding to greetings, narrating, requesting, giving thanks, etc., so that the entire art of letter-writing is presented here: *with the briefest instructions on the art of writing letters added.*

76. **THE HISTORICAL PALACE** should contain more notable narratives on those same subjects, with the Authors and the locations from which each was taken <note>original: "desumptum"</note> noted in the margin <margin>assigned at the margin to the Authors and places</margin>—

<header>JAN AMOS COMENIUS</header>

...drawn from citations <note>original: "allegationibus"</note>.

77. And there are four reasons that persuade us that these *Discourses on Things* should be conceived in a dialogic form.

78. First, nothing is more natural to a human being than conversation: by which one can be led anywhere, gradually and almost imperceptibly. Therefore, these materials can be more easily adapted to youthful minds, so they do not imagine this treatment of serious matters to be either impossible or too arduous and difficult.

79. Second, Dialogues excite, animate, and foster attention. This is due to the variety of questions and answers, and their various occasions and forms, with delightful things being interspersed from time to time. The minds of students are therefore to be enticed <note>original: "Ineſcandi," literally "to be baited" as with a hook</note> with these attractions, so that they may progress through these tasks without boredom.

80. Third, Dialogues serve both to create a firmer impression of *Things* on the memory and to make repetition easier (even among the pupils themselves in private). For just as we more easily remember an event in which we ourselves participated than one we only heard about, so those things which are learned by way of a Play <note>original: "Comœdiæ"</note> or Dialogue stick more tenaciously in the minds of learners—since here we seem to ourselves not so much to hear things as to see, speak, and act them out ourselves—compared to those things which are absorbed by bare recitation.

81. Finally, because the greater [part] of our life...

<summary>Comenius argues that educational texts should be written as dialogues because conversation is natural to humans, keeps children's attention, and helps them remember lessons by "acting them out" rather than just listening.</summary>

part of our life consists of conversation, youth are guided toward it in an elegant and concise way if they become accustomed not only to understanding <term>Things</term> <note>original: "Res" — a central concept for Comenius, referring to the objective study of the world alongside its vocabulary</note>, but also to discussing them with ease.

82. *We desire, therefore, that the entire skill of learnedly conversing and of discoursing about things be handed down here: with opportunities and formulas gathered from every source for questioning, answering, introducing oneself <note>original: "insinuandi se," often meaning to enter a conversation or argument skillfully</note>, explaining matters, pressing a point, making exceptions, wandering from the subject, returning to the purpose, and so on.*

Finally, they will here prepare for themselves a notable supply of the most elegant maxims, which are of very frequent use throughout all* **Learning** <note>original: "Eruditionem" — referring to the whole scope of a scholar's education</note>.

The index of contents for this fourth section, the **PALACE**, will be, in my judgment, a **PHRASEOLOGICAL DICTIONARY** <note>original: "LEXICON PHRASEOLOGICVM"</note>: whether that be from the Vernacular to Latin <note>original: "Vernaculo-Latinum" — translating from the student's native tongue into Latin</note>, or from Latin to Latin. Suppose it is one in which the simple names of things (arranged in alphabetical order) are exchanged for more elegant expressions: that is, let it be shown how the proper names of things are to be expressed through synonyms, periphrasis <note>the use of indirect or circuitous speech</note>, tropes <note>metaphorical or figurative language</note>, and in altogether varied and ornate ways. In this, the lowlier forms should always be put first, such as those pertaining to an epistolary <note>letter-writing</note> or historical style; then the more sublime oratorical phrases; and finally the poetic ones: with the specific locations in the **Palace** assigned where they occur, if indeed they occur there.

89. To this end, the same method can be observed in the construction of the **PALACE** as was used in the **VESTIBULE** and the **GATE** <note>The "Vestibulum" and "Janua" were Comenius’s introductory and intermediate textbooks</note>: namely, that the text of the speech be divided into segments—for example, **Periods** <note>rhetorical units or full sentences</note>—which should be marked with continuous numbering through the various chapters from the beginning of the book to the end; this is, of course, for the convenience of citation. This is the same way I see the most learned **Master Baldovius** <note>Johannes Baldovius (1604–1662), a German scholar of Hebrew</note> has done in his *Marrow of Hebrew Grammar*.

90. So that it may be more clearly apparent what kind of Latin-to-Latin Dictionary I desire, I shall set down as an example how the variety and elegance of the verb **I DOUBT** <note>original: "DVBITO"</note> ought to be expressed step by step.

I DOUBT. <note>original: "D V B I T O"</note> *I am stuck. I hesitate. I am in doubt. I waver. I am uncertain what I should do. It is uncertain to me. I am at a crossroads. It is not clear to me. I am in suspense of mind. I hang uncertain. I hold my reasons in suspense. I call into question. I hold it as a great question whether, etc. This matter pulls me in different directions. I am much more uncertain than I was a moment ago. Poetically: I am doubtful.* Virgil: *I am carried along in doubt.* Ovid: *This renders me doubtful.* Plautus: *This makes my mind uncertain.*

91. And such would be the **PALACE** <note>the third "class" or level in Comenius's system, focused on elegant phrasing and style</note> of the third grade of Latin study.

92. Finally, there will follow the **TREASURY** <note>original: "THESAVRVS"</note> of Latinity itself, the physical material <note>original: "τὸ materiale" — Comenius uses a Greek article with a Latinized word to mean "the raw substance"</note> of which will be the Latin Authors themselves, who explain the whole variety of both things and language: *Natural Scientists, Geographers, Moralists, Physicians,* **POLITICAL THINKERS**, *Theologians, Historians, Orators, Poets, etc.* These include both ancient and modern writers, those already born or yet to be born—whoever brings, or will bring, something remarkably useful, and who employs a polished and pure style of speaking.

93. For the logic of the method we have begun demands that all kinds of authors not only be admitted here, but actively summoned.

94. We have indeed established broad boundaries for this study: the total fullness of both Things and Words—that is, of Wisdom and Eloquence—in as much quantity as is possible. It is therefore necessary that the means [of study] correspond to this end in their own capacity.

96. However, these authors will not provide such completion if we only admit **Historians** along with **Orators** and **Poets** (as has almost been the custom in schools until now). 97. ...for it <note>The "Treasury" or the final stage of the educational method mentioned on the previous page.</note> sets forth **Eloquence**; but this can in no way be possessed without a full **knowledge of Things** <note>original: "Rerum cognitione"</note>. It is clear, therefore, that those aspiring to full Eloquence must traverse the entire circle of Things.

99. For from that which is whole and perfect, nothing can be excluded. Indeed, how foolish is it to wish to speak eloquently about something you do not understand?

100. Nor can **metaphors, adages, maxims** <note>original: "gnomæ"</note>, **apophthegms** <note>Pithy sayings or remarks.</note>, **hieroglyphs** <note>Symbolic images or emblems used in Renaissance rhetoric to convey moral truths.</note>, or various **allusions** (in each of which a great force of Eloquence resides) be truly understood, or properly applied, or sharply grasped, without a proper prior knowledge of the things from which they are derived.

101. These are derived from things **natural, artificial, mathematical, logical,** etc., and from the events that have occurred surrounding them. From where can you learn these better than from their own **Authors**?

102. If anyone thinks that a knowledge of things, as far as is sufficient, can be drawn from "commonplace books" <note>Books where students recorded useful quotes and ideas under general headings for later use.</note> (such as ***Lang’s Polyanthea*** <note>original: "Polyanthea Langii"—referring to Joseph Lang’s famous 17th-century encyclopedia of quotations and examples.</note> and the like), indeed, they have given little thought to where these plans of ours lead! We seek here a **solid** and **mature** <note>original: "virilem", literally "manly."</note> knowledge of Things, coherent within itself, and the power to interpret those Things; not that childish, fragmented, mangled, confused, and blunt sort.

107. It is certainly better to use **Things themselves** than fragments of things; to harvest crops rather than to glean the leftovers; to gather from flowering gardens rather than to collect plucked and scattered blossoms, which are mostly withered and drained of life.

( 3. ) From this, the *City of Olympia* received its name, in which was the Temple of that very Jupiter. And here, in honor of Jupiter, they had established equestrian games or contests of Heroes. ( 4. ) These events, called *Olympia*, were to be repeated at the end of every fourth year, or the start of every fifth. Therefore, from this: ( 5. ) *Olympiad* was the name given to that four-year span, adopted as an epoch for counting the successions of Kings and the deeds of the Greeks: taking its beginning, of course, from the time of the first founder of the Olympiads, Iphitus, in the year of the World 3174 <note>The "Year of the World" (Anno Mundi) is a chronological system dating from the biblical creation. 3174 AM corresponds roughly to 776 BCE.</note>. ->J. A. COMENIUS,<-

Nothing should be left to the boys except to understand and experience that School is not called **Play** <term>Latin: Ludus, which in Roman times meant both "school" and "game" or "play"</term> through irony <term>Latin: antiphrasis, a rhetorical device of using a word to mean its opposite</term>, but that it truly is so.

### General warnings for teachers.

151. *The teacher should not teach as much as he himself is able to teach, but as much as the learner is able to grasp.* For I cannot pour into a vessel as much liquid as I wish, but only as much as the vessel holds; and I cannot pour it all at once based on its internal capacity, but must drip it in as the narrowness of the opening permits. And when I desire to lift something lying on the ground with my hand, I must necessarily stoop down; the object itself cannot raise itself to my hand. Therefore, the Teacher should clearly descend to the level of the student in all things: let him be the active participant, and the Student the passive one. A tablet can paint nothing on itself, but the Painter can; the tablet performs its part well enough if it remains still and receives the pigments skillfully. From which another point follows: namely that:

152. *Whatever difficulties and troubles school studies bring, the Teachers should bear them on their own shoulders: leaving nothing for the Students except the eagerness and ease of imitation.* Indeed, they should act in the way Nurses are accustomed to, offering their little infants only food that has been pre-chewed <note>A common early modern metaphor for making complex information digestible for children.</note>, so that nothing remains for the children but easy digestion.

153. *Whatever (therefore) from the Students is [wanted/required]...*

-># DE L. LINGUÆ STUDIO &c.<-
->### ON THE STUDY OF THE LATIN LANGUAGE, etc.<-

...they wish to be known, they should show it to them with the greatest possible clarity <term>Latin: perspicuitas</term>, and demonstrate it to the eye as if depicted in vivid colors; so that the student cannot fail to see both the thing itself and the manner of the thing. In this way, they cannot help but rejoice in the new light, and always extend their appetite for further things.

154. *Whatever they wish to be done by the Students, they themselves should show the way by doing it.* For it is most natural that everyone says to their leader (even if silently), "Go before me, I will follow": because it is easy to follow one who goes ahead; but to be pushed forward without a pre-designated path is difficult.

155. *Therefore, nothing should ever seem so easy that the Teacher does not labor to make it even more clear and even easier to imitate by various means.* For it is not as easy for the learner as it is for the one who already knows. And even if it were, the mind that is not yet sufficiently strengthened does not trust itself as to whether it correctly conceives or forms what it has been ordered; but when it sees its leader going before it by repeating the task so many times, it follows with spirit. (Moreover, it is very beneficial in every work for fear <note>original: "trepidationem," suggesting a trembling anxiety or hesitation</note> to be absent.) And this will truly be **to lead children** <note>original Greek: παιδαγωγεῖν (*paidagogein*), the root of the word "pedagogy"</note>: to lead the little ones by the hand <term>Latin: manuducere</term> as gently as possible.

156. *Students should never be overwhelmed by the mass of things to be learned; otherwise, they will carry away nothing except nausea and an indigestion of the mind.* For just as it is not those who [swallow] <meta>Catchword: vorant</meta> many things...

## General advice for instructors.

151. A teacher should not teach as much as he himself is able to teach, but as much as the learner is able to grasp. For I cannot pour into a vessel as much liquid as I want, but only as much as the vessel can hold; nor should I pour it all at once according to its internal capacity, but rather drip it in as the narrowness of the opening allows. And when I wish to lift something lying on the ground with my hand, I must lower myself; for that object cannot raise itself to my hand. Therefore, the Instructor should completely descend to the level of the student in all things: and let him be the active participant, while the Student is the passive one. A tablet can paint nothing on itself, but the Painter does; the tablet does enough if it remains still and receives the pigments skillfully. From which another point follows: namely that—

152. *Whatever difficulties and troubles school studies bring, the Instructors should bear them on their own shoulders; leaving to the Students nothing but the eagerness and ease of imitation. Specifically, in the same way that Nurses are accustomed to do, offering their little infants nothing but pre-chewed food <note>original: "præmansos... cibos," a metaphor for breaking down complex information into easily digestible parts</note>, so that only a pleasant digestion remains for them.*

153. *Whatever (therefore) they wish—*
