Thus, they will inevitably rejoice in this new light and always extend their appetite toward further things.*

154. *Whatever teachers wish to be done by their Disciples, they should first show the way by doing it themselves. For it is most natural for anyone to say to their leader (even silently): "Go before me, and I will follow." It is easy to follow someone leading the way; however, being pushed forward without a marked path is hard.*

155. *Therefore, nothing should ever seem so easy that the Instructor does not labor to make it even more clear and easier to imitate in various ways. For a thing is not as easy for the learner as it is for the one who already knows it. And even if it were, a mind not yet fully confident does not trust itself to know whether it is correctly conceiving or forming what it has been ordered to do. But when the student sees their leader going before them, repeating the task so many times, they follow with courage. (Indeed, it is very beneficial for fear <note>original: trepidationem</note> to be absent from every task.) And this will truly be <term>pedagogy <note>original: παιδαγωγείν (paidagōgein); the Greek root meaning "to lead a child."</note></term>: to lead the little ones by the hand as gently as possible.*

156. *Students should never be overwhelmed by a massive weight of things to be learned; otherwise, they will bring away nothing but nausea and a "rawness" of the mind <note>original: ingenii cruditatem; a metaphor comparing an overworked brain to a stomach that cannot digest raw food.</note>. For just as it is not the person who [eats] many things...*

[...those who] swallow <note>original: [vo]rant; completing the word from the previous page</note> are healthier than those who eat only as much as they can digest: so it is not those who read, hear, and commit much to memory who become learned, but those who properly imbibe, digest, and process what they read, hear, and memorize through the understanding, and readily produce it for every use.

157. *Three things must always be formed in the student: the **Mind**, the **Hand**, and the **Tongue**.* The **Mind**, so that they understand the matter being learned; the **Hand**, so that they learn to express in writing what they understand; the **Tongue**, so that they may readily speak out what they understand and know.

158. *These proceed by steps: understanding something is easiest; imitating it with the hand is more difficult; and the most difficult of all—yet closest to perfection—is to express it with the tongue.* For what is done by the hand allows for delay, admitting deliberation and assistance if they are at hand. The works of the tongue, however, are entirely extemporaneous <note>done in the moment without preparation</note> and require a certain established <term>habit <note>original: habitum; in this context, it refers to a settled disposition or fluent skill</note></term>.

159. Thus, it is possible to understand the Latin language (at any level indicated in § 47) before one can either write or speak it. And when the <term>practice <note>original: praxis</note></term> of what has been understood is to be attempted, it should first be attempted with the pen <note>original: calamo; literally a reed-pen</note> rather than with the tongue. This is because during writing, there is no lack of time for deliberation <note>original: deliberandi</note> and the power to consult: either one's own self, by jogging the memory; or another person sitting nearby, by asking; or finally, by consulting books...

<summary>Comenius outlines a three-step mastery of learning: understanding (Mind), writing (Hand), and speaking (Tongue). He argues that speaking is the most difficult stage and should be preceded by written practice to allow for reflection.</summary>

160. *This must likewise be observed in learning the **Arts** and **sciences**. For everywhere this same progression <note>original: gradatio</note> holds: namely, that before all things there is formed in us, through the senses, an **Understanding** of things; and through the Understanding, the **Memory**. Then, with the Memory directing the operation, the **Hand** attempts and carries out its work. But to establish discourse about things belongs only to one for whom an already strengthened Understanding and Memory—regarding the use of things—suggest the matter and words as readily as the **Tongue** is able to speak them. Therefore, the highest step and the peak of progress is altogether this: to readily render things well-understood with the Tongue.*

161. *Therefore, let **Teachers** <note>original: Præceptores</note> take care that whatever they wish to teach successfully to their students, they proceed through these steps without confusion: otherwise they will produce confusion for both themselves and their pupils.*

162. *Moreover, let **Examples** always come first, as the raw material; and let **Precepts** and **Rules** follow, as the form: just as was said above (§ 60). For Precepts and Rules are certain guides for the mind concerning things and speech; but how can something be guided and directed which does not yet exist? And who is not forced to admit that every Rule receives its light from Examples? Why, therefore, is the example not put first?*

### OF J. A. COMENIUS 220

163. *Whatever task is undertaken, let it not be set aside until it is completed. For if one returns to a business at intervals, the labor is not lessened but increased by the repetition: because those same things, left in the same place, will repeat the same difficulties. Test this by experiment: see how slowly you would fill a vessel with water if you only added one or two drops daily; whereas you could easily fill it if you poured continuously.*

164. *Therefore, the Teacher <note>original: Præceptor</note> should never take on more material than what can be proposed, explained, and—through proper exercises—imprinted upon the **Understanding** and the **Memory** <note>original: Intellectui & Memoriæ</note> in that same hour: so that there is no need to return to these things, except for the sake of review. This repetition, however, will be done later while doing something else, and with new benefit; namely, when the following things are built upon those already established. For this true method (which we intend) requires proceeding in order and with a step that is nowhere interrupted: so that preceding things always prepare the way for subsequent ones, and subsequent things always add strength to the preceding ones.*

165. *The first foundations of things must be laid with absolute accuracy, unless you wish the whole structure you have built upon them to wobble. **Physicians** <note>original: Medici</note> know that an error in the first concoction <note>the first stage of digestion in 17th-century medicine</note> is not corrected in the second, nor that of the second in the third. And **Mathematicians** <note>original: Mathematici</note> know that an error admitted at the beginning of an operation increases infinitely as it progresses, and cannot be removed unless the entire operation is destroyed and one returns to the first principles.*

<summary>Comenius argues for "continuous" learning and warns against leaving tasks half-finished, using analogies from physics, medicine, and mathematics to show how early errors or interruptions compromise the entire educational process.</summary>
<keywords>pedagogy, persistence, lesson planning, foundational learning, Jan Amos Comenius, memory, understanding, digestion analogy, mathematical error</keywords>

166. Therefore, whatever the **Teacher** <note>original: *Præceptor*; a schoolmaster or tutor</note> begins to teach, he shall see to it that it is accurate, and thus so firm that subsequent things can be safely built upon it. One must learn **Rightly** before **Quickly**. He hastens enough who tends toward the goal by a straight path. It is better for learners to be slow at first, provided they are accurate; speed will come later, once the foundations are firm. This is certainly the nature of all growing things: they perform their first movements and their first growth imperceptibly, but in their progress, they eventually take on strength and momentum, provided they have been well-rooted. Therefore:

167. If anything has been wrongly grasped or practiced, care must be taken that it does not take root, but is instead plucked out immediately. For the **Mind** is accustomed to entrust whatever it seizes to the **Memory**, and it becomes an idol <note>referring to a false mental image or "Idol of the Mind" that is difficult to correct once established</note> that allows itself to be uprooted only with great difficulty.

168. Therefore, whatever is taught, let it be taught accurately, so that it cannot be snatched away into error. Then, the **Master** <note>original: *Magister*</note> should immediately examine how it was perceived, lest some error has perhaps crept in. And if he notices anything, let him correct it at once: having detected and destroyed the opportunity for falling into that error (which a prudent **shaper of intellects** <note>original: *plasmator*; a creative word implying a teacher who molds a student's mind like a sculptor</note> can easily sniff out from the circumstances). This should be done for that reason: to take precaution so that a similar error is not committed again later.

169. The same diligence must be applied in forming and correcting **stylistic exercises** <note>original: *styli exercitiis*; practice in writing or composition</note>, so that nothing used less than rightly by the student—

171. *By far the greatest shortcut to ease* (for the whole assembly of teachers and learners) *is if the Teacher <note>original: *Præceptor*</note> teaches no one person alone, whatever he teaches, but everyone at once. Or if he teaches one person, given the opportunity, let it nonetheless be in the sight of all: so that whatever is said to one person may benefit everyone.*

172. For just as the **Printer** <note>original: **Typographus**; Comenius frequently uses the printing press—a relatively modern technology in his time—as a metaphor for efficient education</note> fills a thousand sheets with writing from one and the same arrangement of type, and all of them most accurately; so the Teacher, by one and the same explanation of a thing, can illuminate the minds of a thousand students, and by one and the same exercise, polish the styles of all.

173. For this to happen, two things are necessary. First, that students of unequal progress or different starting times are not admitted into the same class: but that all of similar progress are received at the same time and led at the same time; in the same way that seeds in the fields, which are prepared for the same harvest, are scattered at the same—

174. Second, skill <note>original: *arte*; referring to the "art of teaching"</note> is needed to make the students so attentive to those things being done that there is not one among them all to whom everything being taught does not become soundly known and yield practical use.

175. Attention of this kind can be excited and retained in an eight-fold way.

176. First, if the Teacher <note>original: *Præceptor*</note> takes care to always bring forward something that both delights and profits; for in this way their minds will be enticed <note>original: *inescabuntur*; literally "baited," as one lures a fish with a hook</note>, so that they always come eagerly and with ready attention.

177. Second, if at the beginning of every task, their minds are either soothed by a recommendation of the material to be presented, or they are stimulated <note>original: *vellicentur*; literally "nipped" or "plucked" to wake them up</note> by raising questions—either about what has already been proposed, so that they might reach the current material through a logical connection <note>original: *cohærentiam*</note>, or about what is to be proposed, so that, having noticed their ignorance in that area, they are fired up to receive the explanation of the matter more greedily.

178. Third, if the Master <note>original: *Magister*</note>, standing in a more elevated place, casts his eyes around and permits no one to do anything else than fix their eyes upon him in turn.

179. **Fourth**, if he assists attention by presenting any thing <note>original: *rem*</note> to as many of the Senses <note>original: *Sensibus*</note> as he can: namely, not to the Hearing <note>original: *Auditui*</note> alone by spoken words, but also to the Sight <note>original: *Visui*</note> by pictures, and to the Touch <note>original: *Tactui*</note> by offering the actual object <note>original: *rem præsentem*</note> to be handled;

### I. A. COMENIUS

...and to the **Sense of Smell**, etc., whenever objects of that kind are to be explained. For such an application of Things to the Senses, and of the Senses to Things, perpetually stimulates <note>original: *vellicat*; literally "plucks" or "pinches" the mind to keep it alert</note> the imagination and binds it to the matter at hand, so that it can hardly—not even barely—wander off or grow sluggish.

180. **Fifth**, the Teacher <note>original: *Præceptor*</note> will sharpen the students’ attention if, during the lessons, he occasionally interrupts his speech and says: "*You, or you—what did I just say? Repeat this sentence. You—tell me how we arrived at this point?*" and similar questions, according to the progress of each Class. If anyone is found not to have been paying attention, let them be rebuked or corrected on the spot; in this way, the drive for attention will be thoroughly sharpened.

181. Similarly, if you have questioned one student and he falters, skip to the second, third, tenth, or even the thirtieth person, and demand an answer without repeating the question. All this is done so that whatever is said to one student, everyone else strives to pay attention to and put into practice.

182. It can also happen (**seventh**) that if one or two are ignorant of something, the question may be asked of the whole crowd. Then, let the one who answers first, or best, be praised in the sight of everyone, so that their example may serve to spark competition <note>original: *æmulatione*; a common Renaissance educational strategy where students competed for honor and recognition</note>. If someone makes a mistake, let them be corrected, with the cause of the error being identified and rooted out (as mentioned previously). It is incredible how much of a shortcut <note>original: *compendiũ*; an efficient path or "compendium" of effort</note> this will be for the swiftest progress.

183. Finally, when the lesson is finished, let the opportunity be given...

# J. A. COMENIUS

...for we presuppose this: that the student finishes the first and therefore most difficult struggle (since every beginning is burdensome) with *Latin letters*: *that is*, that they learn: (1.) *To pronounce the Latin language correctly.* (2.) *To read it fluently.* (3.) *To write it accurately.* (4.) *To understand and interpret it in some fashion.* (5.) *To distinguish the parts of speech moderately well.* (6.) *To decline and conjugate regular forms exactly.* <note>original: *analoga*; referring to words that follow standard patterns rather than irregular ones</note> (7.) *To express the simple thoughts of a child's mind.* (8.) *To imitate, in some way, models of style already set before them.*

187. To achieve this, some hundreds of short sentences were previously conceived, called the **VESTIBULE** of Latinity: to be perfected hereafter in such a way that: (1.) *Accents are expressly placed over the words.* (2.) *Observations on correct pronunciation are added.* (3.) *Other copies of the same sentences are printed in the same type, but in a faint color (perhaps green would be most suitable): from which the boys may learn the foundations of Latin writing, tracing over the shapes of the letters printed there with ink, and by that method training their hands to form similar letters.* <note>Comenius is describing an early version of a "trace-the-letter" workbook, suggesting that green ink is easiest for a child to see their own black ink over.</note> (4.) *A translation in the native tongue is placed before each sentence.* (5.) *Nouns are expressed in one typeface, verbs in another, and other small words in yet another.* <note>A pioneer in typography, Comenius used different fonts to help students visually identify parts of speech.</note> (6.) *Tables of declensions and conjugations, with necessary instructions, are appended.* (7.) *A good many of the sentences are arranged in the form of a dialogue.* (8.) *At the end of the book, a list of the words...*

198. In the meantime, let the students proceed to read and interpret the sentences, again in order, but with the native-language text placed first (for we advise that the booklet be printed in such a way that the native words precede the Latin) for two reasons. First, because they are not learning their native tongue through the guidance of Latin, but Latin through the guidance of the native tongue: let the guide, therefore, come first. For this is an eternal and unchangeable law of method, that for the **Intellect** <term>Intellectui; the faculty of understanding</term> about to penetrate into the darkness of an unknown thing, it is necessary that the light of some previously known thing be held before it; (For whatever is learned, is learned from things previously known.)

199. Second, this method is beneficial to the **Memory** <term>Memoriæ; the faculty of retention</term>; whose nature is to move forward, not backward. For if I ask a boy, *In the Lord’s Prayer <note>original: Oratione Dominica</note>, after the word* BE DONE <note>original: FIAT</note> *what follows?* he will immediately answer (with memory promptly suggesting it) *Thy will, etc.* But ask, *What precedes that word,* BE DONE? even the best among us will hesitate: specifically because Memory does not know how to go backward, or at least is not accustomed to doing so.

200. Therefore, because both the Intellect and the Memory extend themselves from the known to the unknown (from the native tongue to foreign ones), it is of absolute necessity that the known be placed first, so that the unknown may follow of its own accord. *Come here, you boys. ...they will also learn to render the meanings of sentences, and even be commanded to render them word for word. Specifically, in this manner:
**Come here you boys** <note>original German: Komt her ihr Knaben</note> : *Come, boys* <note>original Latin: Venite pueri</note>;
**Come here** <note>original German: Komt her</note> / *Come* <note>original Latin: Venite</note> : **you boys** <note>original German: ihr Knaben</note> / *boys* <note>original Latin: Pueri</note>.
And so everywhere.

202. The reason for this advice is: (1.) So that the tongue may dwell longer on the same word (for correct pronunciation and fluent reading must still be strengthened); and so that the **Imaginative faculty** <term>Imaginativa facultas; the mental power to form images of things</term> may dwell on the same thing that the word signifies, so that a better impression might be made. (2.) So that the same impression and concept might be more distinct and beyond the danger of confusion. For since a Latin word is sometimes rendered by two words in the native tongue, or because a **transposition** <term>trajectio; a reordering of words</term> occurs in the native language, a boy might not consider sufficiently what each thing refers to if he were allowed only to pronounce whole sentences in a general way.

203. For example: the eighth sentence of the *Vestibule*; *God will help you* <note>original Latin: Deus vos iuvabit</note> consists of three words, and yet in the native tongue <note>here, German</note> it can only be expressed in four; because that **future** tense <term>futurum; the grammatical tense for things that will happen later</term> word (*he will help* <note>original Latin: iuvabit</note>) takes on the little word that indicates the future (**will** <note>original German: wird</note>). Furthermore, a transposition of words occurs: **God will help you** <note>original German: Gott wird euch helffen</note> instead of **God you will help** <note>original German: Gott euch wird helffen</note>. Therefore, so that the boy may become accustomed to discerning these things, this repeated explanation I mentioned (by which word is rendered by word) will be beneficial: **God** <note>original: Gott</note>, *God* <note>original: Deus</note>; **will help** <note>original: wird helffen</note>: *he will help* <note>original: iuvabit</note>; **you** <note>original: euch</note>, *you* <note>original: vos</note>.

If they transcribe these diligently, they will gain a threefold benefit. ( 1. ) They will strengthen their **calligraphy** <term>the art of beautiful handwriting</term> and ( 2. ) their understanding of the words. ( 3. ) Furthermore, they will begin to discern the **construction** <term>the grammatical arrangement and relationship</term> of the words incidentally, while they are occupied with the other tasks.

->III.<-

205. Thirdly, let the *Vestibule* be gone through by repeating the translation from Latin into the native tongue, specifically in the reverse order from the first—but with a similar number of sentences for each turn: likewise rendering first sentence to sentence, then word to word.

206. The reason why we now advise a return from Latin to the native tongue is so that, by this method, the power of the Latin words and their **analogy** <term>correspondence or similarity</term> to the native words might be more clearly revealed. For just as a traveler learns a road better by going and returning, and the structure of some work is better known by weaving and unweaving, so is the relationship of a foreign language to our own better understood by returning from one to the other, and back again.

207. Let the Teacher therefore lead the way again with an example of translating (for our **little recruits** <term>tirunculi; young beginners</term> are still tender; their lips must be shaped for them). For instance: *Come, boys*, **Come here you boys** <note>original Latin: *Venite pueri*; original German: *Komt her ihr Knaben*</note> / *Come*, **Come here** <note>original Latin: *Venite*; original German: *Komt her*</note>; *Boys*, **You boys** <note>original Latin: *Pueri*; original German: *Ihr Knaben*</note> / and so on, translating the whole allotted portion for that hour in this same manner. Then let him command them to do that same thing (each one looking into his own little book) in order. And they will do it swiftly, marveling that such easy things are required of them; because they do not notice—

For in this exact sequence the **Cases** <term>Casus; the various forms a noun takes to show its grammatical role</term> are to be reviewed, so that the **Vocative** <term>the case used for addressing or calling someone</term> follows the **Nominative** <term>the case used for the subject of a sentence</term> immediately—unless we wish to resist the most obvious logic and deliberately torment the students. <note>The Latin phrase *cruces figere* (to fix crosses) is an idiom meaning to cause great difficulty or torture.</note> This is because those two are called the **Direct Cases** <term>Recti; cases that name or call directly</term>, while the others are **Indirect** <term>Obliqui; cases that show relationships like possession or direction</term>: therefore, let those that belong to the same rank remain together. Furthermore, because all the remaining case endings in both the singular and plural are derived from the **Genitive** <term>the possessive case</term> singular ending—but the Vocative singular is not—let the Vocative come first, so that it does not disrupt the pattern of the others later, etc.

216. Once the use of the **Declension Table** has been demonstrated using examples taken from the *Entrance* <term>Introitu; a reference to the introductory text of the Vestibule</term> (showing how single nouns such as *Boy, Tongue, Thing, Wisdom, God, Teacher*, etc., are declined), students will be able to decline both **Adjectives** and **Substantives** <term>Nouns</term> together in combination from the following chapter. At first, however, (for the sake of ease), they should only decline those that belong to the same **Declension** <term>a group of nouns that share the same pattern of endings</term>. For example, from the First Declension: *The Latin Tongue, a beautiful Tongue. The lowest Earth. A nearby Mist. A wide Courtyard,* etc. Then from the Second: *The eternal God. The temporary World. ->ON THE USE OF THE VESTIBULE. 239<-

228. Whenever one comes to indeclinable particles, even if nothing has yet been taught about them, let the teacher nevertheless continue to ask questions. "You, [Name], **FOR** <note>original: *PRO*</note>, (**AND**, **THEREFORE**, **WHERE**, etc.), is it a Noun or a Verb?" For now, it will be enough to know the difference between Noun and Verb, and the use of Genders and Cases, Tenses and Moods, and furthermore to be prompt in declining and conjugating.

229. *The exercise of style will now go deeper. Namely, they will change the Moods of the Verbs, by forming Indicatives from Imperatives, and Subjunctives from Indicatives:* and connecting them by the bonds of intervening subjunctive particles (such as **If**, **that**, **Because**, **Although-nevertheless**, etc., which the Teachers will suggest to them). 243. This is something we experience in ourselves—all of us who were not led by this happy and easy path, but were dragged through various detours. These people are swollen with wordy loquacity; whenever they bring forth and display the powers of their fluency in public, they bring nothing but either the rhapsodies of others or their own "bubbling trifles" <note>original: *bullatas nugas*; a vivid image of speech that looks big like a bubble but is empty inside</note>. Whatever may still be found lacking in this text for completeness and elegance—as shown by more careful observation and more abundant practice—can be gradually perfected through our own care and that of others.

252. *The second is* that which we shall soon provide, with God's help <note>original Greek: "σὺν Θεῷ"</note>, a ***Rational Account of All Words***: that is, an ***Etymological Lexicon***, compiled from the leading etymologists of our age—primarily Martinius, Becmann, Alsted, and Colding <note>These were prominent 17th-century scholars who studied the origins and roots of words.</note>—but with greater brevity and ease (as the work itself will testify) than has been done until now; so that those wise in these matters...

254. And finally, grammatical *precepts and Rules*, arranged *according to the true laws of natural <term>Didactics: the science or art of teaching</term>* for concise ease and rapid practice. The proper use of all these must now be taught here.

255. From this point on, we wish the **DOOR** <note>The "Janua," the intermediate textbook.</note> to be *passed through* ten times repeatedly, just as the **ENTRANCE** <note>The "Vestibulum," the introductory textbook.</note> was before: not only with the eyes and tongue, but also with exercises of the Hand, Memory, and Intellect, so that we may make the students truly fit to be sent into the **PALACE** <note>The "Palatium," the advanced level of study where students would read classical authors.</note>.

256. First, let it be run through in *bare reading*, for the sake of *correct and rapid pronunciation*, and for a *general and preliminary acquaintance with the whole book*. Therefore, let the students read in order, each one a single sentence in a circle: with the native-language text everywhere preceding it. Let the Master be the supervisor, correcting pronunciation and accent.

257. In this way (for nothing more is required), the text of the Door can be run through within one or two weeks.

I shall add: Why do I advise that everything that is learned be written out by the students' own hands? First, so that they may prepare for themselves a practiced hand (for only a frequently repeated action bestows a habit). Second, so that there may be more evident proof for Parents and Schoolmasters that they have thoroughly learned what they ought to. *Third*, as an aid to Memory: which seizes everything more easily and stores it more deeply the more senses it uses, and the longer it dwells upon a single thing. # J. A. COMENIUS

...neither <note>This continues the thought from the previous page, likely referring to the dual goals of eloquence and knowledge.</note> can be obtained without a prior, clear, and distinct knowledge of **Things**, as they reveal themselves through their differences <note>In Comenius's philosophy, "differences" are the specific characteristics that distinguish one object or concept from another, essential for clear classification.</note>. For, if the knowledge of **Things** is confused, speech <note>original: "sermo"</note> will also be confused. Indeed, Language does not touch or express **Things** directly, but rather the **Concepts** of things, as they shine in the mind. Therefore, **Concepts** must be formed first, so that they are correct; and then it will be easy to form the language, so that it expresses correctly what the **Mind** understands correctly.

261. *Therefore, it is simply necessary that, before the **Words** of the Door <note>The "Door" refers to the *Janua*, Comenius's revolutionary language textbook designed to teach Latin through descriptions of the real world.</note> are more accurately analyzed, the **Things** contained under them should first be made known:* which will require some diligence from the **Teachers**. For although the *Door* contains nothing so far above a child's grasp, because children are nevertheless Children—whose minds wander and only touch upon the surface of **Things** everywhere in a passing and hasty way—the mind must be captured in some manner, so that it may grow accustomed to attending more fixedly to **Things** and observing their differences more precisely.

262. *Which can be done in no other way more conveniently than if the **Teachers** conduct an accurate inventory of **Things** in the presence of the students, showing what each thing is, and how it differs from others of the same kind; and if the Door, in its own way, says something too concisely, explaining it more fully as needed.* (Observe diligently, so that the teacher may make all the **Students** completely attentive to him.

# J. A. COMENIUS

(For the seventh time) through the entire Door <note>the textbook "Janua Linguarum"</note>, let the logic of sentence construction be shown in all sentences, using the Rules of Syntax attached to the Door. To make this proceed more efficiently, we plan to mark the rules of the entire syntax with one continuous numbering system: and then to assign those same numbers within the text of the Door itself, so that the Rule explaining why each thing is said in such a way is immediately apparent. In this way, no labor will remain except for comparing any given construction with its Rule, so that through frequent use all these things may finally become a habit. By this method, we seem to be looking out for both the diligent and talented students—so that seeing everything laid out clearly, they may fly through this study of syntax all the more eagerly—and the lazy or slower students—so that seeing that they too are fully capable of moving forward, they may continue to progress.

276. *However, so that those rules of syntax may stick more easily in the memory, let them be written out during these days in the hours set aside for writing exercises. But let them not be bare Rules, as the printed edition will have them: instead, include examples transcribed from the text of the Door, which the numbers placed under each Rule will indicate. This exercise will provide more internal benefit than it appears to promise on the surface.*

280. Ninthly, let the **DOOR** return for a *quasi-logical analysis* through *Questions*. This will be an excellent way to examine the power of Things and Words, looking at their order, connection, and relationship to other things and words. It will likewise foster the skill of wisely and rationally considering any subject and responding to anything. Finally, it will serve the correct and natural practice of Syntax <term>Syntax; the arrangement of words and phrases to create well-formed sentences</term> in such a way that the logic of sentence structure will at last become truly clear and ready to use. For when the Teacher takes the main part—whether a Noun, a Verb, or both—from any period <term>Period; a complete sentence or rhetorical thought</term> to form a question, it will be the student’s duty to construct a response from the remaining parts. Because this answer will not use the same number of words or the same word order as the original sentence, but will be shortened and altered, the student's attention and judgment will necessarily be sharpened here.

281. This will be easy in some places, namely where the questions and answers are already prepared. For example, in section 2: *What does it mean to be Learned?* <note>original: "Eruditum esse"</note> *Response: To know the differences between Things, and to be able to designate each one by its own name.* Elsewhere it may be a little more difficult; however, reason will always dictate everywhere what should be asked and what should be answered. For example, in section 4: *What are the foundations of Learning?* <note>original: "Eruditionis"</note> *Response: The Nomenclature* <term>Nomenclature; a system of names or terms</term> *of Nature and Art.* And again: *These foundations* <note>The text ends mid-sentence here; the catchword "menta" at the top of the page indicates the next word is "fundamenta," continuing the thought.</note>

### ON THE USE OF THE DOOR.

...how are the foundations <note>original: "menta," continuing from "fundamenta" on the previous page</note> laid? Response: By thoroughly learning the Nomenclature <term>Nomenclature; a system of names or terms used in a particular field of study</term> of Nature and Art, etc.

->NB.<-

282. However simple and childish this exercise may seem, it will be just as effective for stimulating the sharpness of a child's intellect and directing it precisely toward Things and Words. Therefore, so that even those who see less clearly on their own may find the path here opened and marked, we will strive to present specific questions—adapted through a certain popular application of logical method—which can be instituted regarding Substantive Nouns, Adjectives, Verbs, and even other small words (within which the emphasis of things lies).

283. No other work for a writing exercise will be necessary here than for those same things which were discussed in the morning hours to be written down: namely, by resolving everything in the entire **Door** <note>original: "Januæ"</note> into Questions and completing them with Responses. It is not easy to say how much utility this beautiful kind of exercise will bring to both style and judgment.

...distinguishing words, constructing sentences syntactically <term>Syntactic; relating to the arrangement of words to create well-formed sentences</term>, forming questions, and responding to them, etc. Let the prize for the winner, if nothing else is available, be public applause and the honor of a higher seat. 285. *Writing style <note>original: "Stylus"</note> may now finally begin to be practiced more freely, after the students have been sufficiently instructed in a wealth of vocabulary, their true meaning, and the art of sentence construction.* They shall therefore translate themes dictated by the Teacher from their native language <note>original: "è Vernaculo"</note> into Latin: with either their Memory or the native language Index (added to the end of the **Door** for this purpose) suggesting the words and sentences. Whether these exercises are, for example, little stories, or parables and fables, or short narratives of another kind—whether invented by the Teacher or taken from elsewhere—it will not matter; provided they contain nothing alien to the form of the **Door**, nothing too figurative or metaphorical, or too far removed from the present humble condition of their concepts and style.

286. For those running through these stages <note>original: "stadia"; referencing the segments of a racetrack</note>, it is enough to be led to the finish line, and no further. We have fixed the goal <note>original: "Metam"</note> of the **Door** once and for all: that children may appropriately express their childish thoughts, as many as can arise from the knowledge of the things contained within the **Door**. If we achieve this, we have hit the target; here we must stop.

And it pleases us also to plant our feet here now, at the exit of the **DOOR**.

## ON THE USE OF THE DOOR.

287. For as much as concerns the use of the **PALACE & TREASURIES** of the Latin language <note>The *Palatium* and *Thesaurus* were the next levels in Comenius's graded language system, following the *Vestibulum* and *Ianua*.</note>, the Architects themselves will be able to give the best advice concerning them in due time: to whom, O **GOD**, grant life and strength, for the honor of Your name!

288. It will be worthwhile to give this one additional warning here. It is very beneficial.

->N.B.<-
<note>Short for *Nota Bene*, meaning "Note Well."</note>

*It will be beneficial for boys being educated by this method if they are given no abundance of books except those destined for their own class: for the first class the* Vestibule <term>Vestibulum; the introductory stage of the curriculum</term>, *for the second the* Door <term>Ianua; the intermediate stage</term>, *for the third the* Palace <term>Palatium; the advanced stage</term>, *etc. There are ready reasons why I advise this. (1.) Attention directed at many things is lessened for each individual thing. By doing many things at once, we do nothing correctly.*

Let them therefore have only these for themselves meanwhile, elaborated with such great zeal for their use: let them attend to these, so they are not distracted by others. *"Constant practice devoted to one thing often conquers both natural talent and art,"* <note>original: "Vsus assiduus uni rei deditus, & ingenium & artem sæpe vincit"</note> says Cicero. (2.) Boys are not yet able to exercise a choice of things; they can easily fall into those things which confuse and entangle them if there is an opportunity to handle anything whatsoever. (3.) What Roman heralds used to shout to those about to enter the Capitol to perform sacred rites, **ATTEND TO THIS** <note>original: "HOC AGE"; a ritual command for participants to focus solely on the sacred task at hand</note>, it is good to train boys in this also, so that they become accustomed to dwelling on authors, not flying over them. (4.) Finally, by immoderate study, the vigor of the mind—especially a fiery, energetic one—is worn away: which must be guarded against.

# J. A. COMENIUS ON THE USE OF THE DOOR. <note>original: *Janua*. This refers to his famous work, *Janua linguarum reserata* (The Door of Languages Unlocked), which revolutionized language teaching by connecting words directly to the things they describe.</note> #

299. But to bring this discussion to a close, let this be the sum and the conclusion of everything that can be said on this matter:

**ONE MUST TEACH WITHOUT ENVY:**
**AND LEARN WITHOUT SHAME.** <note>original: *Docendum est sine invidia: et discendum sine pudore*. This motto reflects Comenius’s belief that knowledge should be shared freely and that students should never feel embarrassed by their quest for understanding.</note>

For all human things that can be improved are in a state of growth and increase.

300. Therefore, let Seneca <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca (c. 4 BC – AD 65), a Roman Stoic philosopher. Comenius frequently cited classical authors to support his modern educational theories.</note> close this work with the words with which he concludes his thirty-third Letter:

> *Nothing will ever be discovered if we are satisfied with what has already been found. What then? Shall I not follow in the footsteps of those before me? Indeed, I will use the old way, but if I find a shorter path, I will pave it. Those who set these things in motion before us are not our masters, but our guides. Truth lies open to everyone; it has not yet been fully claimed. Much of it remains even for those who are yet to come.* <note>original: *Nunquam quidquam invenietur...* from Seneca’s *Moral Letters to Lucilius*, 33.10–11. ...goal is altogether this, and it seems it must be perpetually held and regarded: that **BOYS** be placed, as it were, within the first threshold of Erudition and Wisdom; and thus, according to the measure of their **AGE** and the capacity of their **INTELLECT**, they may be led gradually and step-by-step, not only to the **LATIN LANGUAGE**, to be learned purely from its very beginnings, but also toward the seeds of Human and Celestial Wisdom <note>Vechner emphasizes that language learning should not be separated from moral and spiritual education.</note>, to be grasped gradually and bit by bit along with the first rudiments of the Language.

[pri]mitive <note>original: "primigeniæ"</note> and simple things should alone be considered for admission into the **Vestibulum** <note>The introductory textbook in Comenius's system.</note>; or whether derived and compound things should be carefully excluded. It might seem that a method of teaching and a shortcut to learning require that a beginning be made from the simplest elements, as it is usually the case that once those are grasped, the rest—whether they are derived from or composed of them—open up naturally. This principle is certainly valid in those matters which are grasped by theoretical speculation. However, it is not the same for those matters which must be adapted as closely and as much as possible to use and practice. In such cases, without regard for the first origin, and without an intuition of simplicity, there is often a need for **Derived** and **Compound** things before it is in any way necessary to think about the primary and simple roots. 

In this regard, it has been discovered that the logic of "Simplicity" is quite different: it is not always sufficiently adapted to a child’s understanding and use, nor can it always be safely employed under the assumption that **Derivation** and **Composition** will thereafter be easily managed. On the contrary, it has been noticed that **Derived** and **Compound** words are often much more common than the Simpler and Primitive ones, and are even more familiar in their common meaning. 

To these points, we must add that so many compounds and **Derivatives** descend from the Simple and Primary roots that **Declension**—at least as **Varro** <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BCE), an influential Roman scholar and grammarian.</note> calls it (which we otherwise call **Derivation**) —and **Composition** are by no means "natural." ...it behaves in the same way even in similar cases (as happens in the **Declensions** <note>original: "Declinationibus"; the patterns of noun and adjective endings</note>, as they are commonly called); but it also varies as much as possible, even in very similar instances; and thus it clearly depends on the observation of specific usage. For it is not the case that because one thing is derived from another, it is likewise permitted to derive another similar thing from something else; nor can one compose just anything from anything else at will, without the approval of established usage. 

In executing this successfully and skillfully, an understanding of things is required that is beyond the capacity of children; it can certainly even create difficulty for grown men in some places. And the meaning often varies so much between the **Primary** <note>root words</note> and the **Derived** <note>words formed from roots</note> words that the matter can hardly be understood by any fixed rule; much less would it be easy for children to proceed from a knowledge of **Primitives** through general rules to **Derivatives**. This is especially true since the sense in vocabulary also varies so much between languages, so that what is a **Compound** or **Derived** word in the **Vernacular** <note>the student’s native language</note> may be a simple and **Primitive** word in Latin, and vice versa.

These things being so considered, it can be recognized as better—indeed, necessary—that there should be no restraint at all regarding **Derivatives** and **Compounds** in the **Vestibulum** <note>The "Entrance Hall," Comenius's introductory textbook</note>. Rather, they should be admitted into it with this privilege: that they are not only summoned indiscriminately along with **Primitives** and simple words, but are even preferred over them if they happen to be of more common use and if they suit the grasp...

# ADVICE.

...but also to investigate the **WORD** <note>original: "VERBVM"; here referring to the specific form and meaning of individual words</note>.

In this way, he will also imprint those very Themes <note>original: "Themata"; the root or basic forms of words</note> deep in his memory, if he is ordered to recite and occasionally compete with his fellow students, not only from the Text where the constructed little sentences occur, but also from the **INDEX**, in so far as simple words are concerned.

Generally, in other respects, all words are learned both more easily and more certainly when they are offered in some Structure <note>referring to a sentence or grammatical arrangement</note>, even if they are not presented in the first Case <note>original: "Casu primo"; the Nominative case used for the subject</note> or according to the Theme itself, than when they are presented solitary outside of a Structure. For by this method, the force, meaning, and use [of a word] are both clearly evident and easily retained. In solitary words, the true meaning often lies hidden, and the usage is in no way apparent outside of structure; instead, it is finally hammered in with difficulty through laborious instruction.

Furthermore, so that the Theme may be more easily and immediately apparent with the Text in every place, and so there is no need to consult the Index during the first treatment, it would be advisable to print the more difficult words in the margin <margin>print the more difficult words in the margin</margin>.

...a certain collection of words most familiar to children: and those indicated by that rhythmic method through **Similar Endings** <note>original: "Homoioteleuta"; a rhetorical device where words end with similar sounds, often used to create rhyme or rhythm to aid memorization</note>, should be presented from the beginning: so that in this way, material may be available for exercising **Declensions** <note>the grammatical practice of changing noun and adjective endings</note> alone at the first approach.

If this same thing is done not only with Nouns, but also with certain Verbs, then material will also be at hand for similarly exercising **Conjugations** <note>the grammatical practice of changing verb endings</note> at the start.

And it will be enough for these things to be presented to the children in such a way, and in such a quantity: so that while they busy themselves with inflecting those, all other more important Nouns and Verbs can then be referred to one of them, as they will follow a similar pattern of inflection.

28. By this method, whatever can contribute in that regard to easier understanding and a readier memory will be presented to the children in the most reliable way.

But it is not at all necessary that each item be always placed distinctly under its own Class. It is better for this to be done whenever the occasion arises, under whatever [category]...

<header>ADVICE.</header>

(...so that it should not be obscured or corrupted even in the *Vestibulum* <note>The introductory-level textbook</note>) or that the proper character of the German language <note>original: "Germanicæ propria indoles"</note> be neglected: since words cannot always be connected in the exact same order in this language [German] as in that [Latin], while remaining elegant or even appropriate.

3. However, lest the proper meaning fail to be precisely declared in every instance—and since this cannot be safely left to a less careful teacher <note>original: "Inſtitutori"</note>—it will be necessary to insert in parentheses the proper force of the Latin words, should the German appear to deviate too far from them.

4. It is not necessary for the German to be placed immediately below the Latin text, corresponding to it interlineally; instead, it will be sufficient if they are set on the opposite side <note>This suggests a parallel column layout</note>. This approach is advised because it will make the examination of the boys more efficient, whether they are translating Latin into their mother tongue or expressing German back into Latin. Furthermore, this will work more conveniently for the **WRITTEN WORK** <note>original: "SCRIPTO"</note> which I chose to demonstrate and recommend in the **TEACHER’S GUIDE** <note>original: "INFORMATORIO"; likely referring to the *Informatorium*, a pedagogical manual for teachers or parents</note>, if the Latin words appear distinctly from the German ones.

V.", an abbreviation for *Bene Vale*</note>.

<header>TO THE READER, GREETINGS. 291</header>

Lest the following pages be empty and void, we supplement them with a Catalog of books which the Illustrious Comenius <note>John Amos Comenius (1592–1670), a Moravian philosopher and pedagogue considered the father of modern education.</note> has either already published, or has in hand and still holds back <note>original Latin: "premit," implying works that are written but not yet sent to the press</note>. And all these serve that most excellent end, which as Comenius intends, so we earnestly wish that he may attain it. Indeed, once we are freed from obstacles, we shall be entirely devoted to investigating the truth. There exist, therefore:

I. *The Golden Door of Tongues Unlocked.* <note>original: "Ianua Linguarum reserata aurea," his most famous work, which taught Latin through descriptions of the world.</note>
II. *The Entrance-way to the Door of Tongues.* <note>original: "Vestibulum Ianuæ Linguarum," an introductory primer for younger students.</note>

V. *A Didactic Dissertation* on *Fully Completing the Study of the Latin Language*, with *Appendices.*

->But there are expected<-

I. *The Temple of Christian Universal Wisdom.*
II. *The Door of Things*, or *The Key to Human Understanding*, see page 208.
III. *The Great Didactic.* <note>original: "Didactica Magna," his foundational treatise on educational theory and school organization.</note>
IV. *Metaphysics.*
V. *A Universal Lexicon.*
VI. *An Etymological Lexicon.*
VII. *A Lexicon of Phrases.*
VIII. *A Treatise* on *Homonyms, Paronyms, and Synonyms.*
IX. *A Treasury of the Latin Language.*

## TWO BOOKS

### CHAPTER I.

->*On Political Science and Its Use.*<-

<margin>§. 1.</margin>
Politics is the science that provides the management and method for establishing, preserving, and enlarging the State <term>State<note>Original Latin: *Respublica*, which can be translated as "republic," "commonwealth," or "the public interest."</note></term>.

§. 2. This science must indeed be considered by us in two ways: both insofar as it is separated from practice <note>Original Latin: *ab usu*. This refers to the theoretical study of political principles in the abstract.</note>, and insofar as it relates to it <note>This refers to the application of those principles in actual governance.</note>.

# MARCUS ZUERIUS BOXHORN’S

A

§. 3. Practice and theoretical knowledge <note>Original: *scientia*</note> are for the most part diverse and distinct from each other; yet they are so closely related that it cannot be doubted that the latter contributes greatly to the support of the former. Indeed, theoretical knowledge should not be torn away from practice, and it is best advised that the former be placed before the latter.

§. 4. The foundations of theoretical knowledge are the principle of what is fair and good <note>Original: *ratio æqui & boni*, a classical legal concept referring to equity and moral justice</note>, and the affairs of states <term>States<note>Original: *Imperiorum*, referring to sovereign powers or empires.</note></term> considered in a general sense.

§. 5. The foundations of practice are Prudence <term>Prudence<note>Original: *Prudentia*; the practical wisdom required to make right decisions in specific, real-world situations.</note></term> and the specific affairs of states.

§. 6. Theoretical knowledge ensures that we do not err against those principles which are in perpetual use in the State; Practice ensures that we do not err in regard to this or that specific State, or in these or those specific affairs.

§. 7. Finally, theoretical knowledge considers the State in general and its well-being; Practice considers individual states and their various specific and unique advantages, according to the variety of people, circumstances, and times.

# CHAPTER II.

## What a Republic is, and what is its first origin?

§. 1. A Republic <note>Original: *Respublica*; in this context, the term refers generally to the State or the Commonwealth rather than a specific form of government.</note> is the supreme authority <term>supreme authority<note>Original: *Imperium*; the power to command and the right to be obeyed within a state.</note></term> over many individuals <note>Original: *corporum multorum*, literally "many bodies."</note> for the purpose of acknowledging the majesty <note>Original: *Majestatem*; the supreme dignity and sovereignty of the governing power.</note> of that same authority, imbued with the same laws for all and for each individual, for the sake of the common good <note>Original: *utilitatis causa*, literally "for the sake of utility."</note>.

§. 2. Indeed, supreme powers and public domains have emerged gradually.

§. 3. The first power indeed flowed from natural law <term>natural law<note>Original: *jus naturæ*; the inherent system of rules and ethics thought to be common to all human beings by nature.</note></term>. It is that which we call the power of parents over their children and grandchildren, and those born from them. This is a republic, as it were, of elder kinsmen; it was the form of authority used at the beginning of the human race, when mortals were long-lived and fruitful.

§. 4. <note>The original text repeats §. 3 in error; this is the fourth section.</note> The force and soul of this power consists in devotion <term>devotion<note>Original: *pietate*; a Latin term encompassing duty, religiosity, and the deep-seated respect owed to parents and ancestors.</note></term>; its practice, however, lies in the governance and preservation of a numerous family.

### CHAPTER III.

->*On the first origin of Magistrates, and on the agreement between Sovereignty and obedience.*<-

§. 1. Therefore, there are two parts to any <term>Republic<note>Original: *Respublica*; used here in the classical sense of a "commonwealth" or any organized state, rather than its modern definition as a non-monarchy.</note></term>: <term>Sovereignty<note>Original: *Imperium*; the supreme power of the state to command and enforce laws.</note></term> and obedience. Consequently, there are two types of persons: those who command and those who are subjects.

§. 2. <term>Magistrates<note>Original: *Magistratus*; officials or rulers who exercise executive or judicial authority.</note></term> are those who, based on considerations of public utility and the requirements of the Laws, exercise sovereignty over those below them.

§. 3. Originally, these leaders were either elected and called to office, or they seized sovereignty over others, even when those people were unwilling and resistant.

§. 4. Election is the process by which, through the consent of all, sovereignty over the rest is granted to one or to several individuals because they are seen as preeminent in the greatness of their virtue and their wisdom in counsel.

§. 5. Seizure <note>Original: *Occupatio*; the act of taking power by force or without formal legal process.</note> here is that process by which one or many, being greater in power than the rest, [seize...] <meta>The text ends mid-word with the catchword "pere," indicating the next page begins with "rapere" (to snatch or seize).</meta>

### Political Institutions, Book I

§. 22. (**V.**) If **Rulers** <note>original: *Imperantes*; those holding the power of command.</note> apply their minds and care most intensely to the public and private hardships of their people, whether by preventing them before they occur, by removing those that have already arisen, or finally, by diminishing them through other forms of prosperity or **public generosity** <note>original: *liberalitate publicâ*; refers to the ruler's use of state resources to alleviate the burdens of the citizenry.</note>.

§. 24. (**VII.**) If they lead everyone by their own example in those matters which are harsh and burdensome, yet necessary, which are commanded of the people.

§. 12. §. 14. §. 15. Nevertheless, one may rightly judge a ruler unworthy of Power, and may withdraw from his domination, if he fails to take the people’s liberty into account while overseeing the public safety.

§. 16. That **expressed** liberty is not found to be uniform or identical among all nations, nor even among those where it has been adopted. Depending on the varying character of nations, some embrace total **servitude** <note>original: *servitutem*; here meaning absolute subjection to a ruler.</note> (if you set aside the "tacit liberty" mentioned before), others embrace total liberty, while others choose a path that is neither total liberty nor total servitude. Thus, in some places, the people have reserved more for themselves or granted more to their **Rulers** <note>original: *Imperantibus*; those holding supreme authority.</note>; in some lands, the authority of Rulers is restrained by few laws—or almost none at all—while in others, it is limited by many laws enacted for the sake of the subjects' liberty.

§. 17. Among those nations that prize the glory of liberty above all others, those laws are generally reduced to three main headings.

§. 18. It is necessary that this public good be of the greatest possible magnitude. For this reason, I believe that **Tacitus** <note>Cornelius Tacitus (c. 56–120 AD), a Roman historian whose works were essential to early modern political theory</note> called everything proceeding from the right of rule a **great example** <note>original: "magnum exemplum"</note> in Book 14 of his *Annals* (14.44.7):

> *“Every great example has something of the unjust in it.”* <note>original: "Habet aliquid ex iniquo omne magnum exemplum"</note>

It is called a **great example** because it is concerned only with matters of the highest importance. It is said to have something **from the unjust** <note>original: "ex iniquo"</note> if it is weighed according to private considerations, but not if it is weighed according to public ones, as has already been stated.

§. 13. **§. 14.** Thus, once the boundaries of one's instructions have been described, the **public official** <term>mandatario publico; an agent or representative entrusted with state business</term> must diligently adhere to them in the conduct of affairs. It is from these instructions alone that a justification of their actions is usually sought, and only through them can a proper account be rendered. However, if a serious matter arises that has not been clearly defined—as happens very frequently—it is wiser and safer to consult the **supreme Magistrate** <note>The highest authority, such as a sovereign or a supreme council</note> (provided the nature of the business allows for such a delay) rather than deciding something based on one’s own authority. Indeed, we find it extremely difficult to justify such independent action when the time comes to give an account to the highest authorities.

**§. 15.** Among these high offices, some are perpetual, meaning there is a continuous need for them within the **Republic** <term>Respublica; the state or public commonwealth</term>, such as the **Consulship** <term>Consulatus; the chief annual magistracy in the Roman system</term>. Others are established only for a time as an urgent necessity demands; once that necessity is removed, they no longer exist. Examples of this include the **Dictatorship** <note>original: "Dictatura"; a Roman office granting temporary absolute power to handle a specific crisis</note> and the **Decemvirate** <term>Decem-viratus; a ten-man commission, most famously the one appointed to codify Roman law</term> among the Romans.

<summary>Boxhorn explains that officials must strictly follow their legal mandates to ensure accountability, advising them to consult higher authorities in uncertain cases. He also distinguishes between permanent government offices and temporary emergency powers like the Roman dictatorship.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Boxhorn's discussion on the classification and management of public offices. While the previous page listed temporary emergency roles, this page addresses the criteria for creating new offices and the debate over whether officials should serve long terms or be frequently replaced based on the nature of their authority.</meta>

### Book I of the Political Institutions

For new **Magistrates** <term>Magistratus; public officials or administrators</term> must be established according to the various opportunities that arise within the **State** <term>Imperio; referring here to the realm or the seat of power</term>.

**§. 16.** As for those offices which are perpetual, there is a question of whether those who hold them should be continued in their roles or replaced. What is most expedient in this matter is debated among the authors of this discipline <note>the study of "Politica" or political science</note>; however, both reason and the actual practice of the **Republic** <term>Respublica; the commonwealth or state</term> leave us in no doubt as to what should be decided.

**§. 17.** Therefore, those **Magistrates** should be continued in office whose roles involve more administrative duty <note>original: "curae"; implying the diligent management of daily affairs</note> than sovereign **Command** <term>Imperii; the supreme power to command or use force</term>. In these positions, it is not beneficial to repeatedly replace those who are knowledgeable and experienced in affairs with those who are ignorant and untried. On the other hand, those who possess greater authority and **Command** should not be continued in office, for they may easily abuse a long tenure to seize control of the **Republic**. Indeed, a time limit must be imposed on those whose power cannot otherwise be limited; nor should anyone be kept in the same **Command** for a long time,

### Political Institutions, Book I

...would be <note>This completes the sentence from the previous page: "it would be of practical use..."</note>, if they are not all relinquished by everyone at the same time. Instead, they should be laid down at different times so that as new successors are substituted in, they may become better acquainted with matters previously conducted and decreed—or those not yet fully completed—by learning from those who were present during those events.

**§. 21.** However, here too one must be cautious that close relatives <note>original: "proximi"; referring here to next-of-kin or those closely related by blood</note> do not immediately succeed those laying down their **honors** <term>honores; public offices or titles of distinction</term>. For the **Magistracy** <term>Magistratus; a public civil office or the person holding it</term> seems to be continued in the same hands if it is transferred immediately to those closest to the predecessor.

**§. 22.** In addition to these points, it would be useful—following the example of the Romans—to have and observe **Annals** <term>Annales; historical records or year-by-year accounts</term> and **Laws** <term>Leges</term> that define the age of those who are to hold **Magistracies**. Through these, it can be arranged that **high offices** <term>dignitates</term> involving more physical labor are granted to young men; in these roles, even if a mistake is made—which is common at that age—the core safety of the **Republic** <term>Reipublicæ; the commonwealth or state</term> is not harmed. Nevertheless, in the highest administration of the **Republic**, young men should not be made equal to their elders or to those whose influence carries more weight.

**§. 23.** Just as we praise, following the example of that same nation <note>referring to the Romans</note>, certain and prescribed **levels of honor** <term>honorum gradus; the 'cursus honorum' or sequential order of public offices</term>. Through these, one may arrive gradually from lesser offices to greater ones, and from lower positions to those nearest to the highest. For only he is ultimately worthy of greater responsibilities who, having been occupied with lesser ones, has already shown himself to be equal to the greater; we prepare ourselves best through the similarity of a smaller task that closely resembles a larger one.

**§. 24.** From these points, as well as from what has already been said, it is sufficiently clear that **Magistracies** <term>Magistratus; public civil offices</term> ought not to be sold for a price or put up for auction. For those who have purchased their roles generally sell their services—and along with them, their integrity <note>original: "fidem"; can also mean trust or loyalty</note>—to those who bought them.

**§. 25.** Furthermore, so that **Magistrates** or those who manage public affairs do not prey upon either public wealth or the resources of private citizens, **salaries** <term>stipendia; regular payments or stipends</term> are owed to them. These must be paid from the **public treasury** <term>ærarium publicum</term> to those who have been appointed to those duties by which the **Republic** <term>Respublica; the state or commonwealth</term> is benefited as a whole.

### Book I of the Political Institutions

However, payments must be made by private individuals to those officials whose daily work the private citizens find it necessary to use; in this way, the **treasury** <term>ærarium; the public funds of the state</term> is relieved of the burden. Marci Zuerii Boxhornii

...which, not without cause, a certain one of the ancients called [the public language of the city].

<margin>§. 2.</margin> Before laws existed, the reason of subjects and the authority of Princes served in place of law. However, Laws were born after reason was forgotten and authority was held in contempt by subjects, and likewise after the abuse of power by **Magistrates** <term>Magistratus; public officials or administrators</term>.

<margin>§. 3.</margin> *Moreover, **Law** <term>Lex; a formal rule or statute</term> is a certain form of reason which—defined either by the authority of the supreme Magistrates or by the common consent of the city—either commands what and how things must be done, or forbids when they should not be done, for the sake of obtaining the common good or avoiding evil. It is indeed constant and without passion, without favor or hatred; as **Tullius** <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, the famous Roman orator and legal philosopher</note> says elsewhere, it is a [mute] Magistrate <note>original: 'Magistratus'; Boxhorn is referencing Cicero’s famous maxim that "the magistrate is a speaking law, and the law a mute magistrate."</note>.*

<margin>§. 4.</margin> Furthermore, laws are of various kinds. For there are those which concern the majesty of the State and of those who Rule, the liberty of the people, the establishment, the order, the power of the Magistrate, and the highest interests of the **Republic** <term>Respublica; the Commonwealth or 'the public thing'</term>; these are generally called **fundamental** [laws].

# Political Institutions Book I. 77

...is, and is commonly called **moral** <term>morale; relating to inherent ethics and character</term> in the schools <note>original: "in scholis"; referring to the academic tradition of Scholasticism prevalent in 17th-century universities</note>, but concerning that which is not always such, but is only estimated as such by the judgment of the laws—which we might correctly call **political**—it is not necessary that they be perpetual. (I.) It is better for a punishment to be defined by the **laws** <term>Leges; written statutes of the state</term> than to be left to the **discretion** <term>Arbitrium; the power of a judge to make decisions based on their own judgment</term> of the **Magistrate** <term>Magistratus; a high-ranking government official</term>; for in this way, it will ensure that they are seen to have carried out the punishment not out of some hatred or private impulse, but according to the prescription of the law.

(II.) Severer punishments should be declared by the laws, to be exacted after an **offense** <term>Peccatum; literally "sin," but in this context a legal transgression</term> has been committed. For the laws will be observed more accurately the greater the terror <note>Boxhorn uses "terror" in the classical political sense: a healthy fear of the law that deters potential criminals from acting.</note> that is instilled by them.

(III.) Circumstances of time, of matters, of rank, of age, and other things of this kind—by which someone might seem worthy of immunity from punishment or to be punished more mildly—should not be inserted into the laws, but should be left to the discretion and judgment of the Magistrate. For in this way, fewer offenses will be committed, and everyone will consider themselves bound to the observation of the law or to the punishment <note>Boxhorn argues that if exceptions are written into the law, people will look for loopholes. If the law remains absolute on paper while the judge handles nuances in person, the law maintains its terrifying authority while the judge maintains his flexibility.</note>.

<meta>This page continues the numbered philosophical maxims regarding the administration of justice. It follows page 82's discussion on the necessity of a Magistrate occasionally using severity to maintain order, now shifting toward the balancing role of clemency and equity.</meta>

-># [The Works] of Marcus Zuerius Boxhorn<-

Indeed, just as it is the nature of **equity** <term>Aequitas; the principle of fairness or justice that supplements or overrides strict statutory law</term> to punish those who have transgressed, so it is also equitable to deviate occasionally from strict equity; and it is no less a law of **prudence** <term>Prudentia; practical wisdom or political foresight</term> that **Magistrates** <term>Magistratus; high-ranking public officials charged with administering the law</term> should be merciful.

( §. 16. ) There are, moreover, two parts to **clemency** <term>Clementia; leniency or mercy shown by a power-holder toward an offender</term>: either to remit both the crime and the punishment equally, or not to remit them, but only to mitigate them.

( §. 17. ) Crime and **punishment** <term>Poena; the legal penalty for an offense</term> can be entirely remitted when the spared defendants are believed to be unlikely to harm the **State** <term>Respublica; the Commonwealth or public body</term> or private individuals, and when their punishment would not serve as a beneficial example to others. Meanwhile, those who are spared can be of service by increasing the reputation of the Magistrate's clemency. Where the situation is such, **mercy** <term>Misericordia; compassion or pity</term> is indeed a sentiment better suited to private individuals than to those who govern affairs. <note>Boxhorn is arguing that for a private citizen, mercy is an emotional virtue, but for a ruler, it must be a calculated political decision based on the common good.</note>

( §. 18. ) However, punishment ought not to be remitted, but only mitigated, when the interest of the State is involved, and when the defendant and the crime are of such a nature that it is expedient for the judge to appear equally severe and merciful.

<summary>This page outlines the political and legal theory of clemency, defining when a Magistrate should fully pardon a crime versus simply reducing the severity of the sentence. Boxhorn emphasizes that mercy in government must always serve the practical interests and reputation of the State.</summary>

# Institutes of Political Science, Book I
## Page 91

...nary. **Ordinary** taxes are those which require a fixed and established payment, proportionate to regular public expenditures. **Extraordinary** taxes are those which do not involve a fixed and annually recurring payment, but are instead provided from time to time because of a sudden and often unexpected necessity; at other times they are not demanded at all—such as the **Indictions** <term>Indictiones; originally a Roman assessment of grain or supplies, later a 15-year cycle used for tax purposes and dating</term> among the Romans.

<margin>§. 15.</margin> Furthermore, taxes are either **definite** or **indefinite**. They are definite when a fixed price is declared for a specific item, under which name the tax is collected, as is the case with most taxes. They are indefinite, however, when they are indeed demanded by public authority, yet in a specific manner without a pre-set price, such as the **Oblations** <term>Oblationes; "voluntary" contributions or gifts presented to the Roman Emperor or the State, which often became expected duties</term> among the Romans.

<margin>§. 16.</margin> Additionally, all taxes are usually either collected by public officials or leased out to private individuals <note>original: *privatis elocari*; this refers to the practice of "tax farming," where private citizens pay the state a lump sum for the right to collect taxes and keep the surplus</note>. Both methods are praiseworthy and useful, depending on the varying nature of those things upon which the taxes are imposed.

He concludes by noting that taxes can be collected either directly by the state or through private tax farmers.</summary>

# CHAPTER XL.

## *On Treaties, and their different types.*

<margin>§. 1.</margin> Thus far, we have dealt with those matters by which the **Republic** <term>Respublica</term> <note>original: *Respublica*; refers to the "public affair" or the State as a political entity.</note> is strengthened at home. ## Political Institutions, Book I

In this way, the weaker state, whose territory the others are all competing to invade, may protect itself from each of them individually. This legal status and treaty is generally called **Neutrality** <term>Neutralitas</term>. It consists of nothing more than enjoying the friendship of all parties while leaving the underlying causes of their conflicts untouched. Meanwhile, if this neutrality cannot be obtained, it is beneficial to join the side of whichever power is greater than the rest, provided our cause is most closely aligned with theirs and they are better positioned to bring us aid against the others.

# Political Institutions Book I. 105

§. 12. If **treaties** <term>foedera</term> <note>original: *foedera*</note> are entered into with neighbors who are equals, it is beneficial for everyone to be bound equally to whatever terms are agreed upon, especially where the cause of each individual is the same. For if they were divided, individuals would be no match for greater powers; as they fight one by one, eventually everyone would be conquered. These treaties are stronger than all others and less dangerous because they are entered into with equals.

§. 13. §. 14. §. 17. Finally, faith must also be kept even if we were compelled to enter into a **treaty** <term>foedus</term> <note>original: *foedus*</note> by fear and necessity. For although under **private civil law** <term>civili jure privato</term> <note>the legal system governing interactions between individual citizens</note> it is permitted to rescind an action or a promise that someone made because of force or fear, this is not permitted in public treaties between nations. For if treaties are necessary (as they are), and if almost no treaties are entered into without some degree of force, fear, or necessity (as is usually the case), it is clear that treaties neither should nor can be rescinded for those reasons or under such a pretext. <note>Boxhorn argues that if "being forced" was a valid excuse to break a peace treaty, no war would ever truly end, as the losing side could always claim they only signed out of fear.</note>

§. 18. For this reason, it is also not expedient for ratified treaties to be immediately broken on account of minor offenses committed by the **State** <term>Republica</term> or by private individuals against the **laws of the treaty** <term>leges foederis</term>. Therefore, under the **law of nations** <term>jus gentium</term> <note>an early legal framework for international relations</note>, a system was devised so that public treaties might remain intact despite private injuries; this is called the **law of reprisals** <term>jus Repressaliarum</term> <note>original: *jus Repressaliarum*; a legal mechanism allowing a state to seize property or citizens of another state to compensate for a wrong done to its own people, acting as a "safety valve" to prevent a full-scale war over minor disputes</note>, as they call it.

§. 19. Furthermore, so that treaties cannot be easily violated through slippery interpretation, their laws ought to be drafted in plain and open words...

# CHAPTER XII.

## *On the law of war, and on the correct and cautious method of conducting wars.*

§. 1. Since there are very many Princes and peoples who prefer to be enemies rather than friends or allies, we must now consider how their attempts against the **State** <term>Respublica</term> are to be halted and crushed; this is achieved primarily through a **just war** <term>justum bellum</term>, a just cause for war, and its proper management <term>administratio bellorum</term>.
