§. 2. And indeed, every branch of law permits war: for by **natural law** <term>jus naturæ</term> <note>The inherent rights believed to be common to all humans by nature, such as self-preservation</note>, those things which are necessary are permitted; by the **law of nations** <term>jus gentium</term> <note>The customary laws and treaties recognized by all civilized states</note>, those things which belong to individuals and to all are protected; and by **civil law** <term>jus civile</term> <note>The specific laws of a particular city or state</note>, it is permitted to reclaim by the force of arms those things which have been snatched away from or denied to anyone.

§. 3. Yet it is not enough that all wars be considered just for those reasons, *unless they are also necessary. Therefore, that war is not just which has only a just cause, but that which is equally just and necessary. It is,* moreover, necessary and just when we are unable to claim our **right** <term>jus</term> by any other means.

§. 4. Therefore, the ***justice of wars*** <term>justitia bellorum</term> is reduced to roughly three supreme categories. (I.) *For the defense of oneself and others*, to whom that defense is owed by treaty or by the law of nature or nations. (II.) *For the extraction or reclamation of that which is ours or of our* right. (III.) Finally, *for punishment* <term>pœna</term>, by which, on account of an injury to the Majesty of our Empire, or on account of injuries to our subjects— <meta>catchword: stro- (completing the word "nostrorum," meaning "of our")</meta>

<summary>Boxhorn defines the legal foundations of a 'just war,' arguing that conflict must be both legally grounded and a matter of absolute necessity when no other recourse exists. ...[private] defense is only then just if another’s aggression has preceded it and has actually occurred. **Public defense**, however, is also just before another’s aggression, and regarding what is to come, so to speak. From this it is gathered that a just declaration of war is considered valid not only against those currently invading, but also against those about to invade. Indeed, the threats of war and military preparations by others make a war just for those who—out of fear arising from those threats and preparations—could not remain secure without resorting to war.

§. 7. No less just is a war that arises from the title of **recovery** <term>exactio</term> <note>Also known as "reclamation"; the act of demanding or taking back what is legally owed</note>. This occurs when we use war to reclaim those things which belong only to us, or which belong to us and all people equally. It also applies to those things which, although they may belong to others, nevertheless concern us through the law of a treaty <term>foedus</term> or the bonds of human society <term>humana societas</term>.

§. 8. Therefore, war ought not to be waged solely for the sake of invading or acquiring another’s Empire, or for the purpose of increasing our own power.

§. 9. Furthermore, a war born from those most just causes ought to be considered most just for as long as it is waged—even if those things which were taken away or denied (and for whose sake the war was declared) have already been brought back into our hands or under our power by the force of arms. This is held to be true for the most serious reasons:

(I.) Because in a transgression <term>delictum</term> <note>A legal wrong or offense against the law</note> where an injury has been inflicted, even if that injury is removed through the courage and good fortune of those who declared the war, it is not believed that the **punishment** <term>poena</term> of those who committed the injury before the war has yet been satisfied.

(II.) Because one who has once harmed our **State** <term>Respublica</term> is wisely believed to be a future threat. On account of the injury first inflicted, it is lawful by the **law of war** <term>ius belli</term> to persist in the conflict until the enemy's forces are so worn down and subdued that, even if they wished to do so, they would be unable to harm us in the future. For these same reasons, such wars are also legally extended even to their descendants <note>original: "in posteros"; this reflects the early modern view that the obligations and liabilities of a sovereign state could pass to subsequent generations</note>.

### Marcus Zuerius Boxhorn

it is also beneficial for the **Republic** <term>respublica</term> <note>The state or commonwealth.</note> not to pursue its rights through war immediately, but to wait for favorable opportunities for pursuit. Such wars are no less just in their cause, even if a span of time has passed between the original cause and the actual execution of the war. For the Republic is believed to always keep its rights intact. Therefore, while it is a matter of **Law** <term>jus</term> to be rightfully able to wage war, it is a matter of **Prudence** <term>prudentia</term> <note>Practical wisdom and foresight in governance.</note> to manage that war at the proper time, in the proper place, and according to the needs of the Republic.

->§. 17.<-

One must truly abstain altogether from those wars which—no matter how successfully they are carried out—bring only "modest praise and a modest price of victory," <note>original: "laudem modicam, modicum victoriæ... pretium"</note> as **Tacitus** <note>Cornelius Tacitus (c. 56–120 AD), a Roman historian whose works were essential reading for 17th-century political theorists studying the "reason of state."</note> puts it; yet if they turn out poorly, they bring great mockery and no less damage. For as the same Tacitus says in the second book of his *Histories*: "All those who take up plans for great matters ought to weigh whether the undertaking is useful to the Republic, glorious for themselves, easy to achieve, or at least not too difficult," <note>original: "Omnes, qui magnarum rerum consilia suscipiunt, æstimare debent, an, quod inchoatur, Reipublicæ utile, ipsis gloriosum, aut promptum effectu, aut certè non arduum sit"</note>

§. 12. ### CHAPTER XIV.

### *On the transformations and overthrows of Republics, and their primary causes.*

§. 1. Even when Republics have been established in this manner and strengthened both at home and abroad, it is not possible to promise them any kind of eternity. It remains, therefore, for this first book to be brought to a close by the "end and the exit" <note>original: "finis & exitus"</note> which is the customary fate of almost all empires. Indeed, by a certain eternal law governing all human affairs, whatever things—no matter how excellently they may be established and fortified by reason—are eventually either transformed or overthrown. This holds true for Republics as well, which experience either gradual changes or total collapses.

# Political Institutions, Book II. 141

§. 2. Furthermore, the power or nature of every *Monarchical Government* <note>original: "Monarchici Imperii."</note> is not the same, for it is either a *Principality* <note>original: "Principatus." In early modern political theory, this refers to a monarchy where the ruler acts as a first citizen and respects the law.</note> or a *Dominion* <note>original: "Dominatus." This refers to a more absolute or despotic rule where the monarch rules like a master over a household.</note>. We call it a *Principality* when the *Supreme Power* <note>original: "Imperium."</note> is granted to one person in such a way that it is bound by various institutions and laws devised for the sake of liberty; so much so that *Principality and liberty*—which are usually incompatible under bad *Princes*—are here most excellently joined together. We call it a *Dominion* when the *method of ruling* is either granted to one or seized by one in such a way that he may manage all things according to his own whim; so much so that the *liberty* of the subjects is thus constrained by the judgment of a single man.

§. 3. The form of a *Principality* is generally that where *Princes* have been called to the head of affairs by the consent and election of the people. *Dominion* is generally found where *Sovereignties* <note>original: "Imperia."</note> have become the property of those who seize them, and among those nations who have been driven to obedience by force and terror; which [dominion], nevertheless, when it diverts into the most atrocious *tyranny* <note>original: "tyrannidem."</note>...

§. 5. As to which is greater and more praiseworthy—**Succession** or **Election**—the matter is debated by many with conflicting arguments, and there are indeed very weighty points to be made for both sides. For in **Election**, there is more discord, but also more liberty. In **Succession**, however, there is certainly no discord, but there is also no liberty. 

Furthermore, the judgments of nature—if I may call them that—though sometimes correct, are just as often blind; thus, the worst children are sometimes born to the best **Princes**. The judgments of men <note>original: "Judicia hominum." Referring to the choice made by voters or electors.</note> are more certain, yet even these often deceive and are deceived; for it is not uncommon for those to be elected who, once placed in **Sovereign Command** <note>original: "Imperio." Therefore, to speak briefly, reason fights both for and against each method, and the established custom <note>original: "institutum." The traditional laws or constitution of a specific country.</note> of a nation must be maintained in choosing one or the other.

# Political Institutions, Book II. 151 <note>This work by Marcus Zuerius Boxhorn (1612–1653) is a manual on statecraft, reflecting the 17th-century focus on stability and the "reason of state."</note>

4. Once placed at the summit of power, and secured against rivals—especially those of his own blood—the Prince should strictly and sacredly uphold the acts, commands, and decrees of previous Princes as much as possible, and not easily dismantle them. For a Prince is held in only as much esteem as he himself grants to those whom he succeeds. <note>Boxhorn suggests that by dishonoring a predecessor’s laws, a ruler teaches his subjects to eventually dishonor his own.</note>

5. *If he faithfully observes the laws by which he has bound himself, he will most effectively strengthen both himself and the **Sovereignty** <term>Principatus: The office or position of the supreme ruler</term>; for otherwise, for every bit he takes away from the laws he swore to uphold, his subjects will add a corresponding amount of hatred—to be unleashed whenever the opportunity arises—in place of their obedience.*

6. In short, wherever it is justly permitted, he should pursue with the highest severity of punishment all those found to have violated the **Majesty** <term>Majestas: the dignity, sovereignty, and person of the ruler</term> of the preceding Prince, whose place he now fills. For whatever such offense he fails to punish, he effectively permits others to commit against himself, as if it were lawful.

7. No example of punishment or contempt or undervalued Majesty <note>original: *minus æstimatæ Majestatis*</note> [should be overlooked...]

[...should] *he himself establish against one who bears the same role* <note>original: *personam*—referring to the legal and symbolic "persona" of a sovereign</note> *and has elsewhere received equal authority over his own people. 8. *He should not easily enter into a **treaty** <term>Foedus: a formal alliance or compact between states</term>, or provide aid to those peoples who have stripped their own Princes of their **Sovereign Power** <term>Imperium: the supreme right to command</term>. For just as Princes are often hated by their subjects, those subjects will just as easily follow the example of a **rebellion** <term>Defectio: a revolt or the withdrawal of allegiance</term> that has been approved and promoted by their own Princes against others.* <note>Boxhorn argues that if a King helps foreign rebels, he effectively tells his own subjects that rebelling against a King is a legitimate act.</note>

9. *It should be a fixed and unmovable rule for them not to easily leave the **seat of empire** <term>Sedes imperii: the capital city or administrative heart of the state</term>, or the "head of affairs"—that is, that city or territory from which the **government** <term>Regimen: the system of rule or direction</term> over all things originates. For in the absence of the Prince, and while the seat of Empire is vacant, conspirators almost always take advantage of the opportunity to seize power.*

### 15.
He should place his **children and those closest to him by blood**—those most likely to be faithful—into the nearest, that is, the highest **offices** <term>Dignitates: positions of high rank or honor</term>. For in this way, he will be safer through the loyalty and status of his own kin; by granting the primary power over affairs to his own bloodline, his rule will rest upon many fortifications.

### 16.
If the Prince fears someone because of their excessively eminent qualities—virtues that promise more than is fitting for a private citizen <note>original: *plus quàm civilia*, suggesting someone acting with the grandiosity of a king rather than a mere subject</note>—or because of their fame and favor among the soldiers or the citizens at home, he should exchange their military offices for **civilian ones** <note>original: *togatis*, referring to the toga, the garment of peace and law</note>, and their civilian offices for military ones. By this method, any excessive enthusiasm the people or the soldiers hold for such men will not easily be used against the Prince.

### §. 17.
*No one besides the Prince should claim the glory for a deed brilliantly performed. He must take care, above all, that no one is celebrated in private or public praises above the Prince, however much that person may have deserved it.*

...a Prince ought to be greater than all his subjects, yet he cannot be greater unless he enjoys the love of all or most of them. 27. Nor should he ever oppose the desires of his subjects with such stubbornness that they feel compelled to take up arms, and he is finally forced to negotiate with an armed populace. He who negotiates with those under arms does not so much command as he obeys and is forced; by this one thing, the power of **Majesty** <term>Majestas: the supreme dignity and absolute authority of the state</term> is most greatly dishonored. <note>original: *prostituitur*. 28. He should never delay in executing those things which pertain to his rights, or which the subjects judge should not be postponed. For when such matters are deferred, they are seized by the **Nobles** <term>Proceribus: the high-ranking aristocracy or leading men of the state</term> or by the people, as if they were vacant property; and once they have been seized, they will not easily return to the Prince’s authority.

# CHAPTER IV.

## Concerning the corruption of the **Monarchical state**, that is, **Tyranny**, and the tactics by which Princes cunningly advance toward tyranny and eventually exercise it with cruelty.

<margin>§. 1.</margin> Since a Prince rarely applies his mind to the **rule of one** <note>original: *Imperium unius*. This refers to a system where power is concentrated in a single individual.</note> in a way that restrains his own infinite power, or observes those laws established for the sake of **liberty** upon which he has sworn an oath, the Monarchical state easily falls into a vice that we call **Tyranny**.

§. 2. **Tyranny**, moreover, is such a rule of one person in which—liberty being crushed and the authority of the laws and all other **Magistrates** <term>Magistratuum: public officials or high-ranking ministers who administer the law</term> being violated—everything is directed toward the absolute power of the single ruler, resulting in the ruin of the subjects.

<meta>catchword: §. 3. So much so [Adeò]</meta>

<summary>This page introduces the concept of tyranny as the natural corruption of monarchy, occurring when a ruler ignores legal restraints and his own oaths to prioritize absolute personal power over the welfare of his subjects.</summary>

<keywords>tyranny, monarchy, absolute power, corruption of state, rule of law, liberty, political theory, Marcus Zuerius Boxhorn</keywords>

--- Page 503 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion on the transition from a legitimate monarchy to tyranny. On the previous page, Boxhorn defined tyranny as a system where the ruler violates the law and the rights of magistrates to secure absolute power. Here, he begins to outline the specific methods (thirteen in total) used to achieve this shift.</meta>

<page-num>164</page-num>
<header>*Of Marcus Zuerius Boxhorn*</header>

§. 3. So much so that they are Tyrants who stand out by power usurped from all sides, rather than what is seen as necessary for the state.

§. 4. There are, in fact, certain tactics by which they invade liberty secretly and shrewdly, and others by which Tyrants act openly and cruelly.

§. 5. These tactics can be grouped into approximately thirteen following categories.

§. 6. (I.) They gradually usurp the **duties of the Magistrates and the laws**, as Tacitus <note>Cornelius Tacitus (c. 56–120 AD), a Roman historian known for his analysis of the transition from the Roman Republic to the Empire.</note> puts it. **The duties of the Magistrates**: while they claim for themselves the most important matters and the real power over affairs, they leave the **Magistrates** <term>Magistratibus: high-ranking public officials or ministers</term> with only empty titles or tasks that bring them public hatred. Above all, they strip them of their freedom to vote, and in the place of those who have left office, they install men inclined toward increasing the Prince's dominance. **The duties of the laws**: while they maintain the laws in name only, they meanwhile undermine their true force by interpreting them in their own favor. This is done gradually, because there is a need for intervals and "breathing spaces" of time <note>original: *spiramentis temporum*. This suggests a tactical pause to let the public grow accustomed to each small erosion of liberty before the next one begins.</note>

<meta>catchword: judi- (likely "judiciis" or "judicibus," referring to judicial judgments or judges)</meta>

<summary>Boxhorn identifies the first tactic of a rising tyrant: the gradual erosion of the independence of public officials and the law, replacing meaningful governance with figureheads loyal to the ruler.</summary>

<keywords>tyranny, Tacitus, political tactics, magistrates, rule of law, usurpation of power, political science, Marcus Zuerius Boxhorn</keywords>

# Political Institutions Book II. 165

...they judge [these intervals necessary] to thoroughly carry out those things which might be opposed to the most unjust domination they put forward. If they attempted to pursue these goals with a single blow, they would be overwhelmed at the very beginning by citizens who are still flourishing and breathing the spirit of complete liberty.

### §. 7. (II.)
Even when, at the start, they have perhaps dared some open act against the **laws** and the **higher Magistrates**, they occasionally introduce something pleasing on the other side. Through this, the authority <note>original: *jus*</note> of those same laws and Magistrates seems to be restored more than it actually is. In this way, the hatred incurred by their previous bold actions is cast off and diminished. <note>This describes a "one step back, two steps forward" strategy where a ruler makes a minor concession to pacify the public after a major power grab.</note>

### §. 8. (III.)
By every possible craft, they drive the **higher Magistrates** <term>Magistratus: high-ranking public officials or ministers</term>—to whom the cause of liberty has been specifically entrusted—into dissensions and rivalries among themselves. This is done so that no strong measure can be enacted by unanimous votes <note>original: *suffragiis*</note> against a **Prince** <term>Princeps: the sovereign ruler</term> who is striving for excessive power.

### §. 9. (IV.)
They often think it better to obtain those things that are opposed to **liberty** <term>libertas: political freedom and the rule of law</term> through flatteries, pleas, persuasion, and finally under the pretext of **public utility** <term>publica utilitas: the common good or the "necessity of the state"</term>, rather than seizing them by force. For in this way, while pursuing their most unjust objectives, they are most effectively advanced and strengthened by the very authority of those who ought to be the guardians of liberty. <note>Boxhorn argues that tyrants prefer to use "soft power" and the language of the common good to trick legitimate officials into surrendering their own rights.</note>

### §. 10. (V.)
Having been gradually empowered and thus made bolder, they remove from the scene men of outstanding, great, and upright spirit, or at least cast them down from the height of their status and honors. For they dread the great-heartedness <note>original: *magnanimitatem*</note> of such men, fearing that it might spark a movement to overthrow **tyranny** <term>tyrannis: arbitrary or oppressive rule</term> and that others might be ignited and driven to do the same.

### §. 11. (VI.)
They do not easily tolerate assemblies of **nobles** <term>proceres: the leading men or aristocracy</term> or **citizens** <term>cives: the members of the political community</term>, and they desire above all else that **liberal studies** <term>liberalia studia: the education of a free person, including philosophy, history, and rhetoric</term> and the fine arts be driven into exile. For if the citizens or nobles were called together into one place, it might happen that by the judgment and will <note>original: *votis*</note> of all...

# Political Institutions Book II.

...are decreed against **tyranny** <term>tyrannis: arbitrary or oppressive rule</term>; and through **liberal studies** <term>liberalia studia: the education of a free person, including philosophy, history, and rhetoric</term>, people are most easily filled with the thought of **liberty** <term>libertas: political freedom and the rule of law</term> and a high estimation of the human spirit.

### §. 12. (VII.)
They also take primary care that citizens do not become well-known, intimate, or mutually trusting of one another, as far as can be managed. They ensure that citizens do not form great friendships or kinship ties through **marriage** <term>matrimonia: legal unions often used to create political alliances</term> or other similar means; for tyrants fear **conspiracies** <term>conspirationes: secret plots or agreements to act together</term> arising from what is essentially a "wall" built of many families and mutual affection. <note>Boxhorn suggests that social cohesion and family networks are the greatest threats to a dictator, as they provide a private space for trust to grow.</note>

### §. 13. (VIII.)
No less do they strive to ensure that cities are everywhere beset and made "sticky" <note>original: *viscosæ*; likely a metaphor for a web or trap where every movement is caught</note> by **spies** <term>exploratores: secret agents who observe and report</term> and **informants** <term>delatores: those who denounce others to the authorities for reward or favor</term>. For subjects, constrained by the fear of such people, hardly dare to complain to one another about the tactics of tyrants. Consequently, there is less of a stirring of spirits against the tyrant; furthermore, by this method, the very first and slightest beginnings of **plots** <term>conjurationes: sworn alliances for a political uprising</term> can immediately be made known to the tyrants.

### §. 14. (IX.)
They strive as much as possible to ensure that their subjects distrust one another; for if they are set against each other, they will not easily join together against **tyrants** <term>tyrannis: a ruler who governs without legal restraint</term> to reclaim their **liberty** <term>libertas: political freedom and the rule of law</term>. <note>Boxhorn explains the classic "divide and conquer" strategy: by fostering internal conflict among the people, the ruler ensures they are too busy fighting each other to unite against him.</note>

### §. 15. (X.)
They also strive by every possible means to reduce their people to a state of desperation and extreme **poverty** <term>paupertas: a lack of means that prevents political action</term>. They achieve this through **taxes** <term>vectigalia: state revenues, often gathered through aggressive taxation</term>, through misfortunes deliberately inflicted, through the removal or disruption of **commerce** <term>commercia: trade and economic exchange</term>, and through unnecessary or rashly provoked **wars** <term>bella: armed conflicts</term>. For subjects who are not equipped with wealth do not easily attack tyrants; because they cannot support themselves, they are forced to endure whatever is imposed upon them. <note>The author argues that economic hardship is a deliberate political tool used to keep the populace focused on survival rather than resistance.</note>

### §. 16. (XI.)
They also make use of **freedmen** <term>liberti: traditionally, former slaves, but here referring to anyone of low social standing</term>—or to speak more generally and according to the practice of every **Republic** <term>Respublica: the state or political community</term>, those of lower status and men whose fortunes are depressed below the power of others. To these, they grant the greatest license and often offer the highest dignity. In this way, the tyrants can make use of their most ready and willing service for their own ends. <note>By elevating people who have no social standing or independent power, the tyrant creates a class of officials who owe their entire status to him and are therefore his most loyal enforcers.</note>

### §. 17. (XII.)
They take more pleasure in **foreigners** <term>peregrini: those from outside the state</term> and outsiders than in **citizens** <term>cives: legal members of the political community</term> and locals. Indeed, they believe citizens to be enemies, specifically those they have harmed; for everyone fears the one they have injured. Foreigners, however, having not been harmed, are rendered indebted to the tyrants on account of the benefits they have received. <note>This highlights a psychological reality of power: a tyrant is always looking over his shoulder at those he has oppressed, preferring to trust "outsiders" who have no local grievances.</note>

2. To render them powerless and weak, so that they are unable to rise up.

### §. 19.

### Political Institutions, Book II.

#### §. 28.

#### §. 29.

#### §. 30.
Meanwhile, that evaluation of "highest injustice" must not be based on a subjective opinion that treats empty and trivial evils as if they were most serious; rather, it must be founded upon matters of the greatest weight and the consequences of the most grave affairs.

#### §. 31.
For since it is the greatest of all things to acknowledge a **Prince** as given and established by divine providence, to whom I am most holily bound by the religious obligation of an **oath** <term>jurisjurandum: a sworn oath of allegiance, often seen as a sacred contract before God</term>, there should be no doubt that only the "greatest" of reasons have any place here.

### §. 32.
Therefore, to state it briefly: one must move to cast off the rule of a **Tyrant** <term>Tyrannus: a ruler who governs without regard for law or the well-being of the people</term> when, under his power, the final boundaries of **liberty** have been reached. It is not wise to continue practicing patience until one has reached the absolute depths of **servitude** <term>servitus: a state of political or physical slavery where all rights are lost</term>.

### §. 33.
Indeed, when **liberty** stands at its ultimate crisis—having already been broken and diminished in many ways—a sufficiently just and serious cause for casting out a **Prince** is presented to the subjects. This is because the logic for defending one's life is the same as the logic for defending one's liberty; moreover, the protection of life is a right granted by the laws of **nature** and of all **nations** <term>jus gentium: "law of nations," a set of legal principles considered common to all civilized people</term>.

### §. 34.
But truly, once the extremes of **servitude** have been reached, even though the fear of the **Prince** may be even heavier and the cause of the subjects even more justified, the strength through which the subjects might reclaim their liberty is nonetheless lacking and exhausted.
<note>Boxhorn is making a pragmatic argument here: if you wait too long to rebel against a tyrant, you will be too weak and impoverished to succeed.</note>

### §. 40.

For not only must evils be cut away, but also the fear of those evils; and fear cannot be absent as long as the same opportunities for those evils persist.

### §. 45. 
Therefore, along with a most wicked **Prince** <term>Princeps: a general term for a sovereign ruler</term>, if it can be done, the **Principate** <term>Principatus: the office or form of rule by a single person</term> itself should also be removed. <note>Boxhorn is suggesting that to truly fix a state, one must sometimes move from a monarchy to a republic to ensure the "opportunity" for tyranny is gone.</note>

### §. 46. 
But if, on the other hand, it is not expedient to change the form of the **State** <term>Imperium: supreme power or the system of government</term> because of the specific customs and circumstances of various nations, at least the family should be changed from which the **Princes** have thus far been born and elected.

### §. 47. 
If, however, public peace and security would not permit even that, the **Principate** should be transferred to another member of the same family, with the precaution that the **Prince** is left with the least possible authority in the future, while the subjects are left with more than the usual amount of **liberty**. <note>This describes a "limited monarchy" or constitutional arrangement where the ruler's power is legally restricted following a period of tyranny.</note>

### §. 48.

## CHAPTER VIII.
### *On Democracy, or the Sovereignty of the People, and its genuine constitution.*

§. 1. It follows now that we should examine the final type of **Sovereignty** <term>Imperiorum: forms of supreme power or government</term>, namely **Democracy**, which is to say, the popular state.

§. 2. **Democracy** is that form of **Republic** <term>Reipublicæ: the "public thing" or the State</term> in which all people, however many they may be and of whatever social condition, are participants in the highest honors with equal standing, as well as in the government of the State. In this system, while the power of **Sovereignty** <term>Imperii: supreme administrative power</term> and majesty remain meanwhile in the hands of the people, the government is exercised by a few of a suitable number, who are elected by the people from among the people, and at the will of the people. These people are consulted through summoned assemblies, colleges, classes, **centuries** <term>centurias: a Roman division of citizens, originally based on military or wealth groupings</term>, or **tribes** <term>tribus: administrative divisions of the Roman people</term>, either equally regarding the creation of **Magistrates** and public councils, or only regarding the selection of Magistrates who will manage the State for a limited time. Indeed, **Aristotle** most correctly called this "Arithmetical equality" <note>original: "æqualitatem Arithmeticam"</note>, since in this form, account is taken not of noble birth or other such things by which citizens are distinguished from one another, but of individuals man by man. This does not mean that all individuals command equally in a **Democracy**, however many they are from the peo- <note>The text cuts off here as it reaches the end of the page; the catchword "pulo" indicates the next word is "populo" (people).</note>

<summary>Boxhorn defines Democracy as a state where all citizens share equal access to high office and sovereignty rests with the people, who delegate power to elected magistrates. §. 5. From this, it is abundantly clear what a massive difference there is between ***Democracy*** and ***Ochlocracy*** <term>Ochlocratia: from the Greek for "mob rule," describing a state where the uneducated or lawless populace holds power</term>. For in a ***Democracy***, the care of the ***State*** <term>Imperium: supreme administrative power or authority</term> is in the hands of those chosen from the people who are the most observant of integrity and equality, and who are wise of heart. In an ***Ochlocracy***, however, power is in the hands of those from the lowest level of the people, who lack the virtues <term>Virtus: moral excellence and the qualities of a good citizen</term> worthy of ***State authority***. In the former, the effort is made to work equally for the benefit of all; in the latter, the goal is only to increase the fortunes of these individuals [the mob] while the wealthy are oppressed. In the former, that is believed to be "true equality" in which the equal fortunes of the citizens are protected with equal care. In the latter, the essence of equality is believed to consist of this: that those who are unequal in fortune are made equal through wickedness and the injuries inflicted upon the wealthier. <header># **Political Institutions, Book II.**</header>

Just as **Democracy** is corrupted into **Mob Rule** <term>Ochlocratia: from the Greek for "rule of the crowd," where the legal order of a democracy is replaced by the whims of the populace</term>, so too is **Mob Rule** eventually and entirely overthrown by **Anarchy**.

§. 8. Now, **Anarchy** <term>Anarchia: literally "without a leader," a state of total lawlessness</term> is, as you might say, the absence of any **Government** <note>original: "nullum Imperium"</note>. It is the very funeral of the State—if I may put it that way—and a corpse in which the worst men (who are almost always the most numerous everywhere) no longer follow the commands of **Magistrates** <note>original: "Magistratuum"</note> who are like themselves, but instead follow the impulse of their own insane lusts.

§. 9. This is a greater evil than any **Tyranny** or corrupted **Government**, since it is in the interest even of all good men that bad rulers, rather than none at all, should administer the ***Commonwealth*** <term>Respublica: the public affair or the State</term>. <note>Boxhorn argues here that even a cruel government is preferable to the total chaos of anarchy, as some form of order allows for basic survival, whereas anarchy leads to total destruction.</note>

8. And truly, his opinion shall be accurately stated: no **power** <note>original: "imperium"</note> is secure unless it is fortified by **goodwill** <note>original: "benevolentia"</note>. For this reason, in whatever place a person lives in constant fear and danger, they are no longer in the state of a free city, but must necessarily be overwhelmed by the darkness of the most miserable and foul **servitude** <note>original: "servitutis"</note>.

9. Since the end of every **Tyranny** is most wretched; for in human affairs, nothing ruled by force has a long duration. No violent **Commonwealth** <term>Respublica: the 'public thing' or the state</term> is long-lived.
-> <unclear>Aristotle.</unclear> <-

# T H E  E N D

<note>Vocabulary: Tyranny, power, goodwill, Commonwealth, Aristotle, The End</note>

<summary>This concluding page argues that a government's security relies entirely on the goodwill of its citizens, asserting that any state ruled by fear and violence is a form of slavery destined for a swift and miserable end.</summary>
<keywords>Tyranny, political stability, Aristotle, goodwill, servitude, Commonwealth, Marcus Zuerius Boxhorn, political philosophy</keywords>
